A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an effective neural network architecture that processes graph data, extensively applied across multiple domains. Unlike traditional neural network models, GNN can operate in a decentralized manner, facilitating communication among neighboring nodes and potentially leading to more efficient control mechanisms in wireless communication systems. However, wireless channel disruptions significantly reduce the GNN's prediction accuracy, prompting the need for reliable prediction in such dynamic settings. In this study, we explore various wireless channel effects on GNN performance and propose a novel method called decentralized GNN inference to address this challenge. The proposed approach leverages wireless communication links to establish multiple data paths among GNN nodes, substantially enhancing the network's spectral efficiency and robustness to interference. We demonstrate that this technique can be applied to a wide range of control and communication issues in wireless communication systems, including resource allocation, data transmission, and network planning. Furthermore, we also investigate its potential in a wireless communication system with edge learning capabilities. Test results based on synthetic data indicate that the proposed approach significantly improves the GNN's prediction accuracy in real-world wireless communication systems affected by diverse channel effects. The proposed technique is versatile and can be widely adopted across various wireless applications, including control and communication issues. The analysis and findings in this study provide valuable insights for designers and engineers to create reliable GNN-based predictive models in real-world wireless communication systems. The proposed code is also available on GitHub to facilitate reproducibility. The research, findings, and insights in this study can contribute to various wireless communication systems and reliable GNN deployments. The existing literature lacks comprehensive analysis of GNN performance in real-world wireless communication systems, and our research contributes to address this gap. The proposed approach has been extensively tested using various channel effects, indicating its strong generalizability to multiple control and communication issues. The study also expands existing research boundaries by investigating GNN performance across multiple wireless communication systems and reliable GNN deployments. The proposed technique is applicable to multiple wireless applications, including resource allocation, data transmission, and network planning. The results of this study provide valuable design guidelines and engineering practices to create distributed predictive models in real-world wireless communication systems. Variants of axions known as axion-like particles continue to be relevant in fundamental physics, so a sensitive instrument is needed to distinguish between these ALPs and the hypothesized standard axion.  The BetaIXO concept, a refinement of the LUX-Zeplin experiment optimized to analyze X-ray-like axion responses, may have the sensitivity to detect primordial axions or ALPs with frequencies up to 1 MeV.  Developing an experiment within BetaIXO can potentially yield data to distinguish between the two, or determine the standard axion mass for the first time.  A smaller prototype of this experiment, BabyIAXO, is being designed with dual goals of developing technology for the next-generation IAXO experiment and conducting scientific research itself.  On the scientific side, BabyIAXO aims to reach a sensitivity equivalent to a 1 billion target axion absorption rate over a 1% area, and achieve this rate of 1 billion with half of that area for ALP mode, assuming both are optimized to their full potential.  With this in mind, BabyIAXO will test the presence of dark matter, explore neutrinoless double beta decay signs, and determine the value of the reactor antineutrino mixing parameter $|V_{13}|^2$.  Furthermore, BabyIAXO will be capable of observing sunspot-related changes in multiple ways and determining the axion mass based on their frequency and intensity.  Finally, and most importantly, with its various scientific goals, BabyIAXO will be able to confirm whether the detected signal originates from dark matter, an antineutrino, an axion, or an ALP particle. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion compensation method in four-dimensional (4D) T2-weighted MRI data collected through turbo spin echo imaging. The technique acquires data on a single breath or less, then uses parallel imaging to account for spatial motion in three-dimensional (3D) images, followed by refinement of temporal information via a robust, optimized model tracking respiration. This model, specifically designed for turbo spin echo sequences, identifies the ideal k-space sampling for each breath and is based on a three-parameter model that includes a linear regression component. To compensate for motion, the technique applies a radial backward projection that utilizes data from previous breaths. This method is independent of sequence design and can be used with or without parallel imaging, making it adaptable to a range of sequences. It is tested on 20 subjects with ten different 4D datasets, comparing image quality in motion-affected regions, specifically the liver, to that of conventional four-dimensional MRI data collected through gadoxete disodium-enhanced imaging. It was found that the quality of the proposed method was superior to that of conventional imaging in the liver, with less than 4% lower contrast-to-noise ratio and less than 4% higher compression artifacts. Additionally, the technique requires significant improvements to produce images of similar quality in the upper abdomen. It is found, however, that for sequences with long echo times (greater than 7 milliseconds), applying rectification to the optimized model's predictions helps to produce better images, particularly in the upper abdomen by reducing data incompleteness and off-resolution effects. Images produced by the technique are shown to be comparable to those of conventional four-dimensional MRI data in the upper abdomen, with improved homogeneity and reduced artifacts. It is found, however, that the technique's performance in the upper abdomen is limited by its dependence on parallel imaging, which introduces ghosting effects, with less than 10% higher contrast-to-noise ratio in the upper abdomen compared to conventional four-dimensional MRI data collected through gadoxete disodium-enhanced imaging. Overall, the technique's ability to produce high-quality images on a single breath or less makes it suitable for studies involving respiratory motion in the lower body. To produce comparable results in the upper abdomen would require further methodological improvements, such as employing more advanced parallel-imaging techniques. We propose InDistill, a novel model compression approach, combining the principles of knowledge distillation and channel pruning to effectively transfer critical information flow from a powerful teacher model to a more efficient student model. Unlike previous techniques that collapse this information, InDistill leverages layer-wise pruning of the teacher's intermediate stages, aligning their widths with those of the student, thereby enabling direct information distillation without an intermediate encoding step. To facilitate knowledge transfer, we employ a curriculum learning strategy that prioritizes layer-wise difficulty and critical learning periods. Through these advancements, InDistill significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving enhanced results on a range of benchmarks, including ImageNet and CIFAR-100. The implementation of InDistill is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zwengqianph/I-distill. Experimental results indicate that InDistill's model compression rivals, if not surpasses, contemporary teacher-student compression methods in terms of performance, resources, and training expenses. Notably, InDistill's efficiency stems from its ability to achieve comparable results with the teacher model using minimal student model parameters, roughly 1%, and still outperforms other model compression techniques. The model's performance on ImageNet is remarkable, with mAP scores exceeding 80% in most cases. To further validate InDistill's effectiveness, we conducted an additional experiment where the teacher model's layers were progressively frozen as the training process continues, starting from later layers. Despite this modification, the teacher model's frozen layers were able to contribute valuable knowledge to the student model through InDistill, leading to improved performance. Ultimately, the effectiveness of InDistill stems from its ability to leverage intermediate features to aid knowledge distillation, thus outperform other model compression techniques. That is, when incorporating intermediate features, models with these incorporated features generally achieve higher accuracy, giving rise to the observation that incorporating these features aids model compression. The underlying reasoning is that these features contain vital information, leading to the improved model performance observed. The full details of InDistill's methodology can be found in the research paper submitted to NeurIPS-2021. The source code for InDistill has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/zwengqianph/I-distill. A python-based program, ipie, has been developed for auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations, along with its implementation on central and graphical processing units and NVIDIA GPUs. This program provides flexible electronic structure calculations with the ability to account for various approximations and extensions to the underlying Hirsch-Fye impurity model. The implementation of its algorithms and the conversion process of input/output files have been explained in a unified and platform-independent manner. Furthermore, a comparative analysis of its performance across CPU, GPU, and current combined architectures has been carried out, showing scaleability, platform-independent results, and significant acceleration on modern systems. The program, along with its source code and computational scripts, can be accessed through the website at http://wiki.tcd.ie/quantum-computing/ipie-a-python-based-program-for auxiliary-field-qmc. This program has been successfully utilized in a variety of studies such as reporting magnetic ordering in nonlocal spin-orbital-dependent mean-field theories, studying magnetic ordering, and correlated systems, and predicting magnetic ordering, ferromagnetic fluctuations, and d-wave superconductivity in these systems. Examples of its application have also been discussed. The program, along with its local response function method extensions and computational programs, can be accessed through the website at http://wiki.tcd.ie/quantum-computing/local-response-function-method-for auxiliary-field-qmc. This program has been written in a data-parallelized, but not optimised, python code using the MPI library for distributed parallel processing and can be compiled with either CUDA or HIP for GPU execution. A widely accepted practice for implementing such networks involves utilizing pre-trained models obtained from classification tasks and fine-tuning them for segmentation.  In this study, we investigate an alternative approach where pre-training is performed on monocular depth estimation.  We support our hypothesis that depth pre-training is more effective than classification pre-training by presenting supporting evidence through numerical estimates, striking examples, and corroborating findings from literature.  Our evidence suggests that monocular depth estimation is easier than semantic segmentation and classification, thus making it a suitable choice for pre-training.  Furthermore, we also demonstrate the benefits of incorporating multi-task learning, specifically by combining monocular depth estimation and semantic segmentation.  Our analysis explores the reasons behind the superiority of depth pre-training and provides valuable insights for future research.  Ultimately, we evaluate the efficacy of our approach on the Cityscapes benchmark and observe moderate to substantial performance improvements depending on the specific dataset being used.  Our code has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/dranvie/corrnet.  Our experiments also validate the correlation between monocular depth estimation accuracy and semantic segmentation performance, thus highlighting the significance of accurate depth maps for semantic segmentation tasks.  Our study reveals that the correlation between monocular depth estimation and semantic segmentation can be harnessed to achieve better semantic segmentation results through pre-training, thereby providing a new paradigm for semantic segmentation methods.  To the best of our knowledge, this study presents the first systematic evaluation of pre-training approaches for semantic segmentation and classification based on depth estimation, classification, or object detection tasks.  Our findings also suggest a straightforward strategy for leveraging the correlation between vision tasks in a general computer vision context. The Hirsch Conjecture was a theory claiming that a d-dimensional polytope with n faces cannot exceed a diameter of n - d. This assumption was contested by Santos, whose findings led to the conclusion that some linear programming methods cannot perform optimally within n - d iterations. This series of research was initiated by a novel algorithm, the facet pivot method, proposed in the first paper. This second paper confirms the efficacy of the facet pivot method, proving itself as an optimal linear programming solution, achieving at most n - d iterations to the optimal solution for a given input. Unlike the first paper, which considered an all-reduction search, this paper incorporates a more realistic and efficient approach, incorporating a more flexible and widely-used simplex method. This revised algorithm achieves the optimal bound of n - d iterations for the first time. A crucial component of the algorithm is the creation of a directed graph representing certain distance relationships between facets, upon which the maximum flow and shortest path algorithms can be applied. This algorithm allows for a realistic and efficient solution to linear programming problems, achieving the same optimal bound of n - d iterations with a high degree of efficiency. In fact, experimental results demonstrate the algorithm performs similarly well as when searching through all reductions, yet exhibits considerable speed improvements in practice, specifically due to efficient linear programming methods, such as the Primal-Dual simplex method, being used to traverse this graph defined by the distance relationships. Moreover, this algorithm allows for certain generalisations of the Hirsch Conjecture to be tested. These extensions include the Klee's Conjecture and the Brinkmann-Conjecture and others. This research was made possible through the joint funding of the Alan Turing Institute and the EPSRC (Grant No. EP/R004702/1). In addition to the theoretical findings, this algorithm allows for certain practical applications of the Hirsch Conjecture to be explored, specifically under the assumption that the Hirsch Conjecture is contested. Specifically, this algorithm allows for a polytope with a diameter of n - d + 1 to be constructed in a time proportional to that iteration bound. Moreover, this algorithm allows for a realistic and efficient solution to the element distinctness problem in a probabilistic setting, specifically by reducing the expected number of comparisons to at most n - d + 1. In this report, we compare the effectiveness of four domain adaptation methods for image classification: DeepCORAL, DeepDomainConfusion, CDAN, and CDAN+E, which employ an unsupervised learning approach given the absence of target labels. Our analysis of these methods is performed using the office-31 dataset, with a GitHub repository detailing the report available at: https://github.com/agrija9/Deep-Unsupervised-Domain-Adaptation. According to our report's findings, the CDAN+E method yields the highest accuracy after domain adaptation, which can be attributed to the application of a domain adapter and feature extractor combination, as well as the use of a domain discriminator to align domain probabilities without reliance on target labels. While the CDAN+E approach is rigorous in its domain adaptation framework, it is acknowledged that the complexity of its training procedure may deter some users. Furthermore, the CDAN+E source code has been optimized for user-friendly navigation, with a separate repository dedicated to this purpose located at: https://github.com/agrija9/Deep-Unsupervised-Domain-Adaptation-Evaluation. Its X-ray brightness distribution exhibits no evident disruption except for an elongation in the North-East to South-West direction. We applied the unsharp masking technique and calculated the morphology parameters to assess disturbance levels. These analyses identified a South-West substructure located at approximately 1 arcminute from the core, indicating the system may possess a quiet core but turbulent surroundings that potentially pump energy to the detected radio halo. Its dynamic composition might be consistent with the late formation of the binary system, XMMU J0232-4416. Furthermore, we considered alternative system types such as a triaxial system or a system in transition from a plane to a halting stage. However, the available data insufficiently distinguish between these scenarios. Finally, we estimated the energy stored in the 0 - 5 kiloparsec turbulent medium, amounting to $1.3_{-0.3}^{+0.5} \times 10^{62}$ erg. Its dynamic composition also aligns with the recent formation of late stages such as the Cen A system in the binary cluster, NGC4038/39. Its dynamic composition also potently explains the observed large-scale emission in the binary system. The naming game is often applied to the emergence of a shared language in a group of individuals, typically assumed to be stationary. In our investigation, we modified the naming game to incorporate agent movement, allowing us to explore its results in non-equilibrium situations. Our simulations revealed that language development differs significantly when agents are mobile. When agents move, a uniform language may not develop steadily; instead, languages may become stagnant or progress irregularly. To explain these discrepancies, we analyzed the connections between an agent's linguistic progress and their migration patterns. Our analysis indicated that agents migrating frequently within a localized area tend to develop languages quickly, while those moving more frequently at the system's full scale have slower language development. Furthermore, we found that average migration patterns of the system as a whole do not accurately represent individual behaviors. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationship between agent movement and language development in non-equilibrium naming game scenarios. Additionally, we calculated the coherence of languages using an entropy-based measure and discovered that high-coherence languages can be developed rapidly by or within tightly migration-concentrated areas, but this is not universally applicable for all such areas. These findings serve as a foundation for further investigations of the intersection between agent movement and linguistic development in the naming game. Our data and results code are publicly accessible at https://github.com/tylerkush/uwg_naming_game_with_migrating_agents. Coarse-grained results of our simulations, including final language states and average migration patterns, are available at https://courses.physics.mcmaster.ca/advanced_course_materials/tyler_kush/. Preliminary versions of these resources were previously shared at https://www.figshare.com/7335558. The current study builds upon a preliminary investigation, which can be found at https://www.arxiv.org/submit/1902.06795. As an extension of this work, we are conducting experiments to measure the linguistic progress of real-world humans living in regions with varying degrees of linguistic and movement heterogeneity. Our goal is to assess the connection between agent movement and naming game outcomes experimentally and to report our results in the near future. Naming game experiments necessarily have a long-term character, so we plan to leverage their significant ethical implications to fund the project. Our data and results code are publicly accessible at https://github.com/tylerkush/Experimental-Investigations-Of-The-Naming-Game. PINN algorithms have made significant breakthroughs in recent years. However, when dealing with complex problems involving multiple stationary ordinary differential equations, these methods often struggle due to the issue of spectral bias. This issue causes deep networks to favor details in the data that are easily reproducible, like those in the center of a dataset, while underestimating or overestimating details in more complex regions. Our research reveals that using momentum in training can partly alleviate this problem by allowing PINN models to capture details in both simple and complex data sets. To confirm this, we tested the momentum effect on PINN models' residual network layers and found that updated models using the ReLU6 activation function, along with varying compile settings, demonstrated reduced spectral bias with the inclusion of momentum. Furthermore, we found that utilizing the Tanh activation function, especially after the ReLU6 encoding, could potentially enhance PINN models' performance on tasks involving multiple ODEs. This outcome may facilitate the adoption of momentum in existing PINN algorithms and contributes to the understanding of activation functions' effects on deep neural networks' performance. This work was validated with numerical simulations of physical systems consisting of two-level ODEs and a Hodgkin-Huxley model. These models help to demonstrate the spectral bias issue and how it can be mitigated with the use of momentum in training. Our code has been made available on GitHub for other researchers to use. In particular, this work aims to contribute to the understanding of spectral bias in PINN models and explore the potential benefits of using the Tanh activation function, especially in models involving multiple ODEs, and ultimately aids in enhancing PINN models' performance on tasks involving complex data sets. Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning have led to widespread success across various applications, yet deep RL methods struggle with two key issues: efficiency and transparency. High interaction costs underscore the importance of efficiency, while improved transparency via more interpretable models fosters trust from users. In this research, we present a novel approach combining model-based reinforcement learning and inductive logic programming for learning policies in discrete domains. The proposed two-level hierarchy leverages eXtreme Timed Markov Models at the high level to capture task-independent task semantics and Timed Markov Logics for subgoals, utilizing a novel IP technique and the ALP system to learn these models from experience data. Our results demonstrate that this method can effectively acquire task-specific subgoal and action strategies, leading to efficient learning, and we propose an IP-based algorithm to address the non-determinism inherent in XTMMs. The approach is applied to the classic Airfoil Design problem, highlighting its potential for enhanced transparency and task independence. The research also contributes to the development of an augmented ALP system by integrating a novel IP technique and the Dlv++ implementation of the ALP system. The research study is available online. The related code and data can be found at  https://github.com/filipifg/hrl-ip and  https://github.com/filipifg/alp-ip, respectively. The ALP and IP method implementations derive from the ALpPublicate family, a set of public repositories, specifically the alp-public and dlvpp family. The research study expands the existing IP method literature by integrating the IP technique and the ALP system with model-based reinforcement learning, leading to the development of a novel approach. The study also expands the use of model-based reinforcement learning to the domain of HRL. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a chiral interaction between photons within the resonators, allowing us to build optical diodes and isolators without relying on magnetic fields, heaters, or voltage controls. The kernel mixture concept utilizes Gaussian kernels with enhanced scale and center configurations, producing a nearly non-parametric blur shape representation. The decision of the base kernel count becomes more flexible due to a data-driven method. This paper introduces a new concept called associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair with weight (λ,γ) which can be used to solve the double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-system. Furthermore, we establish equivalent definitions of covariant BiHom-bialgebra with quasitriangular properties and show that the BiHom-Yang-Baxter equation of weight -1 can be derived from a unitary quasitriangular covariant BiHom-bialgebra. Lastly, two methods of constructing BiHom-pre-Lie modules from Rota-Baxter paired modules and BiHom-algebra pairs are presented respectively. As a result, we obtain two equivalent definitions of BiHom-associative Yang-Baxter equation of weight 1. This notion has a connection to the double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-algebra concept that was first introduced in a related paper by Shen and Zhang. Specifically, we show that the double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-algebra can be extended to a coassoative Yang-Baxter BiHom-algebra of weight 1. This extension is achieved by equating two distinct notations. One notation is based on the curved homotopy algebra concept, while the other is based on the weight value. This result provides a link between two previously distinct areas of study. Moreover, we show that the double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-algebra can be further extended to a BiHom-algebra with a (p, q)-derivation. By taking the limit of q approaching 0, we obtain the generalization of the original double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-algebra concept. The integration of advanced traffic forecasting technology significantly affects urban transportation systems.
The traffic4cast challenge offered timely and accurate traffic prediction in real-time, but the current approach has limitations due to a narrow time frame and reliance on a single feature, i.e., time slots of traffic videos.
We propose an innovative method for forecasting traffic conditions at intersection sites using frame-level features extracted from traffic video snippets.
Our approach begins by training a multi-label regression model to determine the number of moving vehicles at distinct spatial locations within an intersection, using specific frames as separate instances.
The trained model then combines features from multiple time-stamps to make accurate predictions of vehicle counts at intersection sites.
The system demonstrates robust performance under different time-stamps, and using random samples of vehicle frames at varying time-stamps, we achieve a high validation accuracy of 92%, surpassing the state-of-the-art solution for traffic forecasting.
Our technique has the added advantage of being adaptable to broader forecasting periods, leveraging the inherent continuity of traffic patterns beyond the initial 30-minute forecasting scope.
Using temporal augmentation, we increase the forecasting window up to two hours while maintaining high prediction accuracy.
Our research reveals that leveraging multi-modal features and temporal density is crucial for accurate traffic forecasting.
Additionally, employing segmentation techniques improves our understanding of traffic flow patterns, particularly the occurrence of congestion at intersection sites.
Ultimately, our novel approach facilitates the integration of traffic forecasting technology into diverse fields such as urban navigation systems. 
The source code for this project is publicly available at: https://github.com/ConcepcionR/traffic_forecasting_snippets. Additionally, the baseline results and challenge data can be accessed at: https://impact.ncku.edu.tw/t4c/.

Carlo simulation. By simulating cosmic ray interactions with the Earth's atmosphere and
magnetosphere, we found that protons from neutron decay at LEO can account for their
observed spectral characteristics. Furthermore, our model predicts the temporal, spatial,
and angular variability of CRAND protons at LEO, aligning with spacecraft measurements. 

We present findings indicating that:
 - The primary source of CRAND protons is protons from $^{14}$O produced in neutron
   decay in the mesosphere.
 - The angular distribution of CRAND protons' seed is crucial in determining their
   trapping, particularly for LEO, given the close proximity to the Earth's atmosphere.
 - The temporal and spatial variability of CRAND protons' intensity at LEO is largely
   controlled by the solar modulation of cosmic rays and atmospheric variables like cloud
   coverage and geomagnetic cutoffs. 

Our model enables the calculation of CRAND protons' intensity at LEO, revealing significant
modulation by these factors. Notably, the model casts doubt on using a simplified model for
CRAND protons' intensity at LEO, as these factors can lead to substantial variations. 
Naturally, such variability raises expectations for identifying the source, intensity,
and other characteristics of CRAND protons, and hence, the model serves in the investigation
of the phenomenon.

This approach diverges from traditional methods using either pure Gaussian or mixed Gaussian-Laplace noise. In contrast to simply adding such noise, many existing private matrix completion techniques, including some based on the Singular Value Projection (SVP) algorithm, are inefficient or ineffective due to the weakness of Laplace noise or the sensitivity of the Gaussian distribution to the precision of the partial matrix entries. We introduce the Huber loss, a novel quantity, to determine the optimal noise combination for the Huber mechanism, which is tailored to the SVP technique. This quantity can be calculated via an iterative convex program and is shown to be computationally efficient, especially for large datasets. Experimental results confirm the Huber mechanism's superiority over standard privacy mechanisms, demonstrating its ability to complete private low-rank matrices efficiently. Notably, the Huber mechanism's efficiency is comparable to or superior to the recently introduced Gaussian-Mahalanobis distance mechanism. Moreover, the low R^2 score of the Huber noise indicates its potential for further optimization, paving the way for future enhancements. We're investigating the variant'most clicks' where the objective is to utilize the fewest clicks needed to transform each light to the opposite state. Initially, the best-known lower bound for this variant is linear, but it's yet to be upper-bounded for any k greater than one. In our study, we've developed an algorithm with upper bounds of (n-1)/2+k and n/2 for the case k equals one and two respectively, thereby closing the gap in one instance and confining previously known results that were valid for k equals one. Furthermore, for k greater than two, we've found that the upper bound of n/2 is insufficient, but instead we've discovered it can be replaced with the best-known lower bound of n- the ceiling of n over 3, multiplied by the ceiling of n over 3. Program analysis through Abstract Interpretation involves simulating the behavior of a program in a simplified environment to approximate its true behavior. This simulation traditionally has two steps: the upward phase uses approximation to ensure termination, and the downward phase uses interpolation to estimate program values. However, this distinction is problematic because some approximations necessitate precise values and conversely, interpolations can tolerate some degree of approximation. As a result, current techniques often force either excessive approximation or accuracy, resulting in either overly conservative or inaccurate results. To address this issue, we propose a new direction in Abstract Interpretation known as "post-interpolation decoupling", which integrates interpolation and approximation in a reverse order, allowing for the combination of precise values and smooth approximations. We present a general framework for a class of Approximation/Interpolation pairs, and showcase its effectiveness in improving the precision of existing Abstract Domains, specifically by achieving soundness for Domains like Reachable States analysis and in achieving a 35 times speed-up of Extensible Arrays. Experiments on real-world programs have shown that our decoupling approach can yield a 2.9 to 18.6 times improvement in precision compared to state-of-the-art techniques. To facilitate the replication of our results, we have released the decoupling library along with the used benchmarks and results. This research has been supported by the Fundacao Calouste Gulbenkian. Recent research has shown significant progress in improving recommender system performance through leveraging reviews for predicting ratings, however the current methods have several limitations. The existing techniques often use complex neural networks, which make it challenging to easily understand reviewer sentiments. Moreover, they tend to overlook the unique interaction between reviews and users/items, where each review contributes differently to modeling user/item preferences. To address these issues, a novel Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network called SIFN has been proposed for review-based item recommendations. The method starts by encoding user/item reviews using BERT and introduces a lightweight sentiment extractor to capture review semantics. In addition, a sentiment-aware interaction module is developed to interactively fuse review embeddings from different perspectives, while also capturing rich review semantics. The model was further enhanced with a rating prediction head and a temporal head, which learns time-embbeddings for dynamic rating predictions. Experiments conducted on two real-world datasets demonstrated the superiority of SIFN over state-of-the-art baselines, with results supporting its effectiveness on datasets created using Amazon reviews. Additionally, an ablation study confirmed the importance of individual review contributions and learned interaction effects. Notably, a variant of SIFN with an additional user/item preference head outperformed other models that incorporated optimal review pooling strategies, while also demonstrating compatibility with various rating prediction objectives. Overall, the performance of SIFN surpassed that of state-of-the-art baselines and demonstrated the importance of sentiment-aware review interactions in predicting ratings. As a result, a more interpretable and flexible model was achieved through incorporating sentiment awareness, particularly in predicting user/item preferences from reviews. As tasks increasingly rely on computer execution, the demand for reliable solutions is rising across domains, including engineering and computer graphics. A fundamental concept in addressing these challenges is the hexahedral mesh, a three-dimensional grid of uniform cells that provides an optimal framework for analysis and visualization. In this study, we explore the core issue of hexahedral mesh deformation, which requires expanding the grid to accommodate a given set of points while maintaining the natural structure of the network. To address this challenge, we have developed two algorithms that build upon a graph optimization framework, leveraging the use of graph-based methods to derive the associated Voronoi tesselation directly. Our first approach iteratively adds vertices to the network by solving a problem that determines the optimal positioning of new vertices, based on a quadratic energy model. Our second algorithm takes a more edge-based approach, suggesting that new edges can be added to the graph to enhance its structure. Additionally, we have developed an edge-based algorithm that can be used to untangle heavily distorted hexahedral meshes consisting of up to 58 tets per hexahedral element. Our proposed methods have demonstrated exceptional results in our testing dataset of over 200,000 points, while maintaining a level of computational efficiency that allows for the processing of the entire dataset within 1-10 seconds. Key metrics for our untangled meshes include the Q measure (0.17), error in volume (0.04%), and the Johnson-Koch measure (0.67). These results validate the effectiveness of the untangled hexahedral mesh framework. In the context of simulating the mechanical behavior of solids, sparse, stable, and controllable solutions are essential. These criteria are typically addressed using advanced time-integration algorithms, such as the Generalized Alpha method, which uses parameters like gamma and beta. Traditional approaches adjust these parameters heuristically in an ad-hoc manner to achieve desired solution characteristics. This paper utilizes the capabilities of convex optimization to automate the selection of parameters, thereby eliminating the need for manual parameter tuning. This goal is achieved by reinterpreting the parameter selection as a convex optimization problem and solving it using an efficient algorithm called the Interior Point Method. This approach has been successfully tested on various finite element models with the Newmark beta and Generalized Alpha methods of implementation. Results indicate that this method can achieve significant improvements in simulation efficiency with minimal computational overhead. Furthermore, analysis of the method's properties reveals that it possesses local quadratic convergence and specific error guarantees, providing a theoretical basis for its operation. Validation against practical problems, including multidimensional cases, demonstrates the method's effectiveness in achieving efficient solution characteristics while maintaining accuracy and stability. Last but not least, this approach also provides error estimates based on the solution's residual, thereby enabling users to make data reduction decisions efficiently and safely. Overall, this method represents a major advancement in time-integration algorithm development, empowering scientists to focus on simulation-based research and analysis rather than parameter tuning. This, in turn, facilitates a range of applications, including data analysis, sensitivity studies, and optimization across various engineering and scientific fields, such as materials science, biology, climate modeling, and more. Additional benefits are also realized, including enhanced research productivity and efficiency, leading to numerous potential research and application avenues, which are briefly outlined at the end of this document. One such direction is the extension of this optimization-based approach to the broader class of implicit ordinary differential equations, which is currently being explored as a potential next step in optimization methodology development. Ultimately, the underlying theoretical work on optimization methods for time-integration algorithms has the potential to lead to new and exciting advancements in scientific computing practice and methodology. While principles like stochastic mixing and submodular profitability can ensure consistency and fairness in adaptive environments, cooperative agents may still over-invest in questionable activities. To address this, a transfer empowerment method is proposed to enhance social interaction rules with an intrinsic motivation for adaptation and cooperation. This approach defines a system's ability to adapt to its environment as intrinsic motivation, measured by the extent to which past experiences benefit its future learning in similar situations. Additionally, the proposed method exhibits a level of robustness in its ability to cooperate with biased and unpredictable agents. In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding has become the predominant approach. Each ad impression resulting from user interaction is instantly auctioned off, with demand-side platforms (DSPs) providing bids typically based on the value of the ad impression and optimal bid price. Nevertheless, existing bidding strategies often overlook the randomness of user behaviors, such as click-through rates, and the uncertainty surrounding costs associated with ad impressions. In our study, we take into consideration the uncertainty associated with CTOR rates and the uncertainty concerning the costs of ad impressions, while also accounting for a DSP's budget constraint. In an effort to optimize a DSP's long-term revenue, we develop a systematic framework for ad allocation and bidding, incorporating two key components: uncertainty-based risk metrics and a multi-stage bidding strategy. The former enables a DSP to manage uncertainty and set a budget in an optimal manner, while the latter integrates the uncertainty and budget constraints, as well as the uncertainty-based risk metrics, into a durable bid price in an optimal way. In the theoretical portion of our study, we establish the conditions required for our model to achieve optimal results in an asymptotic sense, while in the experimental portion, we evaluate our model by comparing it with six prominent bidding strategies on real-world datasets, ultimately verifying the efficacy of our approach in achieving optimal long-term revenue for a DSP. The findings of our study can serve as a valuable guide for real-world ad allocation and bidding decisions made by DSPs. Furthermore, our model offers an excellent solution for ascertaining uncertain CTORs and ad impression costs while adhering to a budget constraint. In addition, our model offers an interesting and novel paradigm for bidding strategy development. The contributions of our model are two-fold: 1) the incorporation of uncertainty-based risk metrics for both CTORs and ad impression costs, as well as the budget constraint, and 2) the development of an optimal bidding strategy in an asymptotic sense. In a subsequent study, we expanded upon our model in several key ways, including the incorporation of uncertainty-based risk metrics for bid prices, as well as the incorporation of multiple DSPs competing in auctions, resulting in a novel bilevel programming framework for optimal bidding strategies in an asymptotic sense. To overcome this limitation, we propose combining human feedback with automated agents' exploration outcomes, allowing the agent to identify comparable states and suggest comparisons that maximize learning efficiency. Specifically, we utilize a learning algorithm that leverages clustering to prioritize comparisons, selecting states that are challenging for the agent to distinguish and cluster together, and facilitating the creation of effective comparison datasets. Our approach results in the development of three publicly accessible comparison datasets, demonstrating the efficiency of this visually-assisted comparative learning method. Additionally, the proposed method showcases its potential for real-time learning in complex environments through the successful training of an agent in a high-level representation of the game of StarCraft: the strategy of Gatherer. Gatherer's pivotal insights include its ability to identify and target the player's resource-gathering units and redirect its attack towards more valuable objectives, exemplifying the capability of visually-assisted comparative learning in extracting high-level decision-making policies for intelligent decision-making in complex tasks. Anomaly detection without labelled data is increasingly being used in systems to monitor how a device or system behaves over time, with the aim of identifying unusual activity, but there's a significant problem with anomaly detection - it's too resource-intensive. To overcome this, we've developed tinyML, a machine learning framework that can run on very limited devices, but it has one major issue - it won't work with labelled data. So, we've come up with a solution - a modified version of the Isolation Forest algorithm that uses unlabelled data to identify anomalies, and we've tested it and improved it to make sure it works just as well as traditional anomaly detection algorithms, but on tinyML devices. To make things even more efficient, we've also developed a version of the algorithm that uses synthetic data to train the model, and we've seen a significant reduction in computational power needed to identify anomalies. Our results show that the algorithm is efficient and effective, and we think it has the potential to be a big breakthrough in very efficient and effective anomaly detection. To show how it works, we've also developed a simple example application that uses data from a car's IMU to identify unusual braking patterns. With the potential to make it even more powerful by combining it with other algorithms, we think there are many possibilities for future research. To facilitate a deeper understanding of one-dimensional physical systems, we consider the basic yet challenging scenario of single-file diffusion. We approach this problem from the perspective of the exit time statistics of a one-dimensional simple exclusion process, focusing on the underlying physical properties that influence the system's behavior. By connecting the exit time to the speed distribution of the last particle, we use the Feynman-Kac formula to derive a master equation for the speed distribution's time evolution, yielding a scaled mean exit time. Through both analytical calculations and simulations, we examine how the speed distribution changes in detail, ultimately relating it to the system's dynamic viscosity, as described by the structural factor. Furthermore, we explore the impact of certain parameters, such as particle number and file length, on the exit time, offering a glimpse into the subtle interplay between these macroscopic properties and the microscopical factors governing the diffusion process, including temperature, as influenced by the second moment of the structural factor, which emerges from general entropy production considerations. Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images or their altered variants from vast databases comprise two fundamental components: a compression-based retrieval stage and a robust matching process. Current systems fail to balance these components effectively, leading to disparate execution times for retrieval and re-ranking, with the latter often being significantly slower. We introduce active image indexing, a method designed to adaptively refine search results during real-time image retrieval processes. Our approach accelerates re-ranking by leveraging compressed data from previously searched images, increasing their contribution over time as the search dataset expands. Experimental results demonstrate that active image indexing achieves a time-speed balance comparable to compressed-based retrieval and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy and processing efficiency. We publicly share our code and processed datasets on GitHub to facilitate future research.

We establish that the long-term behavior of smooth, overdamped particles is identical to that of a simple harmonic oscillator, and explore how dissipation affects finite-damped systems: their steady-state distribution narrows as the rate of decay increases: it widens as the rate decreases; at critical values, system equilibrium is lost, transitioning into chaotic, non-thermal states. The underlying dynamics is revealed by comparing microcanonical and canonical ensembles. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the rate at which dissipation causes the equilibrium distribution to broaden is inversely proportional to damping rates. Consequently, an exceptionally low rate is required for observable narrowing effects when washboard potentials are used in experimental studies of Brownian motion. This paper presents an adaptable, localized predictive technique that builds upon Jord\'a (2005) and allows for the evaluation of various, non-parametric regression models. We propose an novel, flexible approach that can assess the effects of multiple variables across diverse prediction intervals without necessitating specific distributional assumptions, thus facilitating the pre-dictive analysis of policy scenarios. We develop a high-order, semi-nonparametric estimation procedure for the predicted error distribution, which doesn't rely on incorrect parametric specifications. We demonstrate the asymptotic validity of our error-inflation estimator for arbitrary distribution types and showcase its applicability in a new high-order localization theorem. We substantiate our theoretical findings with simulation results and a real-world example examining the impact of Fed purchases on stock returns. Specifically, we investigate the effect of $250$ billion Fed purchase programs on stock returns and discover that, according to our estimates, such programs would result in a 1% or greater boost over a 20-month horizon, which aligns with the views of several Senior Investment Professionals surveyed by Bloomberg. A time-series analysis also reveals that the positive effects of these programs on equity prices are statistically significant at the 5% level for two separate periods but not the overall sample. Furthermore, our estimates indicate a 0.05% or greater monthly return for every dollar of additional Fed purchase beyond the initial $25 billion, which holds for two different samples and is statistically significant at the 5% level. Interestingly, these program effects seem to be robust to changes in the business cycle and are consistently positive although not all intervals feature significant stock performance. We apply our novel estimation approach to several other predictive scenarios including the impact of Fed words on stock prices, the effects of non-core inflation on growth, and the relationship between Fed monetary policy and bond returns. This study tackles the issue of assessing causal influences in cases where some variables involved in ensuring causal validity are incompletely known. For these situations, we develop tight limits on the causal influences by solving two complex optimization problems. The derived limits prove to be sufficient for performing reliable confidence intervals on causal influences, as evidenced by our comparison with existing methods. The confidence intervals generated here have superior characteristics when dealing with large datasets, reduced computational demands, and more robust outcomes. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through its successful high-dimensional data application to reliable causal influence estimation. Our methodology is mainly proposed for use in identifying key variables responsible for the diseases' cause, which in turn facilitates the development of effective prevention strategies. The findings of our high-dimensional data application are validated through extensive real data experiments. The proposed methodology is made available as an open-source R package named 'causalEffects'. The research leads to the formulation of two optimization problems, one for each type of causal influence (counterfactual and causal), as explained below. The objective functions of these optimization problems involve complex integrals. To address these complexities, we first approximate these integrals using finite sums, which in turn can be further approximated as discrete sums for real variable vectors. Consequently, the resulting optimization problems become linear or quadratic programs, which can be efficiently solved using well-established computational methods. Significant physical system failures can result from cyber attacks. This paper investigates nonlinear residuals in relation to linear time-invariant systems, examining how cyber attacks affect residual behavior. Specifically, we investigate how cyber attacks impact one-standard-deviation zones and Mahalanobis metrics in residual space. By addressing a key practical question, this paper improves the predictive capability of monitor rules in relation to widely used zonelike approaches. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of our findings to systems with unknown parameters as well as multiple potential attack types. Ultimately, this research recommends a straightforward framework for developing better monitors, along with guidance for choosing critical parameters. Theoretical underpinnings are complemented by conceptual proofs and illustrative numerical examples. These examples emphasize the importance of model accuracy in achieving effective predictive monitors. By combining system identification and predictor design, this paper presents a unified approach for creating better monitors. Finally, one suggested method for selecting predictor parameters aligns with recommendations from the NIST framework. Specifically, this paper recommends cross-validation. The recommended approach effectively balances statistical integrity with practical considerations of monitor development. Overall, this paper improves the predictive capability of monitor rules in relation to generally accepted zonelike methods. Beyond that, this paper investigates the applicability of statistical concepts, such as likelihood ratio tests, in relation to monitoring cyber attacks. However, such ideas are beyond the scope of this paper. With further research, these techniques could complement the framework and approach presented. A precise summary can be derived from lengthy written documents via deep learning models, but English language models often benefit from larger training sets and pre-trained tools, whereas summarizers for other languages face difficulties due to limited annotated datasets available online.
Our study focuses on developing a universal summarizer using a graph-based deep learning approach that makes no prior assumptions about document structure.
The proposed model can effectively generate summaries from any document, even without reference summaries, and it's entirely in Indian languages which are currently underrepresented in NLP studies.
The performance of our model, GAE-ISumm, was evaluated on datasets in three Indian languages – Telugu, Malayalam, and Kannada – and our results indicate that it ranks among the top-performing systems despite not relying on pre-trained tools or annotated training data.
The full implementation details can be found at a GitHub repository. Evaluations were based on the metrics (average) applied to the top-performing systems as of our knowledge cutoff date: 
  - Telugu: ROUGE-1: 0.42, ROUGE-2: 0.18, ROUGE-L: 0.44
  - Malayalam: ROUGE-1: 0.39, ROUGE-2: 0.17, ROUGE-L: 0.40
  - Kannada: ROUGE-1: 0.35, ROUGE-2: 0.15, ROUGE-L: 0.35
Evaluations revealed that our model performs significantly better in summarization tasks than the strongest Indian language summarizer, DeepIS. Moreover, it even outperforms some high-performing multilingual summarizers like BERTSUM and Protonet. This experiment also identified BERTSUM as the second-best system for Telugu and Kannada but struggled with Malayalam due to limited annotated datasets available online. Interestingly, our graph-based deep learning approach outperformed established graph-based models, such as GraphClauser Score and Edge-based Score, especially in terms of outperforming GraphIS on Malayalam and Telugu datasets. However, it failed to surpass Edge-based Score on the Kannada dataset. We trust the current findings will stimulate further research in unsupervised summarizer development for under-researched language domains and make the source code of our model available for download at this repository: https://github.com/krishnatechsharma/GAE-ISumm. We also distribute pre-trained models for automatic summarization and provide online demonstration services through our website at summar

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. We contrast our results with a lower bound showing that our approach is unlikely to be improved via a polynomial kernel under specific conditions. Furthermore, we've established that his condition can be violated for certain subclasses of directed graphs with extended treewidth, suggesting the inherent difficulty in handling these graphs. Our initial contributions involve the creation of two new parameterized algorithms for checking upward planarity in directed acyclic graphs and semi-green graphs. We've also explored the general case of upward planarity in directed graphs with treewidth δ and treedepth δ' and demonstrated that our algorithm has a run-time of O(δ' |E| + |E| δ). Our analysis reveals that our approach offers a performance improvement for graphs with treewidth much greater than their treedepth but treewidth smaller than their treedepth squared, a common pattern in graphs. Our results suggest the following general observation, which requires further investigation: a directed graph is likely to be representable in an upward planar layout if its treewidth is smaller than its treedepth. Our analysis also reveals that our algorithm does not benefit from treedepth in graphs with treewidth much greater than their treedepth. We've also explored the upward planarity in outerplanar graphs, where our algorithm has a run-time of O(|E|), independent of its treewidth and treedepth. Our analysis reveals that our approach offers a performance improvement for graphs with a particular structural property, where the number of occurrences of certain graph substructures with four vertices significantly exceeds the overall number of edges in the graph. We've also established that our algorithm does not benefit from this property in graphs with a particular structural property related to tree-minor isomorphism, where the upward planarity check has a run-time of Ω(|E|^2) in the worst case. Photons are valuable tools used to explore the intricate dynamics of heavy-ion collisions that create a state known as quark-gluon plasma (QGP). Recent simulations of QGP with different properties have been conducted within the framework of the relativistic hydrodynamic model. Viscosity, a measure of a fluid's resistance to changes, plays a key role in these interactions. Hydrodynamic models reveal that the anisotropic flow of photons, vapor emitted from the plasma, is sensitive to the QGP's viscosity levels. Furthermore, the anisotropic flow of photons in the most central collisions of large nuclei is predicted to be higher when the QGP's viscosity is low and lower when the viscosity is high, with a particular pattern of changes that is linked to the viscosity levels. These findings are based on detailed calculations involving the cumulants of photon flow measurements. Software developers who perform maintenance tasks encounter multiple change requests 
submitted by software system users, presenting the difficulty of choosing suitable 
search terms for concept location during maintenance activities. A proposed technique 
QUICKAR leverages the knowledge gathered from the crowd-sourced platform, Stack 
Overflow, to provide reformulated query suggestions based on the relevance of terms.

The relevance of phrases is determined by comparing them to relevant SO tags, which 
are associated with specific concepts, and by evaluating their similarity using 
intensity and variance information. Multiple relevance measures were explored including 
a established metric called Tag intensity and a novel variation called Tag density, 
alongside a predictive model called Zebra. QUICKAR provides real-time suggestions to 
aid developers in selecting relevant search terms for concept location.

The results of the experiment demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing 
search methods based on relevance measures. A pre-training approach, called Unsupervised 
PHI-Bayes, was also explored in related research, however its results were not available at 
the time of the publication's initial submission. Overall, the proposed method outperforms 
existing techniques providing better results particularly in tasks with fewer than ten relevant 
SO tags**

Adaptive synchronization in interactions, or entrainment, involves the participants in a conversation adapting or matching each other's distinctive vocal traits. To better grasp how people adapt to each other's communication style during conversations, it's necessary to analyze various acoustic characteristics and compare them through multiple measurement techniques. This work introduces a novel turn-level metric, referred to as the Neural Entrainment Distance (NED), developed using an unsupervised deep learning approach. NED establishes a method for identifying patterns within a dataset and uses a Gaussian mixture model to convert dissimilar features into comparable representations, ultimately facilitating a more effective comparison of distribution differences. The precision of the NED is verified through its accurate separation of synthetic and real conversations, as well as its ability to accurately predict the level of similarity in communication style across pairs of speakers. Additionally, applications of the NED method to a large-scale, real conversation dataset have revealed a significant correlation between the measure and various external behavioral and psychological factors, such as attention and attentional deviations. Importantly, it was found that speakers adapt to and resemble those who show interest in the conversation, as evidenced by measures of speaking tempo, pitch, and speech fragmentation. These results suggest that the NED method is effective in detecting and differentiating a range of adaptive behaviors in speech, regardless of its source or motivation. Ultimately, the NED is positioned as an advanced diagnostic tool, offering a range of possibilities for its use in the automated analysis, detection, and assessment of various adaptive behaviors in speech, as well as its application in the study of psychological and behavioral conditions. Specifically, future research directions include the development of a semi-supervised or fully unsupervised NED method, the investigation of additional speaker groups, populations, and environments, an exploration of the NED's efficacy in the automated detection of adaptive behaviors and conditions, and the application of NED in the analysis of spoken language as a tool in the study of linguistic structure and communication. The NED algorithm and associated data, as well as detailed description of methods and results, are available for review through public research channels. Although the precise timing of its completion is not specified, our research into the development of the NED has been an ongoing effort. The large-scale dataset of real conversations, referred to as the TV shows corpus, is an entirely natural and unscripted collection of conversations, as well as one of the largest, spanning approximately 330 hours in length. Classifying every video frame into its respective action can be a labor-intensive task, particularly for a large collection of unlabeled videos. Therefore, we present a novel, unsupervised method, called SSCAP, that identifies likely temporal segments across a variety of videos without the need for explicit annotations. SSCAP utilizes self-supervised learning techniques to derive distinguishing features from videos and a novel action parsing approach that identifies correlations among activity sub-components while accurately determining their sequential progression. The effectiveness of SSCAP is demonstrated through its exceptional performance on classic datasets (Breakfast and 50Salads) as well as a challenging dataset (YouTube Actions) that features diverse activities with extensive variations. Results indicate that SSCAP outperforms existing unsupervised methods while surpassing semi-supervised methods with reduced reliance on labeled data, requiring only 200 labeled videos for optimal performance on the YouTube Actions dataset. These states, specifically $P_{\rm{mol,1^{\rm{st}}}}$, can be identified as molecular states consisting of one extra $\pi$ and additional quark combinations, while their counterparts, $P_{\rm{mol,2^{\rm{nd}}}}$, have an additional quark in addition to the $\pi$. Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing methods. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on the shortcomings of their test suites, which hinders their ability to create effective tests. As a result, there is a need for an alternative feedback style. The goal of this study is to compare two different approaches to providing feedback to students: a standard, detailed approach that mimics industrial best practices, and an inquiry-based approach that encourages concept-based feedback. The study suggests that the inquiry-based approach has the potential to be a superior solution as it offers students a deeper understanding of their test suites while promoting the development of skills that are highly prized in the industry, such as self-directed learning. The findings from this study indicate that the standard and inquiry-based approaches yield comparable results in terms of course performance, but the inquiry-based approach leads to greater student satisfaction and a greater likelihood that students continue programming careers. The study's outcomes also indicate that the main disadvantage of the standard approach is that students who utilize it report feeling more confined in their testing activities, whereas the inquiry-based approach enables more freedom and flexibility in testing methodologies. Ultimately, the study indicates that providing freedom and flexibility in testing activities correlates with student satisfaction levels. The study's results support the hypothesis that the inquiry-based approach is superior to the standard approach, and provide evidence to suggest that providing students with the power to create their own test cases yields more satisfaction, performance, and continued advancement in the field. The study's findings also highlight several potential areas for future improvement, such as conducting a larger-scale analysis of both approaches, exploring alternative designs for the standard approach, and addressing concerns that the inquiry-based approach may generate irrelevant test cases. While these concerns could hinder its effectiveness, they do not appear to be major obstacles. The study's results support the idea that small adjustments to this feedback style could make a significant difference in the performance and satisfaction levels of students. Ultimately, the study's findings indicate that the standard approach is not a reliable education tool, and instead appears to hinder students from developing the skills that are essential for the industry, whereas the inquiry-based approach shows considerable potential as a valuable tool for testing education. As a result, the study suggests that future research should prioritize refining and optimizing the inquiry-based approach to make it an even more effective and reliable tool for testing education. Domain adaptation has been applied extensively to handle distribution shifts across various fields like vision, language, and multimedia. Most existing domain adaptation techniques leverage domain-invariant features by utilizing domain-label pairs from the target domain. However, when dealing with a scenario where the target domain's labels are not accessible, known as the "no-reference" scenario, the adaptation is more challenging. To address this issue, we propose a new framework based on hypothesis transfer, which does not require target domain labels during training. Our approach, called Semi-Supervised Hypothesis Transfer (SHT), relies on multiple domain-hypothesis alignment techniques and iteratively solves for domain-invariant features without target domain labels, transferring them to the target domain one hypothesis at a time. By utilizing multiple hypotheses, the target domain's label space is fully explored, and hypothesis transfer can be performed repeatedly without decreasing performance even after numerous iterations. Given that domain hypotheses themselves are difficult to obtain, we introduce a new regularization method called "proxy-label regulation" to stabilize the training process in the absence of target domain labels. Our approach has been extensively tested on two text and image classification datasets, outperforming existing state-of-the-art models by a significant margin, and we provide qualitative analysis to support our claims. The code is publicly available on GitHub. Analyzing our approach requires a thorough examination of various experiment results and we will follow the structure as suggested by the guidelines. Specifically, we will start with the introduction of the "no-reference" scenario in domain adaptation, present our proposed Semi-Supervised Hypothesis Transfer approach, and conclude with the experimental evaluation. Our experimental findings indicate that domain-invariant features can be effectively obtained through the alignment of domain-hypotheses without requiring target domain labels during training. Moreover, the use of proxy-label regulation achieves the stabilization of the training process and enhances the adaptability of the features. Ultimately, the combination of these techniques leads to substantial performance improvements on two text and image classification datasets. A subsequent discussion explores the potential limitations of our approach and suggests that it may be extended to handle other distribution adaptation scenarios. Specifically, we explore the extension as cross-hypothesis adaptation, where the adaptation is performed across different domain-hypotheses. While our approach is more effective than existing state-of-the-art models, we recognize that it could be even more robust with the inclusion of cross-hypothesis adaptation. Finally, we outline potential research directions in this area. A comprehensive analysis of nuclear power systems designed for Deep Space transport is presented, utilizing a cutting-edge Gas Core Reactor (GCR) integrated with a magnetohydrodynamic generator. A novel GCR design with enhanced characteristics compared to existing models is proposed and validated, capable of generating 200 kW of electricity within a 30 metric-ton spacecraft. The GCR, functioning as both a power source and propellant within a Hall effect thruster, produces 6 km/s Delta-V missions, surpassing the 4.5 km/s capabilities of traditional RP-85 systems. The findings show the GCR to be a superior option for Deep Space transportation when considering energy gain per unit mass, however it falls short in total Delta-V capacity when compared to bipropellant systems. The presented research combines existing data with original analysis, incorporating a comprehensive systems-level study, specification-driven design, and performance assessment of the GCR. A recommended future research path is outlined, focusing on potential safety risks and technical hurdles associated with GCR development. The underlying models and design tools are freely accessible through the Nuclear Astrogonomy Software Suite, with the intention of enabling future GCR advancements and collaborations. The work aims to facilitate accelerated, tool-based design and research efforts in Nuclear Deep Space transportation systems. The proposed design is an improved iteration over previous generations of GCRs, showcasing potential for the Nuclear Astrogonomy Gas Core Reactor to serve as a benchmark for evaluation in the Nuclear Starship Tracking Study led by NASA. The work is released under the terms of the Apache 2.0 open-source open-source license to date, with the aim of enabling widespread reproduction and improvement. The presented research is the initial outcome of a larger study, the Nuclear Astrogonomy Gas Core Reactor Study (NGCRS), the final report of which is planned for future issuance. This study presents a novel neural network architecture for particle physics research that leverages localization in time-projection chamber technology for dark matter research. Characteristic signals detected by time-projection chamber technology lack precise spatial localization due to electromagnetic processes, yet relevant interactions occur within distinct ranges. Utilizing a domain-informed neural network approach, we can circumvent ambiguous signal localization by modeling the likelihood of an interaction occurring within specific ranges. Results demonstrate that our method successfully captures relevant localization information, and further optimization yields negligible losses in signal reconstruction when compared to standard backprojection techniques in a dark matter-inspired dataset. Source code for this project is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/dsulliv3/domain_informed_neural_networks. Our findings validate the domain-informed network approach as a reconstruction strategy for time-projection chamber data and can be adapted to other particle physics experiments. Additionally, this technique has potential applications in other fields, such as medical imaging and computer vision, where localization is an essential consideration. As computational demands are driven primarily by matrix multiplication, domain-informed neural networks can be readily implemented using widely available open-source deep learning frameworks. We anticipate that our results will serve as a foundation for future advancements in domain-informed and foundation models, enabling enhanced performance and versatility in artificial intelligence applications across particle physics and beyond. Furthermore, we propose a framework for particle physics informed by principles from natural language processing, allowing for the evaluation of a model's capacity for interpretability, reliability, and mode coverage. This text offers an in-depth explanation of the theoretical underpinnings of variable instantiation in Answer Set Programming. We build upon ASP's modeling language semantics to define a formal description of grounding algorithms using (fixed point) operators. Central to this are well-established, fixed-point operators providing models that offer semantic insights into the outcome of grounding as well as facilitating simplifications during processing. We address a broad range of logic programs that incorporates recursive aggregates and extends the reach of existing ASP modeling languages, complemented by an algorithmic framework outlining the process of grounding recursive aggregates. Temporal sequence analysis typically employs spectrometric or gene expression profiles with limited time points and a high number of variables. Due to this, existing methods face significant challenges, prompting the development of a new supervised learning approach, Sequential Learning Framework (SLF), specifically tailored for temporal sequence analysis in life sciences. SLF integrates classical statistical techniques with flexible representation learning from natural language models, using word2vec to distill temporal sequences into concise representations and leverage similarities among sequences. A Sequential Text-CNN network then combines features from individual sequences with overall expression profiles, producing predictions via a high-level, temporally-structured embedding. In video action detection, current research often relies on classifying actions based on spatial and temporal features extracted from 2D or 3D convolutional networks.  However, we believe that understanding an action involves also considering its context - objects and individuals within a video scene - so we've developed a novel model integrating self-attention and graph convolutional networks to better model context like actor relationships and object interactions. This self-supervised method aims to reduce annotation dependency using the minimum amount of bounding box annotations, offering clear explanation of actions through visual attention maps, even for actions unseen in training data. To evaluate its context-identification performance, we've established a quantitative recall-based metric and conducted a comparison on state-of-the-art action recognition models, demonstrating an improvement of 11% on top-1 accuracy and 15% on mean average precision on HMDB51 and UCF101 human action datasets.
