Precise and continuous population estimates are crucial for policy decisions surrounding vaccination initiatives and infrastructure development planning. As censuses fall short of providing the necessary spatiotemporal detail, researchers have been turning to independent approaches incorporating remote sensing data and microcensus statistics. We conducted an experiment in Mozambique, specifically estimating the population count in two districts between censuses. Furthermore, we evaluated the feasibility of leveraging open-access datasets to support population forecasting. Our exploration also involved utilizing existing annotated datasets to improve building footprint prediction, coupled with additional annotation of 'dot' features from targeted areas to enhance accuracy. We found that population estimates improved when utilizing estimated building footprint areas derived from this method over solely using available features. Our estimated population distributions in the study districts revealed significant underpopulation in urban areas and overpopulation in rural areas. This has substantial implications for vaccination programs and planning in the mentioned districts. Our proposed approach not only offers accurate estimates but also facilitates the identification of geographical biases and population density variances not captured by the national census, providing valuable insights for health and development strategists. Although with limitations, the precision of our population estimates compares favorably with those generated by the national census, thus offering a promising alternative for health and development planning applications. Our results emphasize the necessity for further research in this area to develop refined estimation and forecasting methodologies. Nonetheless, the gathered population data and corresponding spatial context can already prove useful for planning purposes, thus offering a viable solution despite present limitations. Moreover, the developed code and population data will greatly assist other researchers and practitioners working on similar estimation and forecasting projects, thus contributing to the advancement of this field. Finally, the proposed population estimates were found to have considerable and diverse applications not only in Mozambique but also in other countries, thus emphasizing the need for cross-country cross-pollination through collaborative scientific exchanges to enhance the quality of population estimates and forecasting methodologies. Developing accurate simulations of fluid-impact problems requiring the integration of flexible structures remains an unresolved challenge despite significant advancements in N-body methods. Such scenarios often involve complex multi-phase interactions and fluid-structure interactions at varying scales, necessitating a multi-resolution approach. We introduce an enhanced N-body formulation that extends our previous work on weakly-compressible methods to include incompressible fluid simulations. Additionally, this framework facilitates the interaction between multiple solid bodies, including rigid and flexible structures, by incorporating a multi-body formulation and mesh-free simulation of beams. We validate our new framework through multiple benchmark tests, including low-reynolds multi-phase flows, fluid-impact phenomena, and fluid-structure interactions with flexible surfaces. Results demonstrate that the framework accurately reproduces experimental results and serves as a stepping stone for incorporating additional complexities, such as multi-phase interactions, into fluid-structure interaction simulations. However, we observe inaccuracies in multi-phase simulations due to the requirement of density ratios, likely resulting in a mixture of densities that is not physically realistic. Such limitations highlight the need for a more sophisticated model that can overcome such inaccuracies, representing a remaining area of research for multi-resolution simulations. All the simulation codes used in this research have been made publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/aseaaper/aspoly17framework. Additionally, our framework has the potential to be extended to multi-physics problems through an accompanying supplementary document. Furthermore, our simulation results show that the relative error in multi-resolution framework for non-flexible rigid body simulations ranges from $2\%$, while for flexible simulations, it ranges from $5%$. Nonetheless, our results show that the framework has the potential to be a valuable tool in the study of multi-physics and multi-scale problems in the future. Video illustrations of the results discussed in this research can be viewed at: https://youtu.be/jHsOoV7fH8. Specifically, our results show that the forces acting on a rigid body in a rigid body-fluid interaction have a mean squared error of $0.2\mu N^2$ and the forces acting on a flexible beam have a mean squared error of $0.5N^2$, representing $20\%$ and $50\%$ errors respectively in comparison to the reference values. These results in particular highlight the present limitation of meshless simulations. We believe that the research presented in this document will contribute towards the development of more accurate and robust simulations in the study of fluid-impact phenomena. A recently created TTS model called FastPitch can change pitch, but the amount of pitch change it can make is limited. To expand the range of pitch changes it can make, researchers added a technique to it that adjusts pitch without changing its sound. To test this idea, they used a dataset of cat meows and had listeners compare the sound of naturally spoken meows with artificially changed pitch using the new technique or not. The results showed that the added technique makes it easier for a text-to-speech system to control pitch without changing its sound. To check how well the technique works on words, they compared the sound of naturally spoken words with artificially changed pitch using the new technique or not, but found that the technique doesn't work as well on words as it does on meows. The reason for this is that words can naturally have a wide range of pitches. To fix this, the researchers came up with a new idea to use the technique in combination with a model that changes the timing of words. The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to empower deep neural networks (DNNs) with the ability to tackle a wide array of tasks through pre-training. Despite the widespread utilization of DTL in the field, there is a notable absence of clear guidelines for its practical application. This research work aims to fill this knowledge gap by investigating the transferability in the context of DNNs. Initially, we challenge two commonly held assumptions within the DNN community, namely: (a) the conventional notion that similarities in data distributions and task-related information are key predictors of transferability, and (b) the notion that the reuse of representations is the primary factor contributing to transferability. Through our studies utilizing multiple benchmark datasets and protocols, we gather empirical evidence disproving these assumptions in favor of two new paradigms that are supported by our data: (a) the specificity of a dataset often poses a greater predictor of transferability than task-related information, and (b) the primary factor contributing to transferability is in fact the capability of the model to minimize the disturbance caused by changes in the distribution of the data. Furthermore, we also investigate the impact of the size of the data on transferability, revealing a positive correlation. Finally, with the ultimate goal of facilitating the practical applications of DTL in the future, we also provide a novel framework aimed at systematically assessing and comprehending transferability. The framework comprises two primary components, namely: (a) the establishment of a new metric capable of quantifying and reflecting dataset specificity, and (b) the design of a protocol allowing for the isolation of the effect of dataset specificity from task-related information. Ultimately, applying our novel framework to a wide array of public datasets revealed the empirical evidence confirming the absence of a correlation between task-related information and transferability, in stark contrast to a positive and significant correlation between dataset specificity and transferability. Moreover, as an additional application of our novel framework, we also made the dataset specificity of the iNaturalist dataset publicly accessible for the first time. The associated code has been made publicly available on our GitHub repository. Factors such as the presence of massive asteroids that are not the result of full planet formation models, the constraints on giant planet interior structure, and the constraints on the formation time of the system's gaps all contribute to this uncertainty. Theoretical studies indicate that a turbulent gap, as opposed to a clear cut one, can form when the perturbations in the disk density are not uniform. We discovered that the presence of perturbations can lead to the formation of planets at different radii and masses, and that these perturbations can also alter the shape of the density gap, making it more elliptical. We found that larger perturbations result in the formation of planets at closer distances to the host star. The pressure gaps associated with planar modes have the largest or no impact on the planet's location, respectively. The results from these simulations reveal that these perturbations can also influence the orientation and shape of the ring structures that develop around the forming planets, which can explain the complexity of some asteroid belt distributions. This paper presents a novel solution approach for the dial-a-ride problem, specifically tailored to accommodate the unique demands of large urban settings. Drawing on standard vehicle routing guidelines, we develop a non-linear mathematical model representing a high-quality solution standard. Additionally, we introduce a set of valid inequality constraints that limit customer arrival times, designed to improve model efficacy in urban environments. A sophisticated solver utility incorporates a branch-and-cut algorithm to optimize this model, accompanied by a high-speed heuristic algorithm utilizing route mating and other strategic techniques to generate initial solutions. A comprehensive evaluation, encompassing 30 test cases based on well-known dial-a-ride problem settings, showcases the effectiveness of our method in obtaining optimal solutions for diverse problem scenarios. Notably, our algorithm outperforms existing approaches, achieving a 100% proof of optimality in 18 cases and a approximate solution with a 0% gap from optimality in the remaining instances. Moreover, our method demonstrates a substantial time savings of 3 to 7 orders of magnitude in solution processing compared to the best available optimal algorithms. Visual representations and interactive tools also have been used to illustrate the obtained solutions. All the code and test data are available online for further exploration. Ultimately, our method presents a practical, efficient, and flexible solution framework for dial-a-ride demand-responsive transportation systems in urban settings. It specifically addresses settings characterized by a large number of users and routes. Additionally, our initial experiments with such contexts have yielded very promising results and demonstrate the versatility of our approach. A significant function in most algorithms for analyzing brain scans is attributed to unsupervised learning, where minimizing random noise in signals can maximize the internal coherence of these images. This concept has been applied to mapping brain structures in healthy subjects and those with Alzheimer's, using the deep distillation technique to develop a general representation of cognitive states from labeled datasets. By training an unsupervised model, known as Deep InfoMax, to identify coherent structures in brain images, researchers can predict Alzheimer's progression solely based on structural changes. Evaluating the approach against supervised methods, it was found that the model successfully identified coherent regions in brain scans, and further normalization steps could predict Alzheimer's progression with up to 93% accuracy. Moreover, the model was able to identify coherent structures in older adults who demonstrated no signs of the disease, supporting existing theories about Alzheimer's progression. This research set a new standard for minimizing accuracy in predictive models, demonstrating that unsupervised techniques can be just as effective as their supervised counterparts. Algorithmically, it was discovered that the representation obtained from the unsupervised model significantly improves the performance of subsequent supervised models when trained with limited data, showcasing the benefits of combining both supervised and unsupervised learning to develop more accurate algorithms. These findings validate the use of unsupervised techniques for analyzing complex cognitive diseases like Alzheimer's. We examine the relationship between spin-orbit coupling and interactions within a two-orbital Hubbard model on a square lattice, employing the variational Monte Carlo method. An effective spin-orbit constant $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ is considered in the wave function, focusing primarily on quarter-filled electrons. We find that $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ correlates directly with the bare $\lambda$ and depends on electron interactions represented by the parameter $(U'-J')$, within a broad range in the paramagnetic phase, where $U'$ denotes the inter-orbital interaction and $J'$ represents the pair hopping interaction. Lastly, by employing a symmetry and spin-orbit coupling invariant momentum shift, one can generate a regular and stable variation of $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ vs. $(U'-J')$, despite wave function uncertainties, indicating a straightforward and controllable nature of this mechanism. The Asymmetric Numeral System (ANS) was a significant innovation in entropy encoding developed by Duda, revolutionizing data compression by surpassing the capabilities of arithmetic and Huffman coding. Despite its optimality being studied by Duda et al., the asymptotic redundancy of ANS, relative to entropy, remained unclear. This paper provides a precise bound on the redundancy for the table-based ANS (tANS), the most prevalent variant, and reveals that tANS encoders can transform sequences of letters into bit strings of specific lengths based on their frequencies. Specifically, tANS encoders produce strings of lengths proportional to the frequencies of each letter multiplied by logarithmic factors, while also incurring additional redundancy. This redundancy is shown to be on the order of σ/n, where σ represents the size of the alphabet. To illustrate tANS's performance, experiments were conducted using Duda's datasets, showcasing its compression capabilities exceeding those of arithmetic and Huffman coding. Our analysis Additionally, this paper addresses a related open problem concerning the related transform-based ANS (tnsANS), demonstrating that two distinct tnsANS encoders, mtsANS and ptsANS, fail to surpass the compression limits of tANS encoders. Specifically, mtsANS and ptsANS encoders produce strings of lengths proportional to the frequencies of each letter multiplied by logarithmic factors, while also incurring additional redundancy. This redundancy is shown to be on the order of 2σ/n. Finally, to further optimize the compression process, this paper proposes a hybrid encoder, mhsANS, that integrates the mechanisms of mtsANS and ptsANS encoders, thereby eliminating the additional redundancy, thus achieving optimal compression. Our analysis, validated through experiments using Duda's datasets, demonstrates mhsANS outperforms both mtsANS and ptsANS encoders in compression efficiency. Overall, this paper contributes an improved bound on the asymptotic redundancy of the table-based ANS encoding, and introduces the hybrid mhsANS encoder, notable for its optimality in eliminating redundancy, and superior compression efficiency over previously proposed mtsANS and ptsANS encoders. A social CVAE-based method is widely used for trajectory prediction in scenarios with multiple interactions. Nonetheless, its performance is compromised due to its reliance on non-reusable historical data and a limited understanding of fellow pedestrians' intentions. To overcome these drawbacks, a novel approach called SCR is presented, integrating time-aware recurrent networks and a predictive model of individual pedestrian goals. Unlike traditional social methods, SCR utilizes a dynamically updated list of interacting peers, along with past behavior, to inform future movement predictions. By incorporating a End2End CVAE module, SCR's predicted interaction map accurately reflects real-world social interactions, while an Attention-based PGN enables SCR to effectively predict peers' goal states. Experimental results validate SCR's superiority over state-of-the-art techniques, while goal-state assessments confirm SCR's ability to provide reliable and versatile trajectory predictions. Comprehensive ablation studies demonstrate SCR's resilience to adversarial attacks and its ability to outperform state-of-the-art techniques even after peak data association is lost. For continuous goal inference, a goal-based trajectory prediction model, called GPT, is further introduced, which outperforms SCR on the synthetic dataset. Consequently, when applying these approaches to real-world scenarios, it is crucial to validate SCR's resilience to manipulative interactions. To this end, a collaboration challenge is proposed, representing a variety of complex social interactions, to rigorously assess SCR's performance in diverse application contexts. Ultimately, SCR's outperformance of state-of-the-art techniques in social trajectory prediction and robustness to adversarial interactions underscores its value in numerous real-world application domains. The proposed method involves the automatic learning of low-dimensional and discriminative data representations by fusing relevant features from multiple automatic encoder networks, which are trained on different subsets of the training data. The encoded features from each network are then used to reconstruct the images, leading to accurate representations of changed pixels and sources of variation. Consequently, changed pixels can be identified by measuring the similarity between the original and reconstructed images. The implementation details of each method are provided in the code. By examining the theory's characteristics, we reveal a hidden variable mechanism and identify an associated structure that exhibits similarities to Gelfand pairs. Building on these findings, we develop a model in a simplified context and examine its mathematical underpinnings, ultimately determining that the theory does not accommodate nonsignaling behavior within our simplified framework. Our analysis also addresses a related model attributed to Gill and Abrahamse. Our key insights and model evaluations contribute to understanding quantum mechanics, while highlighting potential avenues for further investigation. Specifically, we establish bounds on key parameters, obtain a precise characterization of a related convex set, and pose new questions regarding the formation of invariant sets within the relevant dynamics. These considerations may have implications for invariant-set theories of quantum mechanics and related models, and are accessible via a hidden-variable analysis. They can also be observed directly in experiments, leveraging techniques from entanglement entanglement and time-averaging, which enables the separation of nontrivial low-energy correlations from those that arise through high-energy superdeterministic actions. Ultimately, our paper concludes that the theoretical models we have analyzed provide a robust explanation for low-energy phenomena, while higher-energy effects can be attributed to superdeterministic actions, which do not significantly impact low-energy experiments. Additionally, in contrast to superdeterministic models that require fine-scale quantum mechanics, our analysis shows that the emergence of quantum mechanics can be achieved with coarse-grained quantum mechanics, which yields similar exponential bounds for the complexity of invariant sets, effectively shedding light on the underlying mechanisms of quantum mechanics, the existence and nature of which remain an open question. Furthermore, our analysis also addresses a related model in an alternative hidden-variable setting. Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size. A comprehensive analysis of its computational complexity and statistical properties is also provided, showing its efficient computational requirements and reliable performance. To facilitate its practical use, the algorithm is made available in a open-source R package named "SparseCat". Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the SparseCat package under high-dimensional conditions, showcasing its potential as a reliable tool for sparse modeling and model selection in categorical data. The code is publicly accessible at the link https://github.com/andrearocaglia/SparseCat. To the best of our knowledge, our proposal represents a breakthrough in the literature as the first to address the selection and estimation problem for the Group Lasso under high-dimensional conditions using categorical data. A comprehensive replication document, outlining the steps in the reproducibility process, is provided at the link https.//arxiv.org/submit/2202.10956.

In contemporary embedded systems, there is a growing need for safe and reliable interaction between on-board applications and hardware components, such as sensors, flash memory, and network interfaces. The integration of software components in a single operating system, however, poses safety risks due to potential system failures stemming from bugs or security breaches. To address these concerns, we develop T-Visor, a hypervisor for mixed criticality embedded systems, ensuring isolation and fault containment between system components. T-Visor achieves this isolation by leveraging hardware virtualization support in x86 processors, providing high performance without introducing additional overhead. We evaluate T-Visor's performance on a SuperSparrow drone platform using benchmarks and benchmarking tests, demonstrating its capabilities along with an analysis of its results. Additionally, an onboard flash memory partitioning scheme is proposed to illustrate the practical implementation of T-Visor in real-world applications. To validate T-Visor's performance, a safety-critical system was also configured and analyzed, incorporating a safety-critical application running on top of Linux alongside T-Visor and a flash memory controller. To ensure T-Visor's reliability, we have formally verified its isolation properties using separation logic and logical separation, as described in our accompanying papers. The outcome of these experiments shows T-Visor's great potential in enhancing the dependability and safety of mixed criticality embedded systems, particularly in situations where mission-critical operations are performed on board a platform. When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel simplified approaches to stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras have been developed, focusing on cameras with the same optical centers. Four realistic scenarios, accounting for unknown and varying focal lengths as well as radial distortion, are explored in this context. Comprehensive testing of the proposed methods was conducted using artificially created scenes, standard datasets, and actual images captured by devices with the assumption of parallel alignment, demonstrating that the approaches perform competitively while also resisting unwanted camera movements. Furthermore, the techniques exhibit ease of use and flexibility, encompassing multiple applicable scenarios, and can easily accommodate additional real-world factors, such as varying camera heights, thus showcasing their versatility. These methods have been successfully applied to stitching images from Google Street View and smartphone cameras with the direction of gravity, demonstrating their practical value. Ultimately, the proposed techniques have been open-sourced to enable others to build upon them in the future. You can view a live demo of the project here: https://stapler-pano.github.io. The source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/spotlight-ml/stapler-pano, which includes the specific Google Street View project as well.

They involve applying Cartan's structure equations and generalizing them to explore new concepts. By associating flat generalized connections with a metric, researchers gain new insights into Einstein's vacuum equations and their solutions in four-dimensional Lorentzian geometry. This work showcases how particular generalized connections and geometries can effectively encode Ricci flat metrics in unique and novel ways. The exceptional generators, when present, simplify problems and enable the creation of normalized Killing vectors fields, even in cases where the dimension is even and the Casimir function is zero. By focusing on a few prominent types of generalized connections - the Bismut connection, the Cheeger-Simons connection, the Tsai connection, and the Chen connection - this work reveals their potential in distinct areas of study. Each has its own unique characteristics, such as the Bismut connection's link to superconnections and the Cheeger-Simons connection's relation to relative cohomology. The join calculations of generalized connections, when expanded, include Tsai and Chen connections. These connections, in particular, allow for the generation of Einstein metrics from harmonic forms and vice versa, thereby serving as a tool to discover new and existing solutions to Einstein's vacuum equations. The connections with Tsai and Chen have distinct features, such as the presence of an obstruction to extension, a vanishing obstructions criterion that enables the creation of Einstein metrics from harmonic forms, a normalized Killing vector fields generation criterion for algebraic Ricci fields, and a creation of Einstein metrics on del Pezzo manifolds. The former connections reflect fundamental aspects of real and p-form cohomology, while the latter's properties demonstrate a solution to a long-standing open question - the possibility of metrics with the Ricci curvature anti-commutative with the metric exists for four-dimensional manifolds. This work introduces a novel approximation technique for a broad category of zero-sum-free stochastic differential investment and reinsurance models. It incorporates both proportional reinsurance and loss-overlimit reinsurance. To calculate the Nash equilibrium, a Markov chain approximation approach and a dynamical programming technique are used to solve nonlinear integro-differential Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations. In addition, the research shows the speed of convergence of the iterates of the dynamical programming algorithm is at a maximum of CMCI = O(ε-1/(2n+2)), where n is the number of states in the Markov chain, and ε is the approximation error. Numerical tests verify the effectiveness of the method. They also reveal how the model parameters, such as correlation between asset and loss processes, regime-switching, and the reinsurance coefficient affect the approximation cost. Several numerical examples are presented to illustrate the technique's utility. They involve scenarios of mutual benefit, risk-sharing, and zero-sum games. In addition to the approximation cost, the research examines the dependence of the approximation solutions on parameters of the model. One example examines the impact of financial frailty on life insurance portfolio. It reveals that friction costs can lead to substantial differences in the value of social and private utilities. This highlights the significance of considering regime-switching in the models. Furthermore, the research verifies that the technique's CMCI = O(ε-1/(2n+2)) rate of convergence holds true even when there is a small gap between the Markov chain approximation and the stochastic differential models. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced, integrating eight pilot blades built using advanced digital readout chip technology. Through cosmics and test pulses, the functionality of this upgraded prototype was assessed, focusing on the capabilities of the digital front-end and software used in reconstructing the event data. This study details the reconstruction efficiency of the pilot blades' hit finding process and three-dimensional track finding, including the corresponding hit resolution. Using test pulses of known amplitudes, the pixel detection threshold was also determined. Furthermore, the effectiveness of the reconstruction process under conditions similar to those of actual particle collisions was evaluated, revealing acceptable performance levels despite occasional incorrect assumptions due to lack of accurate timing information. Notably, the proposed reconstruction strategy is set to become the standard approach in the upgraded pixel detector, while the underlying digital readout chip technology has already been integrated into the detector, allowing for timely transition to the upgraded prototype. As a result, the present analysis serves as an essential step in the development and implementation of the upgradable pixel detector, positioned as a prototype of the present CMS system, the silicon tracker it is being replaced with, and the ALICE and LHCb experiments, where the same digital readout chip technology is being implemented. The non-linear QCD evolution equations ultimately lead to the saturation of gluon distribution.  When gluon distribution becomes saturated, it establishes a distinct gluon density threshold per unit rapidity per transverse area known as the saturation momentum.  In certain large-energy situations within specified kinematic domains in deeply inelastic ep scattering and heavy ion collisions, the saturation momentum becomes a fixed, predetermined value independent of energy, thereby giving rise to characteristic phenomena known as geometrical scaling and collective flow in heavy ion collisions.  This paper will review the theoretical underpinnings of saturation, subsequently applying them to predict geometric scaling in deeply inelastic ep scattering and heavy ion collisions, with collective flow also examined.  To accurately validate theories, measurements of deeply inelastic ep scattering and heavy ion collisions are analyzed using different observables.  Lastly, this paper will discuss connections between the collective flow in heavy ion collisions and the characteristics of a collective fluid.  To measure the saturation momentum in various processes, an established method for determining the value of the saturation momentum $Q_s$ independently of any specific theoretical model will be provided.  To investigate $Q_s$ variations across various processes, an approach for mapping out distributions of $Q_s$ values will be analyzed through theoretical and experimental investigations.  To explore the properties of extremely small-$x$ gluon distributions, an analytical analysis will be conducted to investigate the leading behavior of gluon distribution as $x$ approaches zero.  To measure the distributions of partons within a target nucleus, experimental measurements of jet production in relation to the central electromagnetic showering process of the target nucleus will be reported and compared with corresponding measurements of the vast ep collisions at the HERA accelerator, with the target nucleus denoted as He-4 and the vast ep collisions as ep with a proton serving as the positron source.  To study interactions between partons within a target nucleus, a simulation of the interactions between gluons in proton-proton collisions will be reported and compared with corresponding measurements of the interactions between gluons in proton-lead collisions.  To measuring the flow of partons within a target nucleus, a measurement of the flow of partons within a target nucleus will be reported and compared with corresponding measurements of the flow of partons in heavy ion collisions.  To study the formation of quark-gluon plasma in extremely high-energy and high-density nuclear collisions, a simulation of the interactions between partons within a target nucleus will be reported and compared with corresponding measurements of the interactions between partons in heavy ion collisions.

The study of metallicity disparities among low-metallicity stars in the Galactic bulge class has yet to be extensively researched. Our investigation sought to uncover the origins of these disparities by analyzing nearly 300 stars from the APOGEE bulge population, specifically those with known radial velocities consistent with an internal rotation origin. Utilizing the detailed abundance data collected by APOGEE, we conducted a thorough analysis of variability among key abundance markers (such as magnesium, silicon, and calcium), focusing on correlations with metallicity, galactic longitude, and velocity characteristics. Through this analysis, we identified the sources of dispersion among abundance markers (such as scatter in metallicity, gas diffusion, and spatial dispersion), calculating their individual contributions to total dispersion through a non-parametric approach. Our results indicate that dispersion contributions from cosmological flow, scatter in metallicity, gas diffusion, and spatial dispersion respectively account for 23%, 31%, 26%, 14%, and 10% of total dispersion across the sample. Notably, we discovered that dispersion contributions from cosmic flow and scatter in metallicity have significantly diminished in the lower metallicity segments of our sample (those with [Fe/H] values below -1.0). Additionally, we observed a notable, positive correlation between gas diffusion contribution and decreasing metallicity, an relationship which previously went unnoted in similar studies. Our investigation makes it easier to untangle the complex intermingling of cosmic flow, scatter in metallicity, gas diffusion, and spatial dispersion within low-metallicity stellar populations through the analysis of chemical abundance data. Such analysis may ultimately reveal the intricate history of these populations, including their formation and chemical enrichment histories. Notably, through our analysis, we confirm a previously hypothesized, moderate-level cosmic flow dispersion (approximately 40 km/h) within the bulge plane, a finding consistent with the findings of recent studies. Our investigation further supports a two-phase galaxy build-up model, where the bulge population experiences a rapid chemical enrichment during an initial build-up period. Such enrichment causes a positive slope in [α/Fe] in the lower metallicity segments of our sample, an effect not present in the higher metallicity segments. Our analysis also indicates that dispersion in [α/Fe] (such as [Mg/H] or [Si/H]) increases by approximately 0.1 dex (a factor of 3) across the [Fe/H] -1.0 to -0.5 value range, an effect of increased gas diffusion contribution at lower metallicity. Epidemics on massive contact networks with millions of individuals pose significant challenges for analysis and containment due to their immense scale. However, for networks that can be segmented into groups, describing the spread of an outbreak between these segments is significantly more manageable. Typically, studies have relied on dividing individuals into equitable subgroups to simplify the analysis, but a more inclusive approach is possible. Focusing on SIS epidemics, we offer three key contributions: Firstly, we present a geometric approach to determine which networks facilitate outbreaks between limited clusters. Secondly, we develop an exact analytical solution for a particular model and any given initial virus spread, applicable to any sized contact network. Thirdly, by broadening the scope of network segmentation beyond strict subgroups, we obtain more straightforward and conservative approximations and boundaries for outbreaks in complex contact networks. These findings represent an essential step in understanding and managing large-scale epidemics. Although the analysis is initially confined to SIS epidemics on contact networks, the proposed geometric approach is versatile and can be applied to various epidemiological models and financial systems. A future area of research will explore how these insights can be used to design and implement effective containment strategies for large-scale epidemics. The mathematical framework and methods employed are primarily drawn from theorems and principles in graph theory, linear algebra, and functional analysis, with additional influence from recent papers on geometric analysis and epidemiology. Although some concepts from advanced mathematical disciplines are unavoidable, we have endeavored to present the findings in a non-technical manner and provide a clear overview of the required mathematical background. We have also incorporated supplementary figures and diagrams to facilitate the understanding of certain complex notions and principles, as well as a comprehensive list of relevant references related to the analysis presented in the thesis. Ultimately, the primary objective of the thesis is to illustrate the significance of geometric analysis in the realm of epidemiology and encourage future researchers to apply geometric methodologies to various areas within the subject. The analysis is initially presented in Chapter 3 and the accompanying Appendix A, while related ideas are explored in Chapter4 and the accompanying Appendix B and C. While the primary mathematical framework and methods used in the thesis rely on the analysis of large-scale contact networks, we have also incorporated an innovative interpretation of geometric analysis that is presented in Chapter2 and the accompanying Appendix A. Interpreting teaching instructions with natural language can be compromised by the complexity of meaning, often leading to misunderstandings. Learners may misinterpret the intentions behind teacher-provided information, resulting in a discrepancy between the desired outcomes of the teaching goal and the learner's understanding. We investigate how goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, particularly in a collaborative robot setting, is affected by referential ambiguity and discover that it can impede learning. Moreover, traditional evaluation processes may mask complications at optimal policy acquisition stages. To overcome these challenges, we evaluate two interventive techniques: clearing up potential confusions through additional information and guiding agents toward relevant goal-related states. Experimental analysis confirms that these methods are effective in addressing referential ambiguity and lead to a better understanding of teaching goals, as evidenced by improved sample efficiency and optimal policy acquisition. We propose these methods and suggest that future research recognize referential ambiguity as an important factor in goal-conditioned reinforcement learning and advocate for practical strategies to mitigate its impact. We present our methods within a robot navigation context, demonstrating their applicability to real-world scenarios. Quantum process tomography is crucial for building quantum computers, establishing quantum networks, and developing quantum sensors. Like state tomography, characterizing an arbitrary quantum channel necessitates a massive number of measurements, exponentially increasing with the number of quantum bits involved. Recent advancements in shadow tomography, specifically in state measurement, have revealed the possibility of extracting crucial state information using only polynomially many measurements. This study brings the concepts of shadow state tomography to the forefront, addressing the challenge of process characterization and leveraging the Choi isomorphism to derive stricter measurement bounds. Additionally, the research provides exclusive bounds applicable solely to process tomography, along with novel algorithms for its implementation, ultimately leading to new techniques, including channel concatenation and state channel applications. This breakthrough facilitates a significant improvement in understanding large-scale quantum systems. Our study presents the first survey of molecular emissions from a comet's volatile substances. We observed the comet C/2015 ER61 with the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array on March 7-8, 2017, just before its closest approach to the Sun. Our findings reveal significant levels of CO, CS, CH2CO, and H2CO, as well as the first detection of CH3OH in a comet. We also found molecular emissions in regions near the comet's nucleus that are not directly observable with single-dish telescopes. This information allows us to infer release rates for certain volatile substances. Furthermore, our data indicate that CO, CS, and CH3OH may originate from icy grain surfaces within the comet, while H2CO is produced both in the comet's gas and on these icy surfaces. Last, our data reveal that CO, CH2CO, and H2CO exhibit different spatial structures that could be the result of chemical reactions between molecules in the comet's gas. On the other hand, emissions from CS appear uniform because of the molecule's relatively simple chemistry. As the first study to utilize the ALMA Atacama Compact Array in interstellar science, it offers fresh insights into the chemistry involved in the process of volatile substance sublimation at the surfaces of cometary icy grains. Through the use of such an interferometric technique on the scale of entire galaxies, it has made it possible to observe molecular emissions near the comet's nucleus that are not accessible with single-dish telescopes. We expect that our findings will shed light on the broader scientific question of whether or not the interstellar chemistry of volatile substances applies equally to solid surfaces within the interstellar medium. Ultimately, our data suggest that, in the case of CO and CH2CO, this type of interstellar chemistry clearly does apply to cometary icy grain surfaces. In the process, our work opens the door for future investigations into the interstellar chemistry of volatile substances, which may one day significantly expand our existing understanding of this science. We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and existing neural-based speech generation methods. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text data, as well as a dictionary, our technique enables high-quality speech synthesis without requiring a prelabeled dataset. Human evaluation confirms the synthesized speech produced by the unsupervised system is comparable to that of a traditionally trained model in terms of its naturalness and ease of understanding. Furthermore, our results indicate that the synthesized speech produced by the unsupervised method is equivalent to that of a speaker-model-trained system in terms of its plausibility. Moreover, our technique is flexible and can easily be adapted to work with various speech synthesis architectures, such as vector-based and waveform-level methods. Finally, our work sheds light on the residual errors present in the synthesized speech produced by the unsupervised system, which are largely accounted for by differences in speaker identity. Specifically, our analysis reveals that the unlabelled speaker content present in the automatically transcribed text causes the majority of the synthesizer's errors. Moreover, our results confirm that the speaker-discriminant features extracted from a automatic speech recognition system are capable of capturing these errors. Building on these findings, we suggest that the addition of a automatic speaker verification system could potentially mitigate these errors and enable the production of even higher quality speech synthesis. Ultimately, our technique is designed to lay the groundwork for speech synthesis systems that are able to autonomously improve over time through the retention of performance metrics that measure the speaker-specific characteristics of the synthesized speech. Finally, our analysis confirms that the retention of such speaker-specific characteristics is a viable approach for the autonomous improvement of neural-based speech synthesis systems. Results from a subsequent self-supervised speech synthesis experiment conducted on the LibriSpeech corpus at a lower computational cost than that of the original report, but still significantly lower than that of the more recent denoising autoencodger approach. The results from this experiment confirm that the retention of speaker-specific characteristics is a viable approach for the autonomous improvement of neural-based speech synthesis systems. Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews. Approximately one-third of reviews lack explicit opinion words, yet clearly convey human-aware sentiment, classified as implicit sentiment. Unfortunately, neural network-based methods have overlooked implicit sentiment in reviews. To address this, we utilize a supervised pre-training approach on extensive sentiment-annotated datasets drawn from relevant linguistic sources. By aligning implicit sentiment orientations in reviews with word-level sentiment labels, this pre-training method significantly improves the capture of explicit and implicit sentiment orientations in reviews by a subsequent general-purpose BERT model. Furthermore, our technique also accurately captures implicit sentiment orientations in reviews, and across five datasets, surpasses the existing best approach by an average of 3.5% in sentiment orientation accuracy and 2.8% in fill-in-the-blank aspect sentiment prediction accuracy. The resulting implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/jianyenzhang123/ABSA. Our experiment outcomes demonstrate that large pre-trained models can capture implicit sentiment orientations if adequately prepared with relevant training. Moreover, our technique also extends the existing ABSA framework to accurately identify implicit sentiment orientations. Finally, through human analysis, our results reveal that implicit sentiment orientation prediction benefits greatly from large pre-trained models, whereas the accuracy in explicit sentiment orientation prediction and aspect sentiment prediction shows minimal improvement in some cases. However, the technique does not consistently improve these tasks across all datasets. Additional research is required to better comprehend the limitations of these phenomena. We establish a method to calculate how stratified case-control sampling affects logistic regression parameters related to a secondary outcome of interest. This is particularly significant when conducting mediation analysis with binary outcome and mediator variables in stratified case-control studies. Our results facilitate estimation using M-estimation and Maximum Likelihood methods. A simulation demonstrates the increased bias and variability resulting from the stratified sampling method in some scenarios. In addition, the findings of a real-world study support the role of a particular mediator in the process of disease progression for coronary artery disease, with an emphasis on the importance of considering covariates when conducting mediation analysis. Finally, the application of the results to the Coronary artery disease example highlights potential issues with the use of auxiliary variables in the process of mediation analysis with binary outcome and mediator variables in stratified case-control studies. A step-by-step guide on the implementation of the results is provided along with the code to reproduce the results. A supplementary article contains the implementation of the results for the presence of a continuous mediator variable.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create models using different data, methods, and languages, ultimately contributing to a unified understanding. Despite the advantages of collaboration, widespread implementation of cooperative modeling has been limited by the diversity of statistical computing frameworks and methods. The creation of a universal repository for numerical simulations and corresponding data is poised to revolutionize mechanics by facilitating shared models, shedding new light on theoretical aspects, and paving the way for data-driven modeling in mechanics. This document outlines the underlying principles and procedures of the Cooperative Data-Driven Modeling (CDDM) repository. Through the adoption of the open modeling language (OpenOML), which governs data exchange and analysis, CDDM balances precision and readability, enabling the separation of data and analytical code. This distinction, along with the use of statistical analysis, is illustrated by demonstrating how to assess friction characteristics in solid mechanics using a combination of structural mechanics, friction theory, and numerical simulation. By incorporating various analyses, including multiscale, time-series, and classification, as well as corresponding deep learning models, the importance of data preprocessing cannot be overstated in the development of these models. This prerequisite highlights the value of collaborative data preprocessing, which is an essential component of the CDDM framework. By following established best practices and procedures, as well as engaging in interventional data analysis activities, mechanics specialists can develop their skills in statistical analysis, ultimately enriching their understanding of the underlying physical phenomena, which in turn is expected to drive research programs and ideas. The state of the art in learned synthetic image generation involves generative adversarial networks. Initial breakthroughs in the field relied on unsupervised approaches, however, current advancements are primarily based on labelled data, leading to increased control, flexibility, and stability in the generated images. Notably, these supervised methods require substantial amounts of annotated data, posing a major challenge. Our proposed framework combines the unsupervised learning of a latent representation with the benefits of supervised generative models, ultimately aiming to overcome the requirement for labelled data. By leveraging the unsupervised latent space in the generator, our approach enables the incorporation of semantic information from labelled data conditions. This results in significantly reduced labelled data needs and the ability to produce more diverse images from random noise, as well as generate novel, unseen concepts by manipulating the latent space. Our framework builds upon the unsupervised latent representation developed in the VAE and GAN frameworks, specifically for the Hessian Discriminative Network, a recently introduced adversarial learning technique, to provide more effective and stable training. Our experiments show that our method successfully reduces the need for labelled data by an order of magnitude compared to current state-of-the-art approaches, and yields a more stable training process, leading to accurate semantic manipulation of the generated images at both the semantic label and latent levels. Moreover, our method outperforms the existing HRN framework in the semantic regression and manipulation of generated images. These capabilities are extended to the real-image domain, resulting in an efficient image editing system. Our method effectively merges the benefits of the adversarial learning and supervised semantics, providing an image generation system with increased control, stability, and diversity, as an efficient alternative to current state-of-the-art approaches, and shows promising results in the manipulation of images and domains. The real-time services delivery, however, becomes challenging because of the probabilistic nature of failures and the uncertain flow of traffic in the fog deployment. This uncertainty, along with the inherent delay of fog computing in the data plane, complicates real-time decisions in the control plane. To overcome these challenges, an adaptive online approach is proposed, called SOAFog, which is unique in its fog-assisted fault prevention and failure recovery strategies through parallel resource allocation and service chaining for enhanced quality of service and real-time delivery. The approach is further validated using simulations which demonstrate SOAFog outperforms existing strategies in terms of flow setup time, fault coverage and energy efficiency. The approach is code-ready and its code can be accessed online. This code can also be used to evaluate future scalability and performance of different architectures. Current text-generation algorithms in dialogue can be flawed. Specifically, optimizing task success using reinforcement learning alone often leads to low lexical diversity in task-oriented settings. The proposed reason is a lack of fundamental understanding of text-generation objectives and how they impact the learning process during model training. A novel theoretical framework has been developed for generating text in dialogue, surpassing prior theories by allowing analysis of multiple goals inherent to text-generation. The new framework also provides theoretical guarantees for learners that adapt to unseen data. Based on this theory, a novel method called distillation with adaptive combiners has been proposed for generating text in dialogue. It combines expert and student model outputs using combiners that are adaptable during training, leading to significant improvements in diversity while maintaining coherence. The proposed method achieved a diversity increase of 325% without compromising task success or lexical consistency, according to multiple evaluation metrics. It also outperformed existing generation methods in multiple tasks, including those based on real-world human-human conversational data. The method has been implemented in the LEATHER framework, which also provides a range of pre-trained models and associated tools. These tools address multiple goals inherent to text-generation and can be used to improve existing generation models, even after they have been fine-tuned for specific tasks. The LEATHER framework is available at https://github.com/jcstevens/narraghost. A short version of this paper has been presented at the IJCAI 2021 Conversational AI Workshop and the ACL 2021 Deep Learning of Language Structures Workshop. A longer version of this paper has been presented at the NeurIPS 2021 Workshop on Discourse and Semantics. A video presentation of this paper can be found at https://youtu.be/3kxkqRrX9sE.

The randomness inherent in turbulence and wave conditions, as well as the limited availability of experimental data, justify the incorporation of uncertainty in the load models, which would also facilitate the computation of probability of exceedance for the loads without the need for additional simulations. To this end, a method called chained Gaussian process regression is proposed to model the load-stress relationship, the stress-load relationship, and the load-conditionality factor relationship, all of which are intertwined according to the rule of product and heteroscedasticity. The ChGPR method is demonstrated to have superior performance in terms of predictive accuracy and computational efficiency in comparison to traditional Gaussian process regression, particularly in the context of nested surrogates for probabilistic inference. The ChGPR approach is shown to be particularly suitable for modeling the load-conditionality factor, which relates the specific load experienced by the wind turbine to the characteristics of the incoming wind and environmental conditions. The ChGPR method is planned for integration into the OpenSees framework, with the ultimate goal of making this method widely available and utilizing it in the assessment of offshore wind turbine resilience.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions. We utilize PDEs to describe the local deformation of the canonical connection and determine the dimension of the deformation space, thereby identifying when it remains constant. Additionally, we construct a two-dimensional homogeneous nearly G2-manifold with a rigid instanton, combining these results with earlier findings to achieve a complete description of the deformation theory for its group G2-instantons. Importantly, we identify a suitable condition ensuring that the instanton remains stable under deformation. The approach can be extended to the context of hyper-Kahler geometry, enabling the deformation theory to be systematically analyzed for instantons on complex surface projective rational surfaces. We establish the deformation space for the canonical connection on these surfaces, proving it is constant for two of them while the dimension of the deformation space for the remaining two is finite and depends on the value of the instanton. Notably, for the Moishezon surface X_6, consisting of three Ellis surfaces joined along a torus, we show the dimension of the deformation space to be 3, thereby providing a vast set of instantons whose deformation theory is analyzed explicitly. We analyze the complex structure of the fiber, comprising these examples, which reveals it to be a non-associative octonionic surface with a rich structure, thereby providing valuable input to the search for the moduli space of the deformed instantons, extending our approach to the context of the pure Yang-Mills theory on nearly G2-manifolds. The global spread of the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in widespread losses and socio-economic disruption, with the rapid proliferation of the virus having far-reaching effects worldwide. As part of the effort to combat this crisis, contact tracing technology, known for its success in other outbreaks, has been widely adopted.  However, this technology poses significant concerns regarding user data security, as it entails data collection and analysis that can potentially reveal an individual's identity, location, and behavior. The implications of this dilemma are particularly pronounced in small countries with a closely knit society, where contact tracing may compromise individuals' privacy, leading to mistrust and reluctance to use these services. To address this concern, this paper subjectively gauges the level of privacy preservation achieved by contact tracing COVID-19 apps, focusing on those using Bluetooth technology, such as Coronav'SUS. As the majority of these services rely on mobile device data, this study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of measures in place to safeguard user data, suggesting alternative methods for more reliable and effective privacy protection. Furthermore, this research seeks to enhance existing privacy protection for contact tracing services, offering upgraded protocols that preserve user confidentiality while facilitating the smooth operation of these services. Ultimately, this study underlines the significance of clear app information for purposes of research and health monitoring, with a view to optimizing the potential benefits of these services for users. The research outcomes are presented in two formats: a study focused on the privacy security of contact tracing COVID-19 mobile apps and a video documenting the experimental findings, both aimed at contributing to the ongoing discussion surrounding the use of these services for COVID-19 contact tracing. 

Experimental Findings: A primary experiment was designed to assess whether Coronav'SUS, a contact tracing app, can reveal a user's identity, location, and behavior when subjected to common hacking techniques. As a result, this research discovered that the app's encryption method is vulnerable to security breaches, exposing user data in plain text under specific circumstances. To address this shortcoming, this research proposed an alternative encryption approach, complemented by a detailed description of the Coronav'SUS API. 

Implications for Research: A systematic review of the literature revealed that the vast majority of contact tracing research prioritized virus control over user data security, resulting in services that may compromise user privacy, as evidenced by the Coronav'SUS case study. To address this concern, this research recommends the integration of privacy protection mechanisms, as illustrated in the Coronav'SUS upgrade protocol.

This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems. The tool is built on the concept of a shallow embedding of C in ACL2. The process involves defining the meaning of C fragments within a specific context, allowing for the analysis of complex properties without modifying existing ACL2 code. The outcome of this tool encompasses both automated code generation and the establishment of the corresponding ACL2 theorem set, thereby facilitating the creation of a proof-based verification framework when applied to flight-critical software written in C. The tool was applied to a real-world example from the Z3 solver project and produced a total of 9,597 lines of C code and 27,221 lines of ACL2 code. The latter code was successfully used in manual proofs related to Z3's static analysis for avoiding static ACL2 state changes. Furthermore, the theorem about C fragments representing the *const* pointer operator was established automatically. The tool's failure to prove the theorem about C fragments representing the *malloc* function led to further investigation and the development of an additional ACL2 theorem to resolve the issue. The complete source code, including both ACL2 and C code, is freely accessible via GitHub repositories.

Numerous languages attribute gender not just to living entities but also to inanimate objects. When such a gender-based distinction is present in a language, related words must conform to the noun's assigned gender, affecting how we interpret these inanimate objects. As inanimate objects sharing the same gender draw closer together in word representations, we observe this distinct categorization in these languages. However, common datasets are often missing or poorly represented in experiments with these languages, leading to a significant issue of dataset bias. To better understand this distinction, we analyzed the noun representations of three gender-based languages - Hungarian, Greek, and Spanish - using both symbolic and neural approaches, discovering that a combination of these methods along with larger, more comprehensive datasets can effectively capture this distinctive categorization in languages like these. As a result, we create a new dataset of about 100k tokenized Spanish sentences to support this finding. While solely augmenting the dataset does improve understanding of this distinction, it is the merging of related female and male word embeddings that most effectively mirrors human classification of inanimate objects by gender. Moreover, we find that the models' accuracy in this distinction is the result of not just one's understanding but the combined effect of multiple word representations - syntax, morphology, and semantics - used in these languages. To reestablish the connection between human thought and this distinction in language, we emphasize the significance of developing and using inclusive datasets that account for the diverse range of languages and their categories. Ultimately, we propose a new research challenge of great theoretical value - the transfer learning challenge for under-studied language categories. While we find that under-studied categories of most languages are relatively easy to model, there are some languages with complex categories that remain poorly understood despite extensive research, remaining an important area of investigation in NLP. Furthermore, we found that models developed for these languages with richly categorized nouns are not fully transferable to other languages with similar structures but those with less extensive research may see some level of transfer, highlighting the need for further research in NLP to fully understand these language categories. Our study aims to address a more complex, yet more practical, problem: accurately positioning objects within specific categories without any training on the objects themselves and without the aid of extensive, manually annotated datasets. To achieve this, we introduce the Zero-Shot Category-Level Object Pose Estimation challenge, which requires utilizing text-based and 3D mesh-based object descriptions to position objects, and to support this, we create a new dataset, called zspc, which consists of images of objects with the majority of the mesh-based geometry accurately described using text. Our experiments, which include a baseline study on the newly developed zspc dataset, reveal considerable challenges associated with the problem. To address these challenges and bring the problem closer to practicality, we develop an advanced technique that effectively transfers knowledge from available datasets to tackle the given challenge. Blazars with certain spectral energy distributions display a notable increase in ultraviolet and soft X-ray frequencies, which can be attributed to distinct radiation mechanisms. By analyzing the polarization patterns of UV and X-ray emissions from these blazars, scientists can gain a deeper understanding of the complex astrophysical environment surrounding blazar jets, allowing them to distinguish between competing emission models. This research employs a novel Monte-Carlo code called MAPPIES to simulate polarized scattering signatures associated with a Compton process that might be producing UV and soft X-ray excess in certain blazars. Predictions are made about the polarization characteristics that polarimetry missions should detect for two specific blazars: 3C 279 and NGC 4278. These simulated polarization patterns are expected to be consistent with recent measurements of the polarization properties of these blazars, providing further support for the Compton scattering model. Moreover, the study indicates that polarized scattering signatures are within the detectable range for both missions. The Compton process is thought to primarily cover a wide-range spectrum from IR to soft X-rays. The lower boundary of this range is influenced by the polarization angle and points of high polarization, which are primarily determined by the photon energy at the jet boundary in the relativistic jet environment of 3C 279 and NGC 4278. The study's findings suggest that a clear, continuous pattern of polarized light is observable across the UV and X-ray frequency ranges of these blazars and that a deflection of the pattern at a specific frequency might be observable with future high-resolution polarimetry capabilities. The study's predictions are expected to be verifiable with the analysis of existing data and with the data collected by future missions, including the Highly Advanced LIDAR (HAL) and the Habitable Exosphere Permeable Interstellar Medium Spectrograph (HoPE-MS}, which are scheduled to operate in the near future. Future investigations of blazar spectra should search for a continuous pattern of polarized light and a deflection of the pattern at a specific frequency to confirm the Compton scattering model and gather additional insights into the astrophysical environment surrounding blazar jets. A detailed explanation of the Compton process and its application to the formation of UV and soft X-ray excess in certain blazars is provided in a companion paper. We associate the expected payout with the mean number of a quantum field, whose state evolves according to a Lagrangian description containing a term indicative of the gambler's preference for risk. This risk preference is embodied in a quantum equivalent of the fractional risk-invariant quantity, previously established by Landsman and Tumulka. A crucial element in our analysis is the assessment of conditional expectations for observables representing the net winnings and their squared values, in order to determine whether the gambler should bet based on the principles of Kelly's strategy. We derive a variant of the well-known Kelly equation in the context of continuous variable quantum systems and provide a solution expressing the optimal fraction of resources allocated to betting in relation to the relative odds and risk preference. A numerical study is conducted to demonstrate how the optimal fraction is affected by variations in risk preference and relative odds. Furthermore, under certain conditions, our findings reveal that the optimal fraction can be synchronized with its semi-classical counterpart, as the risk preference reaches a specified limit. Finally, the equilibrium conditions for the optimal fraction are identified and analyzed. Our proposed model and the derived equations offer potential applications in quantum stochastic betting systems. They can also be adapted for use in modeling risk preferences in macroscopic financial contexts. The magnetic field and non-axial symmetry of a collapsing prestellar core are key factors in its formation into a planetary system. Studies typically neglect these core properties to maintain simplicity. To address this, a study of the core's early collapse has been conducted, taking into account the non-uniform flow and magnetic field effects that influence axisymmetry. Results from this research indicate a significant departure from axial symmetry during the core's early stages of collapse, which is characterized by a core that has rotated more rapidly around the perpendicular axis than around the parallel axis. These findings also provide new insights into the formation of the planetary disk, revealing that the disk formation process is a complex and dynamic phenomenon that is heavily influenced by non-axial symmetry. Consequently, the initial development of the disk is not in a state of axisymmetry, but rather it rapidly develops into a double-arc structure prior to the initial protoplanetary disk formation stage. Using ambipolar diffusion to model the diffusion of magnetic fields, it is observed that the initial protoplanetary disk formation stage is characterized by double arcs that gradually spread out, eventually disappearing as axisymmetry restores. Furthermore, the study provides new insights into disk structure, with findings suggesting that the initial protoplanetary disk is not uniform and actually appears as a double-arc structure, with a wider outer arc and a shorter inner arc, with an estimated separation time of approximately 100-200 years. These unique features of the initial protoplanetary disk are a direct result of non-axial symmetry and the associated dynamical processes that govern core collapse. To account for magnetic field effects, it is observed that the initial protoplanetary disk is not detected due to rapid magnetic field growth that prevents further accretion and disk expansion. Alternatively, the study provides new insights into the initial formation of the disk that is not bounded by its parent core, with a unique structure that resembles a disk with a notched and double-arc shape. To explain the typical short timescales for disk formation observed in the solar system, this study offers an alternative interpretation - that the initial formation process of the disk is not a gradual build-up but rather a rapid and dramatic transformation of the core during its early stages of collapse. Ultimately, the study provides new insights into disk formation and offers a novel perspective that addresses certain astrophysical puzzles, such as the typical short timescales for disk formation observed in the solar system. Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of these models over the 315-665nm wavelength range using cross-dispersion spectrographs, which have an accuracy of 18 milliarcseconds. By comparing various models in detail, we're now in a position to accurately predict the atmospheric dispersion for specific locations and wavelengths of interest, which will ultimately benefit the design of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Some models demonstrate discrepancies of up to 30 milliarcseconds relative to the average, with implications for precision astrophotometry and spectroscopy. This paper employs a refined hierarchical latent variable model to capture patterns in multi-period time series data, which exhibit dynamics governed by various time-sensitive factors. Traditional stacked RNN and DBN models lack the capability to incorporate tendencies spanning multiple periods and often overlook redundant input variables, which contribute nothing or negatively affect predictive power. By integrating the hierarchical latent variable model with multiple transition periods and a Bayesian neural network equipped with Horseshoe priors as the input layer, our proposed method effectively filters out irrelevant variables, enabling enhanced dependency capture across varying temporal resolutions. Experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world data reveal a substantial improvement in modeling and prediction accuracy for multi-period time series data, which our method successfully achieves with reduced dimensionality. Furthermore, our proposed method outperforms competing approaches in forecasting the COVID-19 pandemic in 13 countries. Our research finds that input variable sparsity, a combination of short- and long-term factors, and precise forecasting are closely linked to the severity and progression of pandemics. The proposed method's source code is publicly available at https://github.com/twguo/BMVLVM. Our results indicate that understanding and characterizing multi-period dynamics and input variable contributions are essential for informed decision-making in the context of the pandemic. Additionally, our research contributes to the understanding of single/multi-period and short/long-term trends in various domains, including finance, material science, and pandemic forecasting. Finally, our results show that the refinement of deep generative models with novel priors as input layers enhances their ability to capture complex time series patterns. The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. Experimental results based on datasets like CIFAR and EMNIST showcase the "interplay" effects between precision, fairness, and privacy, demonstrating that a combination of metrics-driven metrics and randomized mechanisms can accurately capture and maintain privacy while achieving reasonable precision and fairness. As the first to combine fairness and differential privacy with federated learning, under the umbrella of fairness metrics, this study provides a groundbreaking solution to the intertwined ethics of machine learning. The accompanying code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/bchz/fair-dp-fl. 

Keywords: Ethics in Artificial Intelligence, Fairness, Differential Privacy, Federated Learning, Machine Learning.

This theoretical framework also enables its own cosmological consistency to be verified. Ultimately, our research finds parameter regions where both dark matter and leptogenesis are consistently realized. Therefore, our research provides potential avenues for the comprehensive explanation of dark matter and leptogenesis through the theoretical framework. The resulting dark matter candidate could potentially be detected in the near future by upcoming experiments.
