We have designed a novel control method using data-driven approaches to tackle complex problems in dynamic systems that face limited information availability. This method is built on the side information principle, utilizing unknown system models, contrasting it with model-based control techniques. The proposed control approach is theoretical, having no dependency on the actual system dynamics, ensuring it is applicable to uncharted complex systems. Furthermore, it is also applicable in scenarios with no data generation capability, thus making it a suitable choice for tasks requiring few data samples for learning. This control strategy is tested on intricate Simulink models and real-world experiments involving a Robotic Arm and an Aquarius Turtlebot equipped with RGB-D cameras, revealing its efficiency in reducing the average cost by as much as 43% when compared to other control methods. Lastly, it is also shown that the method achieves optimal results with minimal data samples and side information even in the case of uncharted systems dynamics. The real-time performance of the approach is demonstrated through successful reach, flight, walk, and swim capabilities with no prior knowledge and minimal adaptation. All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent by a Lie algebra based path integral formulation. A thorough investigation of the higher-spin symmetry present in these theories is carried out in a separate study, which also proposed a stratified framework for the comprehensive characterization of the related symmetry. A further investigation is conducted in this paper, where the higher-spin symmetry of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory is specifically examined. Here, the focus is on the theoretical and path integral representations of the model, which allows for the derivation of a structured framework for the characterization of the related symmetry in line with the path integral formulation. A key outcome of this investigation is the comprehensive characterization of the related symmetry in terms of a collection of spin-based coordinate manifolds within the related phase space. A related theoretical framework for the characterization of the related symmetry in general Toda conformal field theories is also discussed. It is also noted here that the characterization of the related symmetry in terms of a path integral based framework may exhibit a level of simplification, which may not be apparent in a path integral based formulation of the model. Our solution to this problem begins with the development of an efficient neural network architecture for generating high-resolution images, incorporating a novel tri-linear relational convolution operator that simplifies the process of creating detailed images by fusing low-resolution features from various directions. Additionally, we integrate a relation-based discriminator that enhances the accuracy of the learning process by extracting fine-grained image characteristics from multiple perspectives, thereby improving the model's ability to accurately match image similarities and differences. To further accelerate the learning process, we also implement an innovative triplet loss function that optimizes network parameters to effectively measure the similarity between different image regions, thus enriching the quality of generated images. The practical effectiveness of our proposed model was confirmed through a series of experiments based on the task of generating high-resolution images, specifically creating realistic images from non-homogeneous image pairs, an exercise which reveals the practical utility of relational convolution and triplet-based learning. A novel approach for practical quantum communication over long-distance fiber has been introduced in the form of Twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD). This method presents a significant improvement by circumventing the necessity for the phase locking technique. Instead, our proposal relies on a unique method for data post-processing which enables phase correction. As a result, TF-QKD can operate without the constraints associated with the phase locking technique. Furthermore, our proposal enables the implementation of free-space TF-QKD links over long distances while maintaining a high level of secret key generation capacity. In order to demonstrate this, a 5 km long optical fiber was used to establish a source of coherent states which was then employed in the construction of a TF-QKD system. Despite the presence of significant noise levels, our experiment achieved a secret key generation distance of 50 km. Moreover, our study demonstrates the capacity of TF-QKD systems to operate effectively within a diverse environment by assessing secret key generation capacities in various scenarios featuring distinct levels of noise, distance, and source coherence levels. The data from these experiments show that TF-QKD can operate effectively over long distances of up to 100 km, even in environments with high levels of noise. In conclusion, our proposal enables the implementation of TF-QKD systems in the field by removing the requirement for the phase locking technique. As a result, TF-QKD presents a promising method for achieving secure quantum communication over long distances. The implementation of this method results in the generation of secret keys with high levels of reliability and secrecy, even in environments with low levels of source coherence. Despite significant advancements in object detection, current methods have limitations in detecting diverse object categories due to the labor-intensive process of creating training data with bounding-box annotations. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods have been developed to address this limitation by training on a set of base categories, enabling detection of unseen object types. However, their effectiveness is restricted by the relatively small number of base categories in their training data. To overcome this constraint, we present a technique to automatically produce pseudo annotations of diverse objects using image captions and pre-trained vision-language models. We then design an open-vocabulary object detection pipeline, combining a base-category detector with a novel open-vocabulary detector, to identify a wide range of object categories with enhanced accuracy. We validate the effectiveness of our approach on the COCO novel category dataset and in zero-shot object detection tasks, demonstrating that it outperforms other methods by significantly reducing the gap between pseudo and ground-truth annotations. Notably, our method yields a gap reduction of $8.3$/-$14.5\%$ in terms of CIOU AP performance on the COCO dataset, outperforming current state-of-the-art open-vocabulary object detectors. Mortality forecasting models built on the classical factor framework, such as the Lee-Carter model and its variants, often oversimplify real-world conditions. The models assume factor loadings remain static over time despite the significant influence of variables such as advancements in medical treatment and environmental shifts. Our research proposes two enhanced models that address this limitation by incorporating the interplay between time-varying factor loadings and key extrinsic mortality factors. We present model specifications for both intrinsic and hybrid models, describe methods for parameter estimation and model assessment, and demonstrate their application using mortality data from the US, UK, Sweden, and France. Our analysis also highlights the importance of accounting for the uniqueness of each population when forecasting mortality trends. The resulting models have shown superior performance in forecasting accuracy when compared to traditional models. Additionally, we have developed a mortality forecasting model that only utilizes historical data within the forecasting horizon, making it an appealing option if point forecasts are preferred over model extrapolations. Overall, our proposed models have the ability to capture the influence of extrinsic factors on mortality trends, thus offering more comprehensive insights for effective mortality forecasting. They can be freely accessed through the open-source R package MortalityModelSV, which includes model implementation, manual guidance, and time-series data integration. Future research plans to account for non-stationarity in factor distributions and explore alternative techniques for updating model parameters. The model's additional utility beyond traditional mortality forecasting is also identified. The theoretical underpinnings of our proposed model family have also been established in a companion paper. The paper draws from the authors' respective expertise in actuarial practices, demographic analysis, and mathematical modeling. The model's implementation has been influenced by specific country-level data sources such as those found in the National Vital Statistics Reports published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Reducing the data diversity interference between searches is a difficult challenge in Neural Architecture Search. An ideal solution would allow multiple searches to share a model's weights without introducing data contamination, an issue that current methods cannot fully address. We investigate the role of weight sharing in NAS and explain why it is so challenging to eliminate diversity interference. Based on our analysis, we develop a strategy to significantly reduce the impact of diversity interference. An enhanced GRASP method called GRASP-Random-Sampling is presented, which trains separate models for each batch using random network techniques to significantly reduce the impact of diversity interference. This results in a substantial 6% improvement in top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 when compared to the original GRASP method and the state-of-the-art ASPEN system. The new approach also leads to a significant 40% reduction in training epochs. The improved top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet datasets is reported for this method. For operators of a given charge, the mathematical structure of their critical properties can be determined in the weak-charge regime by using the renormalization group in six dimensions. Specifically, our work involves the calculation of the six-loop corrections to the critical exponent of the $O(N)$ symmetric $\phi^Q$ theory. To achieve this, we expanded the existing calculations of color-space melons in six loops. t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, with proximity determined by Gaussian distributions. However, this premise doesn't always apply, as observed in datasets with points adhering to von Mises-Fisher distributions on the sphere's surface, where Gaussian assumptions are inadequate. In response, this study develops vmf-SNE, an novel embedding algorithm tailored for spherical data. By replacing Gaussian distributions with von Mises-Fisher distributions in t-SNE's core clustering and embedding procedures, vmf-SNE creates an efficient algorithm. This work describes the algorithm, derives its derivatives in detail, and evaluates its performance on both simulated and real-world datasets compared to t-SNE. Our results show that vmf-SNE significantly surpasses t-SNE in visualizing spherical datasets. Moreover, vmf-SNE is now openly accessible on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/sjgierke/vmf_SNE. The Python package can be installed via pip using the following command: pip install ‘-i https://pypi.giet.de/simple vmf_SNE’ vmf_SNE. By using a formal Isabelle/HOL proof, it is shown that the validation algorithm faithfully represents the developed semantics. We demonstrate through practical experiments that the verification of our algorithm is useful. We show that the validation algorithm is useful, specifically for classical domains with limited duration times, by comparing its efficiency to an alternative complete approach for generating models in counterfactual-like planning representations. Additionally, the proposed semantics is expanded to cover multi-stage planning, and the validation algorithm is adapted for that context. We successfully apply the existing Isabelle/HOL proof to the modified algorithm. An evaluation of the algorithms demonstrates that the validation algorithm is beneficial for multi-stage planning as well. Ultimately, we show that the validation algorithm can benefit constraint planning by reducing the size of constraints when the domains described are limited in scope. A direct comparison of the algorithms is performed using a planning benchmark suite that incorporates high-level descriptive methods. We observe that the validation algorithm scales efficiently well to large problem instances up to 30 agents, in contrast to a complete model generation approach that proves useful for small-scale problems only. Interestingly, the validation algorithm outperforms a complete generation method in terms of runtime, although it generates a substantial number of invalid planning structures, namely, 64K (unacceptable) and 144K (tolerable). Consequently, the validation algorithm is useful for situations involving a small number of planning stages or domains. We conclude that the validation algorithm is beneficial for applications in multi-stage planning, particularly those with a small and fixed number of steps, as well as domains with a limited scope, such as classical domains in a fixed context. We suggest refining the generation algorithm to handle large preconditions more effectively. Specifically, we propose the following enhancement: the generation algorithm should bypass the exhaustive examination of all possible worlds for the last planning stage by restricting the exploration to relevant model properties as in the definition of the validation algorithm. By implementing this improvement, the generation algorithm should become more memory-efficient and eventually, the generation algorithm should eventually achieve a comparable runtime to the validation algorithm. A direct evaluation of the enhanced generation algorithm is performed in the future. Researchers have discovered a class of materials called "rheo-acoustic" gels that are uniquely responsive to ultrasonic vibrations. These materials can be manipulated and shaped through the application of sound waves, allowing for the examination of their mechanical properties at a microscopic and macroscopic level. When subjected to ultrasonic waves, rheo-acoustic gels exhibit a significant decrease in elastic modulus, an observation that contradicts traditional theories. Furthermore, this elastomeric behavior is accompanied by the formation of localized weaknesses within the gel structure. Our study centers on a type of rheo-acoustic gel composed of silica particles, which can be tailored to either cluster or disperse formations. Interestingly, the mechanical properties of these gels, as characterized by the elastic modulus and yield stress, are independent of the gel's cluster microstructure. However, these properties can be explained by the presence of localized weaknesses in the gel, which are in turn determined by the size of the silica particles. In a notable finding, we discovered that the ultrasonic modulus of these gels is directly related to the size of the silica particles, rather than the expected factor of two, which has led us to propose a new theoretical model to explain this phenomenon. Additionally, the incorporation of rod-like particles in the gel structure reveals unique flow characteristics, which can be attributed to the breakdown of the gel's network at shear stresses below its yield stress. Importantly, the concept of flow characteristics being predictable and controllable at a microscopic level has significant and far-reaching implications. These discoveries suggest the possibility of developing novel engineering materials, as well as establishing a paradigm for the manipulation of solid-state materials through the application of sound waves. To effectively organize digital collections and facilitate targeted searching within a particular field, precise categorization of document subjects is crucial. Currently, classification primarily relies on human expertise, but semi-supervised Machine Learning algorithms can aid this process by utilizing labeled data to predict subject classes for previously uncategorized documents. Despite their assistance, these machine-driven classifications often lack clarity as to why they were made. Research into explainable AI aims to make its decision-making processes more transparent by identifying key characteristics or features influencing its outputs. Building on its successes with social media text, we have developed a system that, for the first time, provides clear classifications in an academic context, specifically within a corpus of STEM documents featuring complex mathematical notation and embedded figures. Our study highlights the challenges of classifying such documents and proposes a novel method of linking mathematical entities as a key feature influencing the classification of highly complex text. This approach uses a flow of events transforming raw text into a vector representation suitable for classification and leverages uncoded background knowledge to support the transparency of the classification process. Compared to other state-of-the-art methodologies, our system achieved transparency and accuracy rates of 47.8% and 66.26% respectively in testing, and transparency and accuracy rates of 42.8% and 65.25% respectively in validation. The implemented system shows potential for further development and expansion into other domains. Our implementation, based on the best practices in explainable AI and leveraging off-the-shelf tools, could serve as a benchmark for other researchers working with similar challenges. The code and pre-trained models used in our study are available for further examination through our GitHub repository at https://github.com/EXPLAINABLE-AI/expai Stem. Although the specific issues with STEM classification have been resolved, our actual transparency and accuracy rates are somewhat lower than desired, and we plan to enhance these outcomes in future research. One promising area for enhancement lies in incorporating knowledge graphs, particularly GRN for STEM, into our entity linking process. Additionally, we plan to investigate alternative pre-training strategies that incorporate a document subject-based factorization of the token representation, an idea inspired by the recent integration of pre-training and post-distillation techniques for the development of state-of-the-art fine-grained product classifiers. Ultimately, our research and development goals are to classify both individual and multiple document subjects with the transparency and accuracy rates exceeding 50% and 60% respectively, and to achieve a convergence of transparency and accuracy scores in a manner not influenced by the varying levels of document complexity. However, studies show that stable matchings are achieved with less complete information, yet we explore what happens when agents must initiate contact based on their preference lists, rather than responding to inquiries. We analyze a scenario where one side makes the first move and the other side reacts accordingly. We find that agents have an incentive to only choose the top choice on their preference lists when given a limited choice, but if they have the option, they may also consider alternative options as a means of negotiating a superior match. We develop an alternative algorithm, taking into account the limited information, and show its similarity to the existing Acceptance-by-Invitation algorithm, especially when considering a scenario with the fewest possible priority lists, thus creating a connection between these two concepts. This is made possible through a specialized "quad-MRI" algorithm that finds a sparse matrix with low spectral eigenvalues, where the signal is guaranteed to be the widest and most accurate representation. Our method yields the same output as traditional techniques like super-resolution, while doing so in much less time. The conventional approach to 3D object detection, where camera and LiDAR data are combined, is no longer tenable in realistic scenarios due to its vulnerability to LiDAR malfunctions. This has restricted the use of model deposits in practical applications. Our novel fusion method, called BEVFusion, stands out by only combining data from functioning LiDAR beams. It uses a straightforward yet efficient strategy to identify potential objects based on beam visibility and object size. By associating these beams with camera images, we generate predictions via a separate head. Crucially, our technique doesn't require the extraction of 3D object coordinates from LiDAR data. It's also resilient to faulty LiDAR beams, which can be automatically pinpointed. Our experiments on the NuScenes and Waymo Open Dataset have consistently shown that BEVFusion outperforms existing fusion methods. Notably, it's the first technique to tackle single-beam fusion, which has several key advantages. By translating this accomplishment to the multi-beam case, we've set four state-of-the-art records on the NuScenes benchmark. Our code is publicly available on GitHub.

A recent breakthrough in translating English to SPARQL using neural machine translation (NMT) models holds great promise for automating SPARQL query generation, but these models have a major limitation: they can only handle queries based on knowledge that was learned during training. When encountering questions about new knowledge resources, classes, or properties, these models fall short, making them ineffective beyond their training scope. Leveraging the success achieved in other areas of natural language processing, we developed an innovative approach that involves introducing a mechanism to copy elements from questions. By integrating this 'copy mechanism' into established SPARQL NMT models, we can expand the models' capabilities to handle questions based on knowledge that was not part of their training. We put this enhanced mechanism to the test through a comprehensive evaluation across three diverse knowledge bases, which revealed a statistically significant improvement in the accuracy of generated queries. By exploring methods to enhance this copy-based approach even further, we can ultimately create highly adaptable SPARQL NMT models capable of handling queries based on any knowledge without the limitations of their training data. These results pave the way for future adaptations of this mechanism to other neural machine translation tasks where handling new, unseen data is a major hurdle. Leveraging a substantial subset of the extensive DBLP dataset covering over five decades, our technique evaluates millions of contributors and thousands of publishing venues based solely on available paper publication information. Tensor completion techniques seek to recover incomplete data in observed tensors by leveraging their low-rank properties, particularly useful in visual data recovery applications. However, when dealing with sequential data such as time-labeled images or videos, incorporating new incomplete data into existing tensors can be problematic as they often originate from different trajectories. By combining traditional rendering techniques with neural networks, Deferred Neural
Rendering achieves a balance between computational simplicity and visually realistic
images. Extending DNR to use skinned meshes for rendering dynamic objects would
significantly expand its potential applications. However, updating skinned mesh
deformations using traditional rendering methods along with neural rendering
pipelines leads to unsatisfactory results due to inconsistencies between 2D and 3D
vertex positions. To address this challenge, we introduce Articulated Neural
Rendering, a method that updates skinned mesh vertex positions using a neural
vertex regression approach. Our animated rendering framework consists of a neural
vertex regression model and a layered rendering process, providing high-quality
images in each step. Our experimental results show that ANR surpasses previous
methods in producing clear and non-distorted images of virtual humans,
demonstrating its potential in real-time applications such as virtual try-on,
social media, and gaming. Our code for ANR is now publicly available to facilitate
further advancements in this field. With ANR, we create a new benchmark dataset for
evaluating systematic pose errors in articulated objects, which could benefit the
community in accurately assessing neural avatar rendering quality in the future. Our
research findings are presented in a demonstration video and a paper published at
CVPR 2022. To ensure reproducibility of our research, we also present key code
illustrations in the appendices of this document. Lastly, we propose a range of
potential extensions to the ANR framework, from incorporating multiple objects
into a scene to using frame sequences for enhanced rendering quality, leaving these
potential improvements to the research community for further exploration. To
summarize, we successfully design ANR, the first method to successfully
generate clear images of dynamic objects using a combination of neural networks and
traditional rendering techniques, opening up new avenues for application in the
artificial intelligence domain. The related source code can be accessed at:

Recent advances in artificial neural networks (ANNs) claim to simulate aspects of primates' and humans' neural performance. However, these ANNs primarily rely on basic visual characteristics when performing object recognition tasks. In contrast, humans with normal vision can effectively recognize objects using complex contextual clues, even with severely distorted input. To explore this discrepancy, we consulted medical experts to develop unusually distorted visual datasets mimicking specific eye disorders. We evaluated both human and ANN performance on these datasets to identify any patterns or similarities. The results show that models trained on natural images struggle to adapt to these distorted images just as humans with related eye disorders would struggle. However, our findings suggest that humans and ANNs differ significantly even when presented with minimal contextual information, particularly when dealing with subtle transformations that lie at the edge of their respective visual capabilities. The proposed methodology and resulting image transformations can benefit researchers working on both artificial and human vision. Cr$_2$Al exhibits a tetragonal structure similar to Mn$_2$Au and is of interest in the study of antiferromagnetic spintronics due to its in-plane N\'{e}el vector degeneracy. X-ray resonant magnetism and neutron scattering have been used to determine the magnetic structure and exchange interactions of Cr$_2$Al. Its in-plane magnetic structure is found to be consistent with a specific type known as a $P4/mmm$-B$2$M structure, featuring a simple repeat and in-plane axis. This structure is accompanied by a specific quantization axis. Moreover, the system displays anisotropic exchange interactions, primarily mediated by 2$d$ Cr(Oh) states which are primarily responsible for the in-plane propagation of spin waves, displaying a spectrum that is hyperbolic in nature and has a specific acoustical mode frequency of approximately 4.53 meV. A new kinetic model, the $
u$-model, is proposed to simplify the complex interactions between molecules in rarefied gas flows by incorporating a variable collision frequency depending on velocity. This models collision frequency in accordance with its physical meaning and eliminates the unphysical degrees of freedom present in traditional kinetic equations. Specifically designed for weakly non-Maxwellian flows, the $
u$-model is related to the Boltzmann equation through a generalized version of the Chapman-Enskog expansion. This approach results in a more efficient and accurate solution for rarefied gas dynamics compared to the mode of variable number of collisions. Furthermore, the $
u$-model successfully replicates key characteristics of the hard-sphere collision model, including an exact velocity-dependent collision frequency and a model that naturally reduces to the Maxwell model for undisturbed flows, thus preventing unphysical velocity-dependent distribution functions. Finally, the $
u$-model has been applied to the simulation of rarefied gas dynamics, yielding accurate outcomes for various scenarios. Specifically, the $
u$-model successfully replicated the velocity-dependent redistribution of velocities observed in experiments involving reflected velocity distributions without overemphasizing numerous collision events, resulting in improved agreement with experimental data, particularly in scenarios involving strong non-Maxwellian flows. This approach also resulted in minimal negative oblique momentum in scenarios involving perpendicular incident flows, thus adhering to conservation principles to a high degree of accuracy. Moreover, the $
u$-model successfully replicated the correct shock behavior, accurately reproducing the bimodal velocity distribution characteristic of this scenario. Finally, the $
u$-model yielded accurate outcomes for various other scenarios such as velocity-dependent light scattering, slip coefficient prediction, and generalized force determination, thus highlighting its potential as a valuable tool in the study of rarefied gas dynamics. The kinetic model proposed here, the $
u$-model, successfully replicates key characteristics of the Boltzmann equation through a simplified collision frequency depending on velocity and reduces the complex interactions between molecules in rarefied gas flows to a more manageable solution. This model has numerous applications in the study of rarefied gas dynamics and has resulted in improved agreement with experimental data, particularly in scenarios such as reflected velocity distributions and perpendicular incident flows, thus showcasing its potential as a valid solution to the collision problem. Using ALMA's H30α (231.90 GHz) observations of the metal-poor dwarf galaxy NGC 5253, we estimate the galaxy's star formation rate (SFR) and assess the reliability of other SFR measurement techniques. Based on these observations, the galaxy's photoionizing photon production rate and SFR (0.087±0.013 M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$) are both significantly lower than predicted by standard models. The SFR, as calculated from the H30α observations, is further compared to those derived from other properties such as infrared radiation, Hα emission, and the counts of young super novel radio sources. The results indicate that the global SFR, as calculated from the H30α emission (0.087 M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$), matches those from infrared radiation (0.083 M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$) but is higher than those from Hα emission (0.023 M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$) or the detection of young super novel radio sources (0.018 M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$). The discrepancy between the Hα and H30α SFRs is attributed to the overabundant gas within NGC 5253 as predicted by the 24 μm to Hα flux ratio, while the disagreement between the 24 μm and radio SFRs might be caused by an increased number of dust grains due to a lower metallicity, as predicted by the infrared radiation to infrared radiation flux ratio. The results suggest the presence of a significant age spread among the stars forming within NGC 5253. The discrepancy between the Hα and H30α SFRs, along with the predicted lower metal abundance, implies the use of modified radiation transfer laws in order to accurately calculate the SFR in low metallicity galaxies, particularly under conditions of high nebular optical extinction. The results further imply the need for the use of corrected IR to SFR relations in low metallicity galaxies, as well as the need for the use of corrected Hα to SFR relations in cases of high nebular optical extinction. Designing effective state observers for nonlinear epidemic models presents significant challenges. This difficulty stems from the inherent nonlinearity of these systems, which often follows the law of mass action and results in large, locally-dependent Lipschitz constants, making conventional design criteria unsuitable. This paper introduces a new state observer that improves estimation capabilities for nonlinear systems, including epidemic models, by mitigating the influence of nonlinearity in the error dynamics. To establish the observer's performance, sufficient conditions for convergence are formulated in the form of algebraic Riccati inequalities and linear matrix inequalities. These conditions provide a framework for evaluating and optimizing the observer's design for accurate state estimation. Simulation experiments are conducted to demonstrate the observer's performance capabilities. Furthermore, the proposed observer design is applied to various nonlinear epidemic models to validate its ability to provide reliable state estimates. These applications highlight the observer's versatility and its ability to effectively estimate parameterized models with known parameter values. To the best of our knowledge, the proposed observer design is the first successful application of nonlinear observers to a wide range of nonlinear epidemic models. Moreover, the proposed method addresses the challenge of designing an observer with minimal convergence time. This capability differentiates the proposed observer design from existing approaches in the literature. Several numerical simulations are performed to illustrate the observer's performance capabilities. The observer's design parameters are analyzed to demonstrate its ability to achieve fast convergence. Finally, the proposed observer design is applied to a stochastic SIR model to account for model uncertainty, showcasing its robust estimation capabilities even in the presence of uncertainty. The design parameters of the observer are analyzed to demonstrate its ability to achieve robust convergence. The proposed observer design is evaluated against existing observers in the literature through a comprehensive comparison of its convergence rates. The proposed observer design is shown to achieve a significant reduction in convergence time of up to 50% and 25% when compared to observers designed by Simanek and Faulwetter, and Li et al., respectively. The proposed observer design is shown to outperform the PDE-based observer designed by Leung and Lam by a substantial amount of 74.1%. The proposed observer design successfully estimates the SIR model states with minimal error for both the deterministic and stochastic models. The proposed observer design is shown to achieve faster convergence in both the deterministic and stochastic models. The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings, such as link prediction. However, despite the growing necessity of addressing context, state-of-the-art methods for building temporal knowledge graph embeddings largely depend on model modifications from static graph embeddings, and more often than not, these adaptations come at the expense of decreasing the overall model's capacity for capturing complex aspects of the data. In an effort to rectify this, our study focuses on increasing the model's capacity for handling complexity by converting the static model itself into a tool that generates multiple static models, each tailored to its perceived quality. By doing so, our approach aims to render the static model capable of link prediction in temporal knowledge graphs without needing further temporal adjustments. In a thorough evaluation covering all aspects of the problem, and with the use of the recently created TKG-Benchmark dataset, our results show that the enhanced framework allows for accurate prediction on large and diverse datasets, and more importantly, yields a more streamlined and efficient prediction process. Research driven by ultrashort pulses from Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillators has spawned diverse applications, with theoretical understanding rooted in conventional beam propagation analysis. However, established frameworks are often insufficient for handling the high power levels and strong nonlinearities inherent in high-power oscillators. To address this shortcoming, we employ an integrable coupled-scale perspective, coupled with the paraxial approximation, to explore Kerr-lens mode-locking in high-power oscillators. By developing this combined approach, we provide new geometric interpretations and theories that bridge the gaps in conventional analysis, offering a comprehensive understanding of Kerr-lens mode-locking, including novel design guidelines. To validate our work, we apply our theories to design a ring-resonator oscillator capable of generating 1-nJ pulses at 100-watt average power. A highly efficient and adaptable technique called federated learning is ideal for large-scale nonlinear regression tasks, especially those involving numerous samples and remote devices with limited internet connections and processing capabilities. The conventional federated learning framework, however, fails to account for several practical considerations such as the unequal distribution of data, the limited number of participants, and the energy efficiency concerns in resource-constrained devices. To address these limitations, a new asynchronous federated learning approach asyFEDLE, is proposed. The method addresses the problem of uneven data distribution through data balancing, considers the limited participation of clients with robust client selection, and makes resource consumption visible to the federated server while leveraging the server's central position to optimize energy costs by enabling data processing on server-side platforms. The effectiveness of the proposed asyFEDLE is evaluated against open datasets for nonlinear regression tasks and the results demonstrate its superior performance compared to existing federated learning algorithms in terms of the quality of the learned models and energy consumption during the learning process, leading to a substantial reduction of execution time of about 2.5 times with comparable model accuracy. The study showcases the potential of asyFEDLE for large-scale real-world applications by successfully applying the algorithm to a dataset of 3 million samples. We introduce the semi-inclusive Lepton Flavour Universality ratio $R_\Sigma$ to verify electron-to-muon universality in the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ process at $e^+e^-$ B-meson facilities. This combined observable enhances our capacity to detect potential violations of short distance origin Lepton Flavour Universality, all while retaining a straightforward theoretical explanation if a deviation from its predicted Standard Model value, $R_\Sigma^{\rm SM}=1$, is observed. We outline the method for determining $R_\Sigma$ by describing the relevant experimental conditions and statistical constraints associated with the management of systematic effects, as well as presenting the minimum number of events required to establish a deviation at a 95% confidence level from the SM. This new ratio significantly decreases the number of events needed compared to the inclusive $R_{K}$ ratio, thereby enabling a comprehensive Standard Model analysis even with the limited data collection expected at existing $e^+e^-$ facilities. Moreover, $R_\Sigma$ remains highly resistant to the effects of non-recoil systematic errors and experimental uncertainties in the $q^2$ dependence, which are essential factors governing various CP-violating observables. Finally, with the experimental outcomes from the $B\to K^\ast\ell^+\ell^-$ decays, we determine the lower limits on the relative branchings of the $B\to K^\ast\tau^+\tau^-$ and $B\to K^\ast\mu^+\mu^-$ processes, prompted by the LHCb's latest findings. The proposed $R_\Sigma$ ratio serves as a model for potential applications to additional tree-level observables, such as $b\to s\tau^+\tau^-$ and $b\to s\mu^+\mu^-$ decays, at upcoming $e^+e^-$ facilities. The experimental investigation of these sensitive probes at particle accelerators will be crucial in the precise measurement of Wilson coefficients in the V-A tree-level processes, further reinforcing our understanding of Standard Model parameters and potentially uncovering hints of physics beyond the standard model. We've developed a COVID-19 diagnosis framework that uses CT scan image analysis with a double feature extraction technique via BERT. The initial step utilizes a 3D-CNN to extract spatial information from the CT images and then employs BERT for temporal aggregation of these features. A classification model is trained on these aggregated features to determine non-COVID, COVID, or pneumonia cases. Subsequently, for samples categorized as uncertain or difficult by the initial classifier, we employ a secondary BERT model, which uses a sequential mask-predict process. This process integrates information from the initial classifier and then re-evaluates the features to produce a more refined classification. Notably, the initial classifier's features themselves serve as input to the secondary BERT, which allows for temporal aggregation and more informed decision-making. Experimental results demonstrate that our two-stage approach exhibits superior performance compared to a single BERT model, particularly in data-efficient scenarios. The source code is publicly available on GitHub. The results show that our model distinguishes itself in its ability to avoid false negatives in the re-evaluation process and avoid incorrect classifications in data-efficient settings. The model's performance characteristics suggest its potential applicability in large-scale medical image assessment and data quality enhancement. In a similar scenario but with a larger dataset, a two-stage accuracy of 0.9741, 0.8385, and 0.7530 was achieved for non-COVID, COVID, and pneumonia categories respectively. The model's performance also showed promising generalization to other related classification tasks such as pneumonia classification. The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics is being limited by an exclusive focus on fast-changing ecology and evolution, typically occurring over short periods, as expressed by the eco-evolutionary rate parameter beta. We argue that this perspective neglects potential influences from larger timescales. Therefore, we expand the framework to incorporate beta and any modulators, enabling analysis of dynamics across various timescales. By incorporating modulators, such as environmental shifts and significant evolutionary events, like mass extinctions, polarized selection, or rapid evolution, around 10 to 106 times larger than beta, we can examine the impact of these rate modulators on complex eco-evolutionary models. Our results show that these modulators significantly affect the long-term evolution and stability outcomes of such systems, particularly when rate modulators exceed a certain threshold, suggesting the presence of non-linear dynamics and tipping points. We suggest that such behavior may have contributed to the occurrence of the Late Permian biotic crisis. Our approach provides a flexible framework for investigating different timescales and rate modulators, making it more applicable to diverse real-world scenarios than the traditional beta-focused perspective. It allows for the exploration of long-term evolution and dynamics, offering valuable insights into the interplay between ecology and evolution across various timescales. By incorporating modulators, we can examine the impact of large-scale evolutionary events on the evolution of species and ecosystems, as well as anticipate complex outcomes that might arise from the interaction of timescales and rate modulators. These predictions might be useful for anticipating potential tipping points in contemporary ecosystems. Ultimately, our research suggests that significant ecological and evolutionary processes may be taking place on timescales that have not been previously considered. The extended framework presented here is designed to facilitate the detection and exploration of such processes in diverse real-world scenarios. It also enables the application of eco-evolutionary theory to a broader range of timescales and rate modulators, beyond what has been traditionally considered. Moreover, our approach is not limited to numerical simulations but can be used to inform empirical research by framing the occurrence of mass extinctions, significant evolutionary events, and rapid evolution within an theoretical framework that could help identify potential tipping points in contemporary ecosystems. Our research focuses on the underlying structure of Automated Market Makers (AMMs), 
a prevalent form of blockchain-based, decentralized exchanges. 
We reveal that the power-law behavior observed in the transaction losses of AMMs 
is a consequence of two distinct mechanisms. 
Initially, the initial price volatility facilitated by liquidity providers 
gives rise to a power-law distribution of potential losses. 
Subsequently, the interactions between traders and price changes yields an 
exponential decay in the loss distribution, scaled by transaction amounts. 
To further grasp the price dynamics, we develop a stylized framework 
that accounts for both liquidation and price displacement. 
Through analytical findings, we map out the mechanisms underlying AMM transactions, 
as the price dynamics yield a specific distribution without analytical closure. 
Our research utilizes transaction data from five prominent AMMs to validate the power-law 
behavior and exponential decay observed in the transaction losses of AMMs. 
Additionally, the results show that the mean loss experienced by liquidity providers 
exceeds 25% of their total assets and the median loss experienced by users 
exceeds 0.36 of their transaction value. 
Our research offers novel insights into the analysis and understanding of AMMs. 
It provides a framework for studying a specific regime of AMMs that is lacking in current literature. 
Moreover, the analysis highlights practical implications for users, revealing that the median 
loss experience by users may surpass the transaction fee threshold set by the exchange. 
Finally, the results show that the loss experienced by liquidity providers 
significantly outpaces those predicted by numerical simulations based on the Stein-Jensen model. 
To explain this disparity, the results show that the initial price volatility facilitated by liquidity providers 
is a primary driver of the observed loss distribution. 
It accounts for the majority of the total potential loss experienced by the liquidity provider 
across various transaction amounts. 
For specific transaction amounts greater than $100, the initial price volatility accounts for 
more than 70% of total potential loss. 
Conversely, the subsequent loss associated with the interaction between traders and price changes 
yields an exponential decay in the loss distribution, scaled by transaction amounts. 
Therefore, the initial price volatility facilitated by liquidity providers 
is a primary driver of the observed loss distribution among users. 
It will likely be a dominant effect until the initial deposit is fully liquidated. 
Our research identifies a crucial practical implication for users, revealing that the median 
loss experience by users may surpass the transaction fee threshold set by the exchange.

A new analytical framework, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, is designed to assess information biases in observational studies. The framework centers on the calculation of a sensitivity parameter E, which measures the risk of a false positive outcome when studying the presence of a causal relationship. To achieve reliable results, particularly in the context of missing data, multiple approaches must be developed to estimate E. To this end, we introduce a Bayesian method for estimating E by leveraging the posterior distribution of an incomplete data set's parameter vector. This approach, referred to as the Bayesian E-value, employs Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations to generate multiple samples post-analysis. The method is then validated using simulation techniques and two real-world studies, including one examining the causal link between a genetic variant and a specific disease, and another studying the influence of a particular trait on concert attendance. The latter is an example of a complex real-world problem, as typically seen in epidemiological research. The presented methods are straightforward, efficient, and easy to interpret, providing robust results in the process. Importantly, our proposed methods are highly versatile and can be applied to a wide array of statistical models used for analyzing incomplete data, including linear mixed models, to name one such example. To further enhance the scope of these approaches, we also provide a step-by-step summary of the practical procedures involved in performing the Bayesian analysis, as outlined in an accompanying supplement, available at the website [1]. The goal of this work is to facilitate the reliable calculation of E by means of a standardised protocol. To this end, we also provide supplementary material on the practical application of one such approach, including results in the context of logistic regression, for the sake of example's sake. A separate software package, referred to as BayesianBias, is used to implement the presented results, as available at the website [2] for the time being. The presented results are unique in merging concepts from missing data analysis and sensitivity analysis together, including simulations in the process. The goal of this work is to shed light on the critical issue of information biases in the process, including real-world examples in the context of observational studies. To this end, we also provide a critical review of existing research on the topic, including a long-standing framework for assessing such biases, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, as well as an accompanying document on the practical application of one such approach, including results in the context of logistic regression, for the sake of example's sake. The escalating demand for bigger cooling systems to support increasingly larger numbers of cryogenic qubits in quantum computing applications is prompting innovation.
In response to this challenge, we have developed a groundbreaking 1-meter-by-1-meter experimental space at Fermilab, which utilizes a cutting-edge cryogenic platform to achieve supercooled temperatures below 10 millikelvin.
This cutting-edge cryogenic platform, fueled by a 400-liter liquid helium dewar, can support and maintain up to 100 qubits, allowing for the demonstration of quantum error correction and accelerated quantum computing advancements.
By integrating our custom cryogenic device with three-dimensional microarchitecture and advanced radiation shielding techniques, we have successfully minimized stray magnetic fields and heat leaks, while also facilitating cryogenic processing, communication, and RF antenna connectivity.
This newly designed cryogenic platform, featuring a user-friendly and visually accessible remote control interface, has been successfully tested and is now ready to support groundbreaking quantum research at Fermilab's quantum computing hub, which is poised to become a leading research center in the field. The facility will focus on the intersection of quantum computing and cutting-edge scientific instruments to enhance the detection and analysis capabilities of rare subatomic phenomena, including the search for new physics beyond the Standard Model and the deepening understanding of fundamental particle properties, such as the weak mixing angle. We introduce an advanced technique for localizing and classifying objects within complex urban settings using aerial imagery, drawing inspiration from the effectiveness of crowd-sourced classification. The proposed VALUE system distributes object detection tasks to multiple agents, which then vote on class distribution in a decentralized manner. Furthermore, we've developed an innovative mechanism for updating class weights based on voting results. Experimental evaluations conducted on two comprehensive datasets demonstrate that VALUE outperforms state-of-the-art models in object detection and classification tasks, particularly when class imbalances exist. Furthermore, we found that VALUE's performance resilience in such scenarios directly correlates with the depth of the class hierarchy. Building on these findings, we outline a plan to harness the capabilities of contemporary edge GPUs to execute VALUE, paving the way for its deployment on drones equipped with affordable and low-power computational units. By integrating VALUE with such platforms, we aim to create a pioneering vision-based aerial surveillance system capable of automatically detecting and classifying objects within real-time video streams. We address the challenge of deconvolving sparse signals within seismic reflection inversion to retrieve the subsurface reflection coefficients with high resolution. Our model uses a synthesis-based sparse method involving both convex and non-convex regularization terms to yield l0 pseudo-norm approximations. This leads to an iterative algorithm utilizing proximal averaging that can be reformatted as a trainable neural network, optimizing through data-driven training. Our effectiveness is proven through numerical evaluations using synthetic data from 1D seismic traces and 2D wedge models in comparison to established techniques. Furthermore, we provide additional validation with real-world data from the Sigsbee2B dataset in 3D seismic reflection imaging. Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed through machine learning. Although the problem is largely solved for contemporary languages, historical corpora pose significant challenges, primarily due to limited native speaker interaction and a lack of training data. Compounding this issue, historical texts lack standardized sentence structures and orthographies, making automated POS tagging more complex and error-prone. In light of these complexities, instead of assigning single tags with uncertainty, POS tagging algorithms should allow for probabilistic outcomes. We propose applying the concept of set-valued prediction, enabling POS taggers to suggest a set of potential tags rather than guessing a single one. This approach not only reflects the uncertainty of the model but also promotes the examination of set-valued prediction techniques, paving the way for the development of more refined tools in natural language processing, particularly for historical texts. We introduce a novel metric to evaluate the quality of set-valued predictions and introduce smulder, a deep neural network-based model, designed to generate sets of tags. Through comprehensive experiments using Finnish and English data, we demonstrate that the proposed sets of tags are of higher quality in relation to existing single-tag predictions, ultimately reducing the total error rate by 25%. We believe that the employed set-valued prediction technique has the potential to benefit not only POS tagging but other natural language processing tasks that struggle with uncertainty, such as machine reading or named entity extraction. This approach aims to provide more accurate and robust results, analogous to the existing state-of-the-art achieved in contemporary languages. Furthermore, the developed model is expected to serve as a potential solution for other complex natural language processing tasks across languages, including those with limited training data, such as those in South America or sub-Saharan Africa. Additionally, the developed model is expected to facilitate the annotation of emerging text collections, such as news articles or social media posts, and could further the development of more linguistically informed models, bridging the gap between linguistics and natural language processing, particularly for minority languages. Eventually, the developed model is expected to enhance the quality of annotations in collective efforts across the broader Automatic Semantic Rendering spectrum, such as the Automated Part-of-Speech tagger, the Human Annotation collaborative platform, the Generalized Event Representation Framework and the Annotation Cooperative. Despite research-based promising outcomes with ML models, there is an underlying barrier to integrating these into clinical practices.  One major obstacle is the varied formats of annotation and prediction data along with the numerous toolsets to interpret them.  To resolve this, the DICOM standard was developed to unify the annotation and exchange of imaging data, with highdicom being a Python library that both reads and generates DICOM data.  In this study, we detail highdicom's functionality in managing ML model outputs alongside traditional image analytics, showcasing its potential with a multi-headed UNET model for tumor segmentation in computed tomography scans.  To make highdicom usable for users new to DICOM, the library features automatic conversion of ML model outputs and image analytics data to standard-compliant files as well as supports automatic DICOM message decoding.  Additionally, the library includes a model output converter, a UNET model class for tumor segmentation, and demonstration examples in the form of a CT-based tumor segmentation challenge. In recent times, deep learning models have been effectively utilized for categorizing DNA sequences based on various tasks. A major challenge often arises due to the lengthy and complex nature of these DNA sequences. In our current research, we have developed a novel deep representation model capable of autonomously learning DNA's intricate characteristics. Our model's key component is a specially designed representation module that effectively splits the input DNA sequences into localized, easily processable segments using a novel transformer-based approach. Additionally, we have devised a novel objective function that employs structural similarities within the variable-length input DNA sequences. A new, systematic method referred to as the Clebsch canonization has been proposed to convert Lie-Poisson equations into equivalent canonical Hamiltonian systems through a momentum map connection. We outline both an algebraic and a geometric approach to this method, with the latter presented here for the first time. Moreover, we discovered an additional momentum map, resulting in a dual pair of momentum maps, which under specific conditions can represent the process of Lie-Poisson systems collectivization. Consequently, applying symplectic Runge-Kutta methods to solve the system in its canonical form leads to integrators preserving coadjoint orbits and Casimirs precisely. We provide two case studies: the Kida vortex, which corresponds to Lie-Poisson systems on $\mathfrak{so}(2,1)^{*}$, and the heavy top, which corresponds to Lie-Poisson systems on $(\mathfrak{se}(3) \ltimes \mathbb{R}^{3})^{*}$. In the former case, we present an original momentum map technique to exhibit the phase space conjugates in the canonization process. In the latter case, we present an original momentum map technique combined with coadjoint orbit quantization, which yields a time-preserving Hamiltonian for the classically equivalent vector field following the Madelung form. All methods and properties are presented in a context-free framework with the aim of achieving maximum clarity and simplicity. The code for these methods has been written in a Julia language, which is provided alongside, with the goal of facilitating the further development of novel momentum map-based integrators. Julia also enables the generation of visualizations for the integrators and their application to the exact solution of the Kida vortex. Importantly, the provided code is also executable within an interactive Mathematica context, which is achieved by importing the Julia code and enabling the subsequent interactive use of the code. Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are insensitive to orientation. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while adapting to different orientation classes. Our experiments demonstrate that OCNs outperform traditional DCNNs in orientation-invariant image recognition tasks, and show promising results for complex multi-oriented classification problems. Furthermore, our proposed approach accelerates training and improves the overall efficiency of deep learning models. These findings suggest that OCNs based on LGFs are a valuable tool for image recognition and classification in various orientation-induced scenarios. Our project's source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/asharakeh/OrientationConvolutionNetworks. Ashraf Alvarado, an undergraduate student, contributed significantly to this research. Our experiments, conducted under full orientation variability, verified the effectiveness of OCNs across different training and testing data splits and demonstrated their superior performance in multi-oriented classification problems as evidenced by their 98% accuracy on the Wikipedia dataset. Moreover, I successfully applied the LGFs approach to a 1 million image classification challenge, where the resulting model surpassed the existing state-of-the-art performance. These advancements pave the way for future research in orientation-free learning. Ashraf specifically explored and validated the efficacy of LGFs on a wide range of orientation-invariant datasets, where the results confirmed their ability to resist circumferential transformations while enhancing the model's generalization capabilities. Interestingly, the proposed LGFs are insensitive to axial rotations, where the resulting score remains constant. We develop a systematic method to study the impact of mass on the pole mass in comparison to short-distance masses like the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ mass for a heavy quark, specifically with an emphasis on the top quark, through virtual loop insertions from heavier quarks. Our method adheres to heavy quark symmetry constraints, allowing us to decompose and gradually remove the effects of lighter massive quarks as well as the intervening momentum regions, all while accurately controlling high-order asymptotic behavior. By employing this method, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of massive flavor contributions, calculate fourth-order corrections from three heavy quarks (including the top quark), determine first-order corrections from four heavy quarks, and provide an upper limit on pole top mass variations due to massive flavor interactions. We validate our method by confirming agreement with existing, lower-order results, and the accuracy of our proposed corrections. Ultimately, we present a set of numerical outcomes for the pole top mass and $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ top mass, taking into account the effects of massive flavor interactions. Our method can be adapted for application in future theoretical corrections and experimental analyses. For completeness, we also outline the general framework of heavy quark effective theory without assuming any specific heavy quark limit, and discuss the general structure of massive flavor contributions, including pole mass corrections, in the context of both pole and $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ masses. Additionally, we provide a first-order estimate of the four-loop massive flavor correction, and comment on the interplay between these interactions and other sources of uncertainty in the determination of the top quark pole mass. The numerical outcomes and analysis presented here are anticipated to extend smoothly to the treatment of bottom quark masses. The detailed derivation of our method is documented in the accompanying notes (Supplemental ), where we also extend the derivation to the general mass spectrum in the gauge theory and convert the resulting framework into a systematic method suitable for precision calculations. Furthermore, the underlying code of our method, implemented in Mathematica, is made available for future use at this link: https://github.com/hyenhuiyong/MBMcode.git. Currently, the diagnosis of COVID-19 relies on laboratory tests, which have their own set of challenges, such as delayed results, limited sample availability, and the need to isolate patients. To improve diagnosis while minimizing costs and the risk of spread, researchers are exploring alternative methods. One such approach is digital radiography, specifically the analysis of chest CT scans. However, this requires high-dose machines that expose patients to increased radiation levels and still carries the risk of false negatives. To overcome these limitations, there is a need for more sensitive methods that can detect early patterns and lesions in low-dose scans. We present a new method, based on a human-level two-stage time-distributed capsule network, that utilizes pattern recognition to identify COVID-19 patterns in low-dose and conventional CT scans. By training on datasets from China, Japan, and the US, we successfully replicated human-level performance in COVID-19 diagnosis, according to AUC scores, and provided statistical analysis support. We further validated the robustness of our model against corrupted data, extended its capabilities to other infectious diseases such as MERS and SARS, and used feature matching to explain its decision-making process. This outcome suggests that our method could be applied to other infectious diseases with similar lung patterns. To facilitate this, we share our source code with the research community. We hope our work contributes to the accelerated detection of COVID-19 through improved data analysis technologies. Ultimately, the outcome of our study could positively impact the global health community by facilitating the timely detection of infectious diseases. To accelerate this process, we openly share our source code with the research community. We successfully trained the model on different datasets while replicating human-level performance according to AUC scores, providing AUC values of 0.8269 for low-dose scans, 0.9601 for conventional CT scans, and 0.9606 for combined analysis. To generate top-quality quadrilateral meshes on complex computer-aided design (CAD) models efficiently, we propose an integrated solution. A versatile mesh with numerous irregular points is initially created, which allows for intricate quad configurations due to its unstructured layout. Subsequently, we build upon this foundation with a flexible T-mesh structure, which can be manipulated to optimize the mesh topology by assigning varying lengths to its arc segments. Utilizing advanced optimization techniques in the form of integer linear programming, we efficiently resolve the mesh simplification process and refine the resulting topology. Ultimately, we extract high-order quadrilateral meshes from the optimized framework, showcasing excellent results on various CAD models through rigorous testing that highlights its speed, accuracy, and overall effectiveness. These findings demonstrate the significant improvement in mesh quality when utilizing higher-order quadrature methods, which can lead to enhanced accuracy and efficiency when paired with related computational methods such as finite element analysis. To facilitate easy integration of our approach into existing design and simulation workflows, we have developed mesh generation software that can be seamlessly incorporated into the vtk framework. A comprehensive evaluation, accompanied by additional resources and implementation details, is provided on our website at https://qmesh.lne.de. The associated code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/pmeester/qmesh. The MeshBench benchmarking tool, used to benchmark the quality of our generated meshes, can be found at https://github.com/pmeester/meshbench. All CAD models employed in the study, as well as the resulting meshes and quadrature schemes, are also publicly accessible at https://qmesh.lne.de/demo. Additionally, a detailed comparison study of our approach with similar mesh generation methods is presented in an article that can be found at https.//doi.org/10.1017/hprj.2022.56. Pearson's correlation coefficient is frequently employed as a measure of association in statistical analysis. The strength of evidence for linear correlation is often evaluated using a hypothesis test, resulting in a p-value. Under certain data transformations and assuming normal distribution of a dataset, a t-statistic provides an exact p-value; otherwise, the result is an approximation. The p-value can be estimated by analyzing how a sample correlation coefficient behaves under different permutations of the data. Although such estimates may rely on approximations of distribution moments, an inductive approach in this paper offers a precise formula for expressing sample correlation distribution moments in terms of the dataset's central moments, allowing for the development of novel estimation methods to compute the p-value. Experimental comparisons demonstrate that these methods outperform existing ones, thus providing an improvement in statistical analysis. We investigate the two- or three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations defined within a bounded region. This model takes into account an external force that introduces instability and is constrained by no-slip boundary conditions. The goal of our work is to stabilize such systems through finite dimensional feedback controls in the vicinity of an unstable equilibrium in critical Sobolev and Besov spaces that approximate L^3(Omega) in three dimensions. This research setting has substantial implications as the uncontrolled dynamics' well-posedness issue has been solved in the critical space L^3(R^3) in recent studies. By localizing controls in a small subdomain within Omega, this study provides a solution to the uniform stabilization problem in the critical space and also offers an improved, simplified solution in the slightly stronger H^3(Omega) space. This work derives uniform bounds over a finite time interval of L^3(Omega) in the presence of boundary conditions, extends the work's scope to the critical Besov space B^{1_{p'}}_{q} (Omega), and also considers the two-dimensional case in a somewhat coarser space. This work was completed with the support of a grant from the NSF, referred to as 'Mathematics: Inference and Identification', and is available at https://www.nsfdedicated.org/. The presented results' power lies in their capacity to provide a solution in the critical space for the global interior semigroup's uniform stabilization problem as well as the classical finite dimensional boundary localized feedback control in the subcritical space. Moreover, this work showcases the effectiveness of the distance principle in the context of Navier-Stokes equations and the power of localizing controls in extending the work's scope and achieving the desired uniform bounds in more delicate cases. Finally, this work combines critical problems from both analysis and control engineering disciplines to facilitate the resolution of these challenging problems. The growing interest in transparent AI has led to an increase in research on explainable recommendation systems. Among these, post-hoc methods have been identified as the most practical solutions for intricate models that operate as "black-boxes." Recent studies have exposed limitations in local surrogate models used in post-hoc explanation techniques, such as misinterpreting user preferences or attributing results to random factors. In light of these findings, this work develops LIME-RS - an enhanced post-hoc explanation framework for recommendation systems, built on top of a general optimization approach. LIME-RS addresses the shortcomings in the original LIME model, ensuring accurate and stable explanations that align with user expectations, and we make all implementation details publicly available. Empirical evidence demonstrates the effectiveness of our method in various recommendation settings, highlighting its ability to provide consistent and adherence-oriented explanations for user-generated content on video platforms. Notably, the implementation will be integrated into the most widely used open-source recommendation platform - RecBoard, facilitating future research in this domain. As a result, this study hopes to stimulate discussions and inspire reliable explanation techniques for recommendation systems in the future. Research has shown that certain complex models require significant data to learn reliably, and that data with label noise may not be sufficient, despite being locally similar to a suitable model. We investigate the concept of data being locally similar to a model using certain criteria, and find that Demuth et al.'s definition of local similarity in 2021 is too narrow. We develop a broader definition and demonstrate its increased utility in identifying suitable data for learning. Specifically, our definition leverages the principle that locally similar data should contain useful information for model optimization, and we apply criteria such as dense subset inclusion and query-level stochastic loss to define our local similarity criteria. We find that these criteria can accurately capture the concept of local similarity, and that they align with intuitive understanding and existing definitions. Furthermore, our analysis provides novel insights into the relationship between these criteria and the problem of learning from robustness. We propose two new definitions of local robustness, and prove that our large class of criteria can be viewed as specific instances of these definitions. We apply these new definitions to develop generalizations of four established decision tree theorem results. These theorems provide increased insight into the connection between our local robustness definitions and the concept of model modularity. Consequently, our analysis leads to the creation of an algorithm to find locally robust data, and we find that certain datasets contain multiple examples that can significantly aid learning, and that these data are identifiable using our proposed algorithm and analysis. Our research also reveals that our local robustness definitions can be applied across a range of complex model types by proving the definitions applicable to NFTs and FTPs. We propose an algorithm to identify robust data for FTPs and NFTs and demonstrate its increased effectiveness through our analysis. Furthermore, our research shows that our local robustness definitions can be used to develop strategies for actively collecting reliable data, and that our analysis and algorithm can be applied across a range of real-world data configurations. We demonstrate this applicability by collecting and evaluating local robustness definitions for two high-accuracy models, and finding that our data and analysis lead to significant improvements in model performance. Ultimately, our research and algorithms enable us to identify and utilize certain data for learning that were previously unknown and inaccessible. We collect and evaluate local robustness definitions for multiple models and demonstrate their increased effectiveness, and our results and parameters allow future researchers to replicate and apply our findings to a range of learning scenarios. Our previous research significantly sped up Sinkhorn iteration by taking advantage of a kernel matrix's inherent properties, transforming its $O(N^2)$ complexity to $O(N)$ efficiency. This paper delves deeper into kernel matrix characteristics by defining and applying two key concepts, Lower-ColLinear Triangular Matrices and Upper-ColLinear Triangular Matrices. By showing that multiplying these matrices with vectors can be achieved in $O(N)$ operations and demonstrating their closure under specific operations like Hadamard product and matrix scaling, we resolved two critical challenges for IPOT complexity reduction. This breakthrough further enables the creation of an accurate and precise solver for IPOT, a crucial requirement often underestimated in literature. Our new algorithm is surprisingly simple, yet effective and efficient, outperforming current state-of-the-art IPOT solvers by several orders of magnitude, as shown through extensive numerical tests. Notably, with our new method, even large-scale IPOT problems with millions of points can be solved in a matter of seconds, opening up new application avenues. We explore novel view generation -- the challenge of generating distant, unseen views by virtually navigating a given image -- through a new, promising approach. Our contribution is DiffDreamer, an unsupervised system that synthesizes new views by conditionally generating images based on the given perspective and a pre-trained representation of a scene's layout. Our method employs a cutting-edge diffusion model, paired with an advanced layout representation built from a pre-trained unsupervised scene parser, to generate high-quality, distortion-resistant images even at extreme distances. Our diffusion model is specifically designed to maintain scene consistency and spatial accuracy, along with realistic image details, by fine-tuning and refining samples through multiple stages of optimization. Our experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses existing layout-based approaches in quality and extension, while also showcasing the potential of advanced image synthesis models without explicit training data. Many complex systems feature interconnected components that follow nonlinear patterns of interaction, presenting complex dynamics when modeled using nonlinear equations or random processes. Recent advances in analytical tools and experimental methods have generated vast amounts of data containing hidden connections and patterns. This paper presents a novel, data-driven framework rooted in graph theory and machine learning for identifying complex systems, even when modeled using stochastic or nonlinear equations. It utilizes dynamic time warping for aligning data sequences and developing predictive models of complex systems, even in cases where data is scarce. Furthermore, under certain conditions on the initial values, we assess and discuss the stability within the Lagrangian Lagrangian framework, while also demonstrating that solutions are stable in the Eulerian Eulerian framework without imposing additional constraints.
