We further investigate and discuss specific scenarios, including the transition from the inviscid Hunter-Saxton to the viscous Hunter-Saxton equations, as well as the relationship between these equations and the geometrically interpreted dynamics of certain active strings. Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging is particularly difficult for individuals without prior experience. A newly developed robotic scanning technique combines deep learning with controlled pressure to accurately follow spinal curves. This method was tested against manual scanning by examining the spinous process angles in 23 scoliosis patients using ultrasound. Two human evaluators measured and compared the coronal image angle (CIA), posterior rib angle (PRA), and sagittal spinal angle (SSA) for each scanning method. Results showed that robotic scanning yielded higher degrees of freedom, similar spinous process angle correlation to manual scanning, but a lower posterior rib angle correlation. Overall, robotic scanning performed equally or better in scoliosis assessment in comparison to manual scanning, making it a reliable and dependable method. This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling incremental synthesis. This method is in line with a broader goal of concurrently modelling durations and auditory costs. Furthermore, the aim is to tailor the training of the model durations to align with the acoustic qualities of a reference dataset, a process known as auditory normalisation. The application of this method is shown through a demonstration of naturally spoken German sentences synthesized without the influence of duration annotations. The results indicate a notable improvement in duration accuracy, specifically a 57.0% reduction in the root mean square error compared to a previously established method, specifically the deep neural neural network-based duration model introduced by Krueger et al. in 2017. The synthesis system underwent a second stage of training where the duration model was combined with an advanced spectral representation technique. The resulting system exhibited high quality in both duration and tone accuracy, specifically with a mean absolute percentage error of 6.94 and a root mean square error of 29.82, respectively. The synthesis of sentences without the influence of duration annotations by the model is shown. The source code for the method has been made publicly available. Identifying online hate speech is increasingly critical due to its capacity to inflict emotional and psychological harm on minority groups. A recent study from TU Berlin's research team analyzed the performance of different Natural Language Processing models on subtasks one and two of the 2021 Indo-European language shared task, which focused on detecting hate speech and derogatory content. Our team assessed the effectiveness of models that rely on word and character-based recurrent neural networks and those employing transfer learning via BERT, all of which utilized a shared task dataset. It was discovered that models employing transfer learning outperformed others across both tasks. Models leveraging the BERT model's pre-trained knowledge on English demonstrated superior accuracy but with the drawback of only being applicable to English. Our team adapted an alternative model, which uses a character-based recurrent neural network, to classify multiple languages and explored its suitability for task two. An investigation of the model's accuracy showed that it can efficiently eliminate a significant amount of derogatory content on social media platforms. Through an evaluation experiment, it was observed that our character-based model achieved an F1-score of 0.512 for task two, indicating its capacity to filter 52% of social media platform content. Our team also evaluated the model's ability to not mark as hate speech identities texts that are objectively derogatory, and interestingly, it was observed that models employing transfer learning are more inclined towards such a classification in comparison to other models. Our research team's performance highlights is further complemented by an analysis of the model's classification and localization characteristics for task one, which was performed using TU-Berlin's dataset as well as datasets from other reputable research sources. Our investigation into the model's characteristics signals future research directions to complement the current state of the model. In standard numerical approaches, the solution speed declines dramatically as the potential energy approaches its final asymptotic value, a limitation that has hindered realistic simulations of solvated molecules for decades. To address this issue, we present a novel quadrature scheme based on a multi-center approach that overcomes the this limitation. In this method, the traditional analytical formula for the potential energy is replaced with a numerical quadrature expression, allowing the solver to efficiently converge even at large non-uniform grid points. We present theoretical justifications and supporting evidence for this method. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this multi-center quadrature scheme is compatible with both mesh-free and mesh-based solvers, making it a versatile tool. To validate the scheme, we present convergence data for various test cases with up to three distinct solvation models. We show that our multi-center quadrature scheme facilitates the realistic simulation of solvated molecules, a breakthrough that enables the generation of accurate solvation free energies without being plagued by excessive computational time. To showcase the scheme's effectiveness, we present two case studies. Firstly, we present a realistic simulation of a small peptide in water using this multi-center quadrature scheme. Interestingly, the computed free energy of solvation agrees well with the experimentally observed value. Secondly, we present a multi-ion water box model that requires the satisfaction of two specific conditions to simulate accurately, a problem that is easily solved using our numerical approach. To conclude, we present a comparative study of the computed solvation free energies generated using different models based on the multi-center quadrature scheme. The results show that this scheme facilitates the generation of solvation free energies that are well within the acceptable error range from the actual values, a significant advancement in computational methods. One of the major advantages of this scheme is its compatibility with a wide range of computational models, a fact that has been demonstrated in this study. To further enhance our understanding of the scheme's effectiveness, we present a supporting study that showcases its application and effectiveness in a realistic peptide simulation. To conclude, we outline the upcoming research directions based on the findings presented in this study. To address this issue, our study introduces the Bayesian Statistics Guided Label Refurbishment mechanism (BSG-LR) to accurately classify medical images even when faced with significant label noise. By combining multiple reliable features derived from images and incorporating Bayesian statistics, the BSG-LR model is able to accurately detect and correct noisy labels. Experimental results show that the BSG-LR model achieves an accuracy of 94.714.7% in the medical image classification field, outperforming existing noise mitigation techniques. Furthermore, the code for the BSG-LR model can be easily adapted for use in other fields. To facilitate this process, our study provides step-by-step instructions on how to implement the BSG-LR model. Ultimately, the code for the BSG-LR model is available on GitHub under the open-source license. To visit this repository, the following URL can be accessed: https://github.com/huangyunxian-BYU/BSG-LR. The BSG-LR model has the potential to greatly improve the accuracy of medical image classification, even when faced with significant label noise, which has the potential to save countless lives by improving the quality of medical imaging. By improving the accuracy of medical image classification, the BSG-LR model may also be able to enhance our understanding of the underlying medical structure through improved analysis of medical image content. To achieve this goal, our study provides guidance on how to implement the BSG-LR model in the form of "Guided Reading". By reading and understanding the key papers in this field, our study shows that the BSG-LR model is based on two critical concepts: the Bayesian statistics and the label refurbishment mechanisms. In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new approach that simplifies termination proofs without overly utilizing the clock mechanism, particularly illustrated through the context of functional big-step semantics for programming language interpretations. By comparing different clock embedding techniques, we conclude that a novel, low-intrusion embedding surpasses existing methods. We also expand the HOL reasoning framework to accommodate more natural and high-level definitions of non-terminating functions, building upon a existing concept. The developed approach is versatile, applicable to diverse interpretation semantics, as shown in a range of case studies. Furthermore, we showcase its capabilities by applying it to a representative language example, demonstrating the results of a new abstraction refinement strategy in proof development. The developed approach is available for public use, with the source code openly accessible on GitHub, incorporating both the embedding of clock mechanisms and the definition of non-terminating functions, as well as the application to a range of case studies. Additionally, the developed approach is accessible via a web-based demonstration through the Coq-based, non-HOL reasoner, Critica. The source code of Critica is openly available for collaborative improvement. The developed approach is accompanied by a critical examination of potential attacks on its design, including a detailed investigation of potential countermeasures. The analysis of the developed approach is further accompanied by a discussion of its potential extension to total higher-order automated reasoning. This study demonstrates the presence of self-dual (topological) solitons within a modified baby Skyrme model that incorporates Born-Infeld term governed gauge field behavior. The effective implementation of the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield framework yields an energy lower bound, with corresponding self-dual equations whose solutions manifest as the limiting solitons that achieve this bound. The lower bound energy, resulting from the Bogomol'nyi bound, differs from the Quotient energy which accounts for the Skyrme term's full influence. Furthermore, this work illustrates, through both analytical and numerical data, how the Baby Skyrme model's nonlinearity parameters impact soliton deformations and how they affect both the radius and stability of these solitons. Notably, we find that both radial dimensions and stability are influenced by corrections to the quark-like interactions which lead to soliton deformity. Moreover, we show that corrections to the pion-like bilinear terms also play a crucial role in soliton stability. Using a technique of superposition, this work also examines and compares the geometric characteristics of solitons resulting from various coupling parameters. Lastly, this work calculates and compares the magnetic field produced by the solitons in question. The presence of surface magnetic fields, resulting from baby Skyrme effects, can be inferred for all configurations whose solitons exhibit stable geometries. Conversely, configurations whose solitons exhibit unstable geometries possess interior magnetic fields. The Skyrme model's nonlinearity parameters and quark-like interactions clearly define soliton geometric characteristics and stability, while pion-like bilinear terms define soliton magnetic properties. Consequently, this work sheds light on how quark-like and pion-like interactions impact soliton geometric characteristics and stability. Moreover, this work illustrates how baby Skyrme effects lead to distinct soliton characteristics that can be experimentally verified. For a three-dimensional Majorana-Weyl fermion with arbitrary charge neutrality and magnetic flux applied within a cubic lattice, our findings indicate a phase transition from a topological neutral liquid with time-reversal symmetry to a time-reversal-breaking semi-metallic phase, even at a zero magnetic field. When a minimal amount of magnetic flux, equal to a quantum, is present, this transition can occur for any number of lattice sites. For instance, if we consider a cube with 8^3 sites, without magnetic flux, it exhibits neutral topological behavior. However, when a unit of magnetic flux is applied, it transitions into a time-reversal-ineffective semi-metallic state, featuring 3 non-zero Berry curvature vectors located at the Fermi level, one directed along each spin axis. Furthermore, our analysis shows that magnetic flux equal to or a multiple of the quantum (e.g. 2π, 3π etc.) removes time-reversal symmetry from the system regardless of lattice size. Conversely, neutral topological behavior is observed for certain fractional flux values (1/3, 5/3 etc.) for any lattice size (e.g. 8^3, 9^3 etc.). The theoretical predictions have been validated through full diagonalization of the model. The proposed model, based on the minimal model of Dirac fermions at the conic points, may provide the groundwork for the stable creation and precise manipulation of time-reversal-ineffective semi-metals with quantum flux. It can also be experimentally developed through superconducting magnetic arrays coupled with ultraclean two-dimensional semimetals. Ultimately, this model may facilitate advancements in quantum processing, one potential application being the stable storage of information through chiral Majorana modes located at the edges of magnetic textures. Consequently, this model may enable the accurate representation and manipulation of time-reversal-invariant quantities, for example, the natural handedness found in chiral edge states located at the edges of magnetic atoms, even in the absence of overall system symmetry. As a result, this model may lead to stable and precise local inversion symmetry breaking, alongside other related phenomena, such as the stable and precise influence of parity here and now. Mechanical screening, a widely recognized phenomenon, is utilized across solid-state systems.  Nucleation of defects, scars and folds in curved crystals, rearrangements in disordered systems and glassy transitions all involve this screening effect.  However, researchers discovered that granular matter, a non-screened medium, exhibits an unexpected screening effect.  A grain that undergoes high-velocity collisions experiences an instantaneous reduction in normal force upon collision and loses 'age.'  Our study involved creating and losing age events in granular materials and measuring the distribution of ages between events.  Due to the absence of screening in granular matter, we developed an anomalous screening theory.  Our model is based on the idea that events must occur within a time-limited 'window.'  Each subsequent event begins age counting from the most recent one.  To validate our theory, we analyzed experimental age distributions using both numerical simulations and analytical models.  Our results show excellent agreement among the experimental, simulated and calculated age distribution results.  This agreement confirms our initial hypothesis and proposes a general approach for detecting screening effects in diverse materials.  Our numerical approach can also facilitate the identification of screening effects in various systems.  A critical parameter determines whether events form clusters or a continuous distribution, and this parameter is easily identifiable in granular materials.  Our research opens up new avenues for investigating screening effects in wide-ranging materials.  It also inspires an important area of investigation: analyzing power-law distributions with exponents greater than one.  Our approach offers an understanding of screening effects in disordered systems in mechanical equilibrium, and suggests methods to modulate and adjust mechanical properties through adjustments to the collision velocity.  Ultimately, this allows for alterations to mechanical behavior, and to diagnose and diagnose screening effects in various systems.  Investigating this fascinating phenomenon has far-reaching implications for various fields, and our numerical and analytical findings provide reliable indicators of screening effects in granular materials and potentially other systems as well.  While screening and age concepts are widely applicable, their interplay is most easily observed in granular materials.  Therefore, identifying screening effects in materials lacking distinct events is a more challenging task, and our approach may serve as a starting point for investigating and validating screening and age models in various systems.  It also inspires an important area of investigation: understanding and validating the theoretical model of anomalous screening that we developed.  Our approach can also be used to investigate and validate screening and age models in various systems, and to identify potential applications of these concepts to materials science and physics.

Utilizing first-principles calculations, our research involves analyzing silicene in relation to hexagonal boron nitride substrates. The findings indicate that boron nitride can effectively stabilize silicene layers. The impact of manganese decoration on the electronic characteristics of silicene is also explored, showing that certain patterns of manganese placement can result in the formation of a manganese-based semiconductor. Furthermore, manganese decoration gives rise to both localized and delocalized unhybridized states of silicene, suggesting the appearance of a manganese-induced transition in the system. The transition can be described as a reversible shift from an A4x4 structure to a hydrogen-passivated 4x4 structure. Additionally, our research examines the response of the system to strain, demonstrating that silicene's interaction with the boron nitride substrate is diminished as the level of strain increases. The strain is observed to have varying effects on the positions and energies of the manganese-derived bands. The findings of our study indicate that silicene's electronic properties can be fine-tuned through manganese decoration and external strain, presenting potential applications in the creation of manganese-based devices. The accompanying total density of states analysis not only validates these conclusions but also provides a clear understanding of the underlying mechanisms. The study concludes by highlighting potential applications of the system in the form of device design. The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses a mystery with age estimates ranging from extremely young, around 1-2 thousand years, to a significantly older, 10 thousand year estimate. Our objective is to create a straightforward simulation of a supernova explosion occurring within a dense gas cloud near the galactic core, to determine feasibility of a young age estimate. We employed a one-dimensional simulation of a type II supernova explosion occurring inside an expanding gas cloud. To account for asymmetry, we included an influence function representing the precursor stellar wind from the exploding star. Using this model, we tested various precursor positions and angles to replicate an observed east-west symmetry of Sgr A East, concluding that an accurate fit is only achievable with a 10 to 30 parsec radial distance from the galactic core and a precursor position approximately 20 to 40 parsec away. Based on these findings, we estimate the precursor position to be around 26 parsec from the galactic core. Furthermore, we calculated that a supernova explosion occurring at that position would result in a radiation energy of 10^48-10^49 erg/s, which would be visible as a bright source only recently, on a time scale of 50-2000 years, depending on the galactic gas density and the distance from the galactic core. The study examines various oversampling methods to classify multi-class topics, particularly focusing on the performance of SMOTE, a popular method for generating new samples based on minority class examples, and its five variants (SMOTE-Tescent, Borderline, ADASYN, Random SMOTE, and Stochastic SMOTE) in combination with classification algorithms (support vector machine, k-nearest neighbor, and naive Bayes). Through data classification, the research elevates understanding in the field of text classification using synthetic oversampling techniques. Findings indicate that using random SMOTE in conjunction with support vector machine results in the highest overall accuracy, outperforming other combinations of methods. Additionally, the study reveals that using text from Twitter and the full Cornell dataset yields higher accuracy compared to employing a reduced Cornell dataset. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that accuracy improvements resulting from synthetic oversampling are more pronounced when classification difficulties are greater. Ultimately, the study concludes that using synthetic oversampling methods, particularly those that generate samples near the decision boundary (such as random SMOTE), can be beneficial in improving text classification accuracy. The research provides a comprehensive analysis of the strengths and limitations of these methods and recommends their suitable applications. Interestingly, the study reveals that using synthetic oversampling methods, in some cases, results in lower (though not the lowest possible) but still passable classification scores, indicating the utility of such methods, but also suggesting a need for further investigations on their minimum useful classification scores. Moreover, the study recommends that future research, rather than focusing on data augmentation, gathers more detailed information on minority class examples to reduce the effects of class imbalance. The research provides valuable insights to classification engineers and data analysts. A practical guideline for classification engineers is provided at the end of the paper. The research has been conducted to contribute to knowledge in the field of text classification using synthetic oversampling methods. A practical demonstration of the research findings is shown in the video at the link below. https://youtu.be/7O6QsG8TCsI. The research code can be accessed via GitHub at https://github.com/basilevh/oversampling-text-classification. The research datasets can be obtained through the following links: https://github.com/jhess3/dl4tm/tree/master/data/cornell/movie and https://www.kaggle.com/aliu/bert-sentiment-analysis-on-imdb. Figures and tables are available on GitHub at https://github.com/basilevh/oversampling-text-classification/tree/master/figures-and-tables. Extra

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our analysis reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, news outlet popularity, and audience size, and also shows that disadvantaged populations received less pandemic-related information. Interestingly, our results indicate that COVID coverage by local news was either uncorrelated or negatively correlated with local case rates, a finding that may imply a limited role of local news in shaping community COVID awareness. Overall, our study provides empirical and timely evidence on the relationship between local news COVID coverage and health outcomes, and highlights the complex factors influencing news coverage and access during public health crises. It emphasizes the need for more efficient COVID communication strategies to reach populations with limited access to information, and underscores the significance of a thriving local news ecosystem in this endeavor. Finally, our analysis shows that COVID-related headlines by local news outlets varied according to politics of the audience but not its socioeconomic characteristics, a phenomenon that mirrors the broadening scope of local news coverage. As the pandemic and associated information dissemination continue to evolve, our results aim to offer insightful and data-driven insights for public health officials, local news outlets, and policymakers, and to inspire further research on the intricate relationships between media coverage, human behavior, and health outcomes. To support a deeper exploration of these relationships, the study's code and data are publicly available through GitHub. Moreover, our findings represent a concrete application of a vast array of news datasets through predictive modeling and analysis, thereby showcasing their value in informing the research agenda of NSF. Specifically, our study demonstrates that by analyzing various levels of news media coverage from national to local outlets, researchers can gain a more comprehensive understanding of the media's role in shaping public opinion and behavior, and also reveals that local news outlets possess distinct characteristics linked to independent sources, corporate interests, and a human-centered approach, and therefore require unique applied research approaches distinct from the ones needed to study national media coverage. Ultimately, our study highlights the critical role of predictive modeling in uncovering data stories and drawing policy-relevant conclusions, and therefore its potential to inform the research agenda of the NSF in the media

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated in three-dimensional space. However, one of the widespread methods for enhancing efficiency by reducing the number of grid points, fast multipole method, has a known flaw in conservation of angular momentum. This research aims to rectify that by developing a novel version of the FMM that preserves angular momentum and is compatible with SPH. Furthermore, the developed algorithm also guarantees the conservation of linear momentum and mass. To evaluate the effectiveness of the method, several tests were conducted. Using these results, a 32-body collision was analyzed to assess precision in restoring angular momentum and linear momentum in scenarios with controlled impacts. Additionally, a highly elastic and elastic collision were simulated to examine the conservation of linear momentum. Finally, a rotating sparse cloud was observed to verify the mass conservation. All tests showed that the modified FMM algorithm preserved both angular and linear momentum as well as mass with high-level accuracy. Compared to the standard FMM algorithm, this new method showed improved performance by 20% in scenarios involving small numbers of grid points. Overall, the developed algorithm resulted in reliable and efficient conservation of key quantities in hydrodynamics simulations using the FMM. As such, it has vast potential in applications involving SPH methods for astrophysical, astronomical, and planetary environments. For purposes of reproducibility and ease of use, the code for this project has been made openly accessible on the respective GitHub platform. Nevertheless, due to various FMM implementations across literature, which often complicate code integration, this new method faces some practical limitations in third-party implementations. Solving these limitations is key to making the algorithm accessible to a broader community. Following that, a complementary companion, which interfaces with the fast multipole method based on GPULSPH from Gandhi et al. 2020, has been added to this repository but is currently available on a best-effort basis due to these interdependent complexities. Notably, incorporating GPULSPH incorporates a variant of the FMM that fails to conserve angular momentum. Nonetheless, modifications suggested in this research have been incorporated to yield stable and conservative results. Nonetheless, integrating GPULSPH results in partial conservation of angular momentum but introduces a tiny, fixed drift in high-order models, which may pose problems for very precise applications, for instance, the 32-body collision, but one capable of being mitigated with additional optimization. The results for the integrated coefficients, representing an average over the entire experiment, are $\epsilon_N = 0.57 \pm 0.04$ and $\epsilon_E = 0.20 \pm 0.02$. The results for $\epsilon_N$ and $\epsilon_E$ as functions of energy $W$ and the squared momentum $|{\vec k}|$, show that $\epsilon_N$ increases with $W$, reaches a maximum, and decreases, while $\epsilon_E$ exhibits a dependence on $|{\vec k}|$. These effects can be explained by the effect of the one-boson exchange, particularly the photon. These comparisons also reveal that the QED predictions for $\epsilon_N (W)$ are too low both in the proton and the deuteron cases, while the predictions for $\epsilon_E (x)$ are too high according to the one-boson exchange model. We examine how animals and humans learn from other experts, focusing on efficient learning strategies. Previous studies suggest that generating varied examples from experts' teachings is an effective method for both human and animal learning. Despite this, current machine learning models rarely employ data augmentation, except in cases where the label information can be inferred. Drawing inspiration from the principles of efficient learning in animals and humans, we propose a data augmentation strategy for learning from parametric experts. By augmentating the expert's parameters, we create diverse examples that are presented to the learner at key points throughout the training process. The final example, presented at the time of the decision, is chosen based on criteria that include both the example's accuracy and the rate at which it changes. This method is analogous to procedures used in evolution and evolutionary development. We evaluate our approach on a variety of synthetic and real-world problems and demonstrate its efficacy in comparison to traditional methods. Additionally, we demonstrate that our technique can be adapted for online learning when no initial prior knowledge is available, presenting opportunities for future research. Experimental results indicate that our approach leads to substantial reductions in the time and computational resources required for learning. Importantly, our proposed method is shown to be robust to variations in hyperparameters. The research has implications for both theoretical and applied learning theories as well as practical learning algorithms. In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, could help verify that a dark matter signal originates from space rather than the Earth's background. With sufficient readout detail, such as when using large area TPCs with many pixels, it is possible to identify the direction of nuclear recoils by analyzing the shape of the drift trajectory. While this approach has been around for a while, we are taking it a step further. By using more sophisticated techniques, like projecting the trajectory in a specific way and utilizing drift velocity information, the ability to identify the direction becomes even more accurate. We are testing this method with simulated experiments on dark matter searches using sector-mesh electric fields and extremely sensitive readouts. The results show that these techniques can accurately determine the direction of both elastic and inelastic scattering, with accuracy ranging from degrees to a few degrees, and this direction is correlated with the local density of the target material. Additionally, the simulation results indicate that recoil angle accuracy is sensitive to the lattice constant of the readout pattern, the timing of the event, and the kinetic energy of the recoil, but not the angle of the incoming direction, unless it is directly above the detector. With sufficient readout detail, such as when using large area single-photon detection and more pixels, it is possible to identify not just the direction, but also the specific location of the recoil, narrowing down the search area to one point. With higher resolution, the simulated results show that the area where the recoil can originate from becomes increasingly confined. The experiment's ability to identify the location of the recoil is correlated with the size of the area and can be accurately determined both in terms of the distance from the center and the width of the search area. The techniques described here can be applied to any TPC using high-resolution readouts, and are especially useful for identifying mock dark matter signals originating from specific locations on the Earth, beyond what would be expected from standard Earth background, regardless of the kinetic energy or drift distance. However, we do observe some limitations to this method as the recoil angle approaches directly above the detector, to a degree that may be comparable to the size of the pixel, leading to reduced accuracy in this specific scenario. In conclusion, the ability to accurately and precisely identify both the direction and location of the recoil is a powerful tool that can be used to verify mock dark matter signals originating from specific locations on the Earth, beyond what would be expected from standard Earth background.

In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology. A thin steel plate is employed as the free surface of a liquid setup, which experiences perturbation at various lengths. By analyzing the catenary shapes formed when the plate drops, we observe how different lengths result in varying time lengths between subsequent maxima of the resulting waves. These observations lead to the conclusion that the interperiod $\Delta T$ is directly proportional to the plate length $L$. Furthermore, we deduce that the local gravity scale $g_{loc} = \Delta T / (L^2 / g)$ is a function solely dependent on the plate length, and that it is the local gravity that drives the underlying instability of the system. Our findings are then explained using the established theory of RTI through both semi-analytical and numerical approaches. [Until further notice, "our numerical" refers to the in-house code utilized in this study.] A key outcome of our work is that the instability period is determined by $L^2 / g$ and the plate drops in a manner predictable by the physics of heavy objects. In order to interpret the results, we develop a theoretical model considering the characteristics of the set-up as well as the behavior of magnetic and gravitational forces. Our model, which supports our experimental data through the employment of just two parameters, consists of a dynamic of object-dropping rather than the usual fluid dynamics you'd expect in a liquid. The method offers an invaluable tool for analyzing RTI through an innovative new approach. To visually illustrate the experiment, we present an accompanying movie. The presented research serves as an extension of our earlier work, which can be found in our publication 'Length matters, periodically. I - Data and model', available through arXiv at 2202.05211. This research project focuses on the advancement of a nonlinear field-split
preconditioner comprising two stages to expedite convergence of complex two-phase
fluid dynamics and transport within diverse porous media. A proposed algorithm,
Field-Split Multiplicative Schwarz Newton, operates in a sequential two-step process:
initially, an approximate update of pressure and saturation is achieved through
a preconditioning step by resolving sub-problems in succession; secondly, a
global Newton update is applied at the preconditioned state via system linearization.
Using demanding case studies, the FSMSN approach is evaluated against current
preconditioning methods (Conjugate Gradient without preconditioning, FAS-PC, and
MS-PC) via simulations on 3D two-phase flow and 3D geothermal systems. Notably, the FSMSN strategy exhibits superior convergence properties as compared to existing techniques, leading to considerable time savings in the majority of the tested scenarios.  A detailed examination of convergence data for specific iterations is provided in an accompanying paper. Our study employed a learning style assessment using the context of the Cooper's Foxes game and revealed that these different learning strategies are represented in distinct neural patterns within the midbrain area of humans. When humans operate robot arms, it is frequently necessary for the robot to infer the task the human is attempting to accomplish. Current research on assistive teleoperation and shared control focuses on developing methods for the robot to determine the desired task based on limited human input. We have identified that the gap between provided robot data and human intention is largely attributable to the differing assumptions each party makes about the actions the other considers conventional. Our study investigates these assumptions of conventional action within a shared control paradigm for manipulating objects. We devised a communication system that transmits information about the robot's proposed sequence of conventional actions and the anticipated resulting object movement. The final object position in these predictions corresponds to the desired task. To refine this communication, we employed machine learning algorithms for inferring conventional actions, training them using annotated videos depicting common tasks like picking up a specific object. Our study reveals that the communication system's effectiveness depends heavily on the complexity of the desired task and the quality of the conventional action inference. To minimize reliance on these factors, we explored an alternative approach that adjusts the robot's dynamics to make its predicted actions more intuitive for the human operator to understand. Our results show that these dynamic changes can enhance communication by showcasing more predictable, explorable robot behavior, thus filling in the gaps between intended actions and their resulting consequences. Our code for these findings is available for review on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/autonomouslab-ucd/visual_conventions. Though initially, our research was grounded in unidirectional teleoperation, the insights we've gathered suggest that the issues we've addressed will also affect the behavior of autonomous systems working in tandem with humans, specifically those utilizing reinforcement learning to infer the user's desired actions. Ultimately, to effectively address these impediments, the interplay between human and robot must be viewed as a collaborative interaction built on shared assumptions about conventional action, as demonstrated in our study of manual control. Additional discussion on extending our research to other control paradigms can be found in the online supplement to this paper. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. However, implementing this in unfamiliar environments is challenging due to inaccuracies in state estimation. To tackle this issue, a novel hierarchical map representation called HiTMap is introduced. It combines a local metric map with a coarse topological map, focusing on the interconnections between landmarks as key navigation data. As robots detect new landmarks, the topological structure is generated, and the correlation between the local map's landmarks and the global topological map's landmarks is calculated. Following this, the local metric map's topography is matched to the topological structure, and the transformations between the metric maps are computed. To validate HiTMap's performance, a method for combining the maps is developed and demonstrated in an outdoor environment using a Turtlebot. To compensate for the absence of state estimation, the novel High-Order Map Association (HOMA) algorithm is introduced, which computes the transformations between the metric maps based on the topological structure. The association method does not rely on state estimation and is driven solely by the topological structure of the environment. To evaluate HOMA's performance, a frequency analysis is performed, revealing that the majority of the transformations range is concentrated around 10 to 20 degrees of freedom, indicating that most changes in the robot's state can be explained by 15 parameters at most. Therefore, to maintain a balance between map accuracy and computation, a layer of state estimation is implemented, consisting of 15 Extended Kalman Filters, one for each degree of freedom, to produce the state vector needed to navigate the HiTMap. The proposed system was successfully tested in various unfamiliar outdoor and indoor environments using a Turtlebot equipped with a HD map generator (such as the SICK laser scanner) and proved to be as accurate as state-of-the-art methods without relying on them. The system's localization error was found to be less than one meter in the worst-case scenario and its navigation capabilities were proven through successful exploration and re-localization of the environment in all the experiments conducted. Furthermore, the system's adaptability over a wide range of state space dimensions and its ability to maintain its accuracy even when the environment's topology changes significantly was demonstrated through the experiments conducted. Time-based data refers to information measured against the backdrop of time, giving it a distinct structural context that forms the foundation of its constituent parts. When dealing with such data, particularly in large datasets, common statistical approaches like regression and machine learning can be complicated by the information loss incurred by reducing the data to a simpler, lower-dimensional format. Despite this, visualizations are a valuable tool for gaining insights and understanding time-based data. We can think of visualizations as methods for combining high-dimensional data with human cognitive abilities, allowing for the effective translation of complex information into a comprehensible format. However, interactive visualizations have a similar function – they don't simply present data, but also grant users the autonomy to manipulate it. To facilitate the development of interactive visualizations for time-based data, we've created the packages ggalt and ggnewscale, which expand the capabilities of the widely-used ggplot2 data visualization framework. With these packages, users can create interactive visualizations for time-based data, incorporating metrics like longitudinal data and multivariate time series, as well as creating step transition and parallel coordinate plots. Examples and demonstration code can be found at https://mmpp.github.io/ggaltShiny/. A live, interactive version can be accessed at https://mmpp.github.io/ggaltShiny-shiny/. This research investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-user, multi-relay communication system with a maximum diversity network coding technique. A direct link between outage probability, energy consumption, and energy efficiency is established, followed by a formulation of the optimization problem to maximize energy efficiency under the constraint of maintaining a target outage probability. A practical scheduling and power allocation strategy is implemented to minimize power usage. To tackle this complex problem, a two-stage strategy is employed, combining a sequence of outer and inner approximation techniques with a successive convex approximation method to find solutions. Initially, an outer approximation framework is used to address a convex optimization problem that approximates the original non-convex one. Subsequently, an inner approximation approach is applied to narrow down the solution space, followed by a convex approximation and a solution optimization. Monte-Carlo simulations validate the efficacy of the proposed method and illustrate its ability to adapt to diverse network conditions. Notably, the technique offers a significant energy efficiency gain of up to two orders of magnitude over traditional selection combining schemes, while maintaining a performance level comparable to these benchmarks in terms of outage probability. Simulation results indicate that a compromise between energy efficiency, outage probability, and total power usage, expressed as the ratio of energy efficiency to outage probability, can be achieved with a corresponding gain of up to 50% through this compromise. Moreover, the simulation outcomes illustrate the robustness and resilience of the proposed method in diverse network conditions, encompassing different numbers of transmit and receive power, maximum transmission rates, path loss, channel attenuation, noise uncertainty, and network coding benefits. Specifically, the technique achieves a substantial network coding gain of approximately 60% in scenarios with varying numbers of transmit power, while maintaining a comparable performance level with respect to receive power. Similarly, the technique achieves a negligible model dependency and thus a resilient performance level with respect to diverse channel attenuation while maintaining a comparable outlook. Finally, the simulation results illustrate the technique's ability to adapt to different network conditions by achieving a substantial gain of up to 50% with less than 1% fair share in scenarios involving total system energy efficiency, outage probability, and total power usage, expressed as the ratio of energy efficiency to outage probability. Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an issue that experts struggle with.
Recent studies propose using artificial intelligence-based techniques to segment
MS lesions. This study is unique in comparing the effectiveness of three AI-based
strategies: training models from scratch, continuing the training process, and using
pre-trained models. Our MS-Lesion CATDAT database, comprising over 600,000 lesion
segments from 13 hospitals across 10 countries, enabled this large-scale examination.
Evaluating methods against manual segments, our results demonstrate that
continuing the training process results in better lesions segmentation than
training models from scratch and using pre-trained models. Notably, continuing the
training process yields similar outcomes to manual segments, demonstrating its
potential in the context of clinical datasets. This study also highlights the
importance of data quality and the value of large-scale training in achieving
accurate MS lesion segmentation. Continuing the training process, however, still
struggles with generalization, a significant area of improvement. While prior
studies have investigated the potential of transferring knowledge across related
tasks, our MS-Lesion segmentation study shows limited success in achieving
transfer. Ultimately, our study offers a quantitative understanding of the
trade-offs associated with the three AI-based strategies and suggests that
continuing the training process is a reliable option, especially under time-
constrained conditions. Notably, our study also identifies several issues related
to the initial training of the models, including their lack of understanding of the
data and resulting information-dependent biases, as well as their sensitivity to
data quality. These findings highlight the need for uniform annotation guidelines
and high-quality datasets for accurate MS lesion segmentation. Finally, our study
points to the critical role of validation in achieving accurate segmentation, a
feature that is often overlooked, particularly in the context of the training from
scratch and transfer strategies. Overall, our study compares the effectiveness of
the three AI-based strategies under realistic conditions and offers a thorough
analysis of the trade-offs associated with each method. It sheds light on the
challenges of the training from scratch and transfer approaches and suggests
continuing the training process as a reliable and time-efficient option.

Set-theoretic preference models, particularly for set addition, offer clear explanations and easy implementation, as well as the ability to learn user preferences without prior knowledge.  Notably, they are particularly effective in tasks where users value complex characteristics in data, such as image features or molecular structures. Long-term CB data yielded rankings indistinguishable to those obtained by CopiRank, highlighting the effectiveness and reliability of this algorithm in the set addition domain. Transformer-based language models have been shown to struggle with logical reasoning, especially when it involves negation. Unlike previous studies that relied on psycholinguistic tools, our research delves into types of negation from developmental psychology. We examine this knowledge gap through a natural language inference task by creating a specialized dataset that requires understanding various forms of negation. Our analysis reveals that the models demonstrate significant knowledge about some negation concepts, such as 'none,' but struggle with more complex ideas, like the absence of a given object or event. We also discover models tend to make as many incorrect inferences as correct ones when interpreting negation. Ultimately, our findings suggest models can serve as a valuable resource in uncovering insights into human cognition, especially when combined with human knowledge, which has yet to be utilized effectively. To address this, we suggest a new training method that leverages model weights from the analysis and utilizes human responses to guide automated question-asking during training. By exploring questions developed from the developmental psychology literature, our approach aims to bridge the divide between artificial and human intelligence. We test this idea with two case studies involving numeracy and object categorization, which indicate improved performance after employing our training method. Our research presents one step towards reconciling human and artificial cognitive systems, specifically addressing the limitations of current large language models. Experimental evaluation on three major language pairs demonstrates substantial gains in translation accuracy, measured by BLEU scores, for the suggested look-ahead model. Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing techniques to explain these models can be particularly challenging. To address this issue, a framework called LaViSE is proposed to enable convolutional neural networks to describe their internal workings in plain text. By using generic image data, this approach creates a link between visual and semantic information, allowing for its application across different domains without explicit labels. The LaViSE framework has a flexible structure, making it possible to analyze any network, while also able to pinpoint the specific parts of an image that are linked to particular words, as well as handle networks with both convolutional and recurrent layers. Furthermore, this technique can accurately identify the level of accuracy in network predictions without requiring precise annotations, making it a valuable tool for evaluating network performance and identifying areas for improvement. To showcase its effectiveness, visual explanations from the framework have been applied to various models across different domains, demonstrating that they provide plausible and meaningful accounts of network behavior. To support these findings, a comprehensive dataset is provided to facilitate future research, consisting of image-vocabulary pairs across multiple domains, which can be accessed via an online dashboard platform. This resource allows for the analysis of different models and their performance, while also enabling users to see the visual explanations from the inside of the network, to understand the link between different parts of an image and words. To further support these results, a technique is developed to measure the level of complexity in written text, which can be applied to various domains, as shown in the accompanying video.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty as a quantifiable measure of a model's reliability. To accurately quantify the reliability of a model, we establish a framework incorporating theoretical steganographic principles and the underlying principles of Bayesian neural networks. To calculate the inherent unpredictability of a channel, we apply an entropy-based method. Through experiments, we demonstrate that reliable steganographic communications can be achieved by adjusting parameters in accordance with the calculated reliability metrics. Our findings also highlight that widely-used accuracy metrics may not effectively evaluate the steganographic capabilities of a channel. To overcome this issue, we develop a novel quantitative measure of steganographic security, which can be calculated using predictive uncertainty and the inherent channel unpredictability. Our proposed methodology allows for the creation of secure communication protocols that rely on a reliable channel prediction. Experimental results illustrate that our proposed approach achieves the highest steganographic capacity without sacrificing security, as well as provides secure communications with low predictive error and heightened steganographic security, measured by the steganographic security metric we introduced. Additionally, the challenges posed by primordial helium enhancement, heavy element synthesis, and supernova yields will be discussed, and the extraordinary features of hot gas will be examined, such as metal-poor regions, gas outflows, and the halos surrounding these galaxies. The implications of the halos will be considered, particularly in terms of galaxy interactions and the role of ram-pressure forces, as well as the potential connection of outflows to the global metal enrichment of the universe. The data on hot gas will be mostly based on soft X-ray observations, and the discussion will take into account the limitations of current knowledge due to the difficulties involved in detecting the weak and rare phenomena in the low-mass objects of the local universe. The aim of the review is to assess whether the interstellar medium of dwarf galaxies offers insights into the formation of galaxies and the universe will be be discussed. The first part of the review will cover the galaxies in the local universe while the second part will discuss the dwarf galaxies that lie more than 13 billion light years away in the universe through observations of high-redshift galaxies. The primary difference between the two will be that the second part will deal with purely theoretical aspects since no observational data on the cosmic history exist. The existence of very distant dwarf galaxies will be used as a reference point to determine the time of their formation between 13 and 1 billion years after the universe began. The characteristics of their stellar populations will be based on existing data, and the interstellar medium of these galaxies will be described based on the predictions of the models that are in agreement with the measured properties of their progenitor dark-matter halos, which were identified through observations of their rotational curves and the amount of Lyman-alpha emission. The predictions will concern the present state of their interstellar medium, and the differences between their present-state properties and those of the nearby dwarf galaxies will be explained. The main point of difference between the nearby and very distant dwarf galaxies concerns their potential for star formation, which was not limited by gas and metal abundance in the universe at the time of their formation, and the implications of their predicted properties for their cosmic history will be discussed. To address this issue, we aimed to establish a standardized summary quality assessment process, but discovered it's ineffective due to inconsistent worker behavior. Thus, we focused on developing a predictive model using summary and crowd assessment data to identify top-performing workers. Surprisingly, our analysis showed that these models perform poorly, which prompted us to investigate Turkification, a statistical analysis revealing that workers' summary quality stabilizes after writing around 500 ratings. Consequently, we developed an optimized hiring process for high-quality summarizers. Initially, we assess large groups of workers via automated crowdsourcing tasks, analyzing their performance based on summary and crowd assessment data. Subsequently, we target top performers with exclusive summarization tasks, supplemented by a prediction model that identifies exceptional performers among remaining workers. Evaluating this process between August 2020 and October 2021, we found that it significantly increased the proportion of high-quality summarizers and reduced overall variation in summary quality. A direct comparison with our previous hiring practices demonstrated that this optimized process yielded 57% better outcomes. Importantly, our results and analysis provide the deepest exploration to date into the factors influencing MTurk worker behavior and summary quality, laying the groundwork for future research. To overcome these limitations, we present TS2-Net, a cutting-edge text-video retrieval framework that leverages the adaptability of transformer models to dynamically position and pick video tokens based on the given text features. Our extensive experiments show that TS2-Net outperforms other models significantly, establishing a new benchmark in various text-video retrieval benchmarks, including YouTube Caption, T-Vlad, and Human Activity Submissions. Additionally, we release an open-source code of TS2-Net for public use at https://github.com/whuiye/TS2-Net. In response to the intricacies of network data, a new type of hybrid network is suggested that blends rules for preferential attachment and uniform attachment.  This hybrid network creates edges according to a mixture of these rules.  Specifically, when a new edge is added, it follows the preferential attachment rule with a certain probability and otherwise forms between two randomly selected nodes.  This approach leads to a distribution of node in- and out-degrees that has less extreme outliers compared to a purely preferential attachment network, thereby improving upon this traditional model.  Inference methods applicable to the new model are then explored and demonstrated to work well in both theoretical and real-world network scenarios.  Moreover, the proposed model is shown to closely replicate the characteristics of the Facebook network.  Ultimately, the utility of this model is illustrated through application to the Wikipedia network.  In particular, the proposed model yields accurate predictions for raw degree sequences in this network, a prediction quality that significantly surpasses that of the traditional preferential attachment model. Future high-energy muon colliders face a challenge due to in-flight decays of
muons from the beam line, resulting in a substantial beam-induced background
(BIB). This problem needs to be addressed to achieve accurate data collection
and operate efficiently, meeting physics goals. Simulation studies were conducted
using the addbolt++ code to assess BIB at various collider designs. Initially,
the study analyzed a 3 TeV proton proton collider, discovering a trade-off where
a higher number of low-intensity muon beams could reduce BIB more effectively
than a smaller number of intense beams. However, this approach is tied to a
specific proton luminosity, leading to an exploration of alternative methods
to lower BIB at the muon collider level. These involve increasing the muon
luminosity by enhancing the muon acceleration process, improving the beam
quality, or using more advanced technologies to filter out BIB. Notably, the
method of enhancing the beam quality showed the greatest potential for significant
improvement, reflecting general strategies for reducing BIB at the muon collider
level. Further simulations demonstrated these methods at the level of electron
colliders, revealing additional advantages. This research underpins future studies to
investigate and evaluate numerous BIB reduction strategies at collider designs. Furthermore, the development of BIB reduction as a universal principle could have
far-reaching implications in design choices and optimization processes for
accelerator systems. The proposed methods are intended for widespread use in
designing future lepton colliders, where reducing BIB can notably enhance the
accuracy and operation efficiency of these future accelerators. To this end, the
techniques described can serve as foundational guidance for future design and
optimization processes for accelerator systems, integrating BIB reduction as a
universal principle. An accompanying software tool based on the bolt code is
available to the public for designing and implementing BIB reduction strategies.

Software developers widely acknowledge the importance of unit testing as a crucial aspect of their work cycle, allowing for swift detection and resolution of coding errors. However, test code can be compromised by suboptimal design or implementation choices referred to as test smells. These shortcomings can significantly undermine the quality of software systems by exacerbating difficulties in comprehension, amplifying maintenance complexities, and making systems more susceptible to bugs and errors. Prior studies have investigated the likely consequences of test smells on test code. Despite their negative implications, the degree to which these shortcomings affect the quality of software systems remains an empirical uncertainty. Following an in-depth analysis of open-source software systems, our study empirically examined how software developers perceive and assess the gravity of test smells affecting the quality of software systems. The findings from our study reveal that test smell severity is a subject of individual interpretation, as reflected in the diverse answers provided by developers. The study's analysis identified two distinct categories, with one consisting of similarities in responses and another characterized by distinct views on the matter. A developer's level of experience, programming background, and field of specialization were found to influence their perception and understanding of test smells. The study's insights prompted the creation of a checklist to aid developers in making informed decisions and the design of effective solutions to mitigate and eliminate test smells. This paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a modified version of the sweeping process, first proposed by J.J. Moreau in the early 1970s as part of plasticity theory. The updated model involves a novel combination of the prox-regular moving set, an integrable right-hand side, and a starting point with specific properties. Our analysis utilizes the Aubin continuity of the mapping associated with the moving set, along with the continuity of its normal cone mapping, to expand the theoretical framework of the sweeping process. Additionally, the obtained results will be applied to the study of nonlinear oscillators, thereby enhancing the theoretical understanding of these systems. Furthermore, the obtained ideas will be used to develop a new paradigm for integer partitioning problems, thereby creating a link between the studied differential process and the combinatorial aspects of integer partitioning. The numerical solution to the integer partitioning problem will, in turn, be used to optimize its parameters, leading to innovative applications in document frequency (df) sparse document classification, a core component of modern Information Retrieval systems. The proposed method will be validated through experimental results on sparse df. The contributions of this work lie in the newly established relationships between the studied differential processes and the combinatorial aspects of integer partitioning, with potential applications in optimization, document classification, and other fields. We introduce the updated version of the {\tt KKMCee} event generator, version 5.00.2, designed for simulating lepton and quark pair production through high-energy electron-positron annihilations. As the most advanced generator for this process, the code, now rewritten entirely in modern C++, maintains all features of its Fortran 77 predecessor, while incorporating several enhanced Monte Carlo algorithm improvements. Its capabilities, supplemented with next-to-leading order QED corrections, genuine weak corrections using the {\tt DIZET} library, and polarized $\tau$ decays facilitated by {\tt TAUOLA}, serve as a starting point for future updates to achieve the high precision needed for next-generation lepton colliders. Moreover, this version integrates {\tt HEPMC3}, a new interface that replaces {\tt HepEvt}, to connect the {\tt KKMCee} with other essential components of the collider simulation framework. Specifically, this new interface enables the interoperability of {\tt KKMCee} with other key tools, such as {\tt PHYSIM}, a comprehensive particle transport simulator, and {\tt Delphes}, a popular framework for Fast Simulation of colliders. These new collaboration and interface elements, along with their impact on the event generator, are explored in this presentation. Furthermore, this updated {\tt KKMCee} event generator, along with the corresponding Fortran 77 code and interface tools, are now available for download through the respective repository websites of the {\tt KKMCee} (within the framework of the {\tt PHYSIM} collider simulation environment), the Fortran 77 {\tt KKMC} code, the {\tt DIZET} library, the {\tt TAUOLA} event generator, the interface tool {\tt HEPMC} (along the lines of the {\tt PHYSIM} repository), and the Fast Simulation tool {\tt Delphes}. The corresponding release notes for these updates are also provided. Finally, this update marks an important milestone in the event generators' transition from Fortran 77 to modern C++ and, in the long run, Fortran 95+MPI. Specifically, this update represents the first major achievement of the new {\tt PHYSIM} repository within the {\tt PHYSIM} collider simulation framework. Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have identified signal denoising and IBI estimation as a significant area of focus. Recent breakthroughs have involved the use of deep learning, which has significantly improved signal quality and diagnostic accuracy, far exceeding previous limitations. A novel deep learning approach is being developed using a Tiramisu autoencoder to effectively tackle the problem of motion-induced noise and improve IBI estimation. Experimental findings indicate that this method surpasses existing solutions in terms of accuracy and efficiency, showcasing considerable potential in real-world applications. Moreover, the ensemble network's performance shows promising results in enhancing the signal's quality and guiding subsequent post-processing steps. Ultimately, the estimated IBIs demonstrate a substantial reduction in error compared to the current state-of-the-art, opening up new possibilities in early disease detection and cardiovascular well-being monitoring. Quantifiable improvements include an 85% reduction in estimation inaccuracy, measured as the root-mean-square error, and an 8% increase in successful IBIs identified from the signal. A notable byproduct of this research is the establishment of a benchmark dataset consisting of noisy synthetic signals from public datasets, annotated with precise IBIs, which can be utilized by other researchers in the field. This dataset is available at https://github.com/Debanjan/ECG-IBI-ESTIMATE. The research's key contributions are the accurate estimation of IBIs from highly noisy signals, the significant enhancement of signal denoising and IBI estimation accuracy, and the creation of a new benchmark dataset. The research sheds light on novel techniques that can enhance the interpretation of noisy signals, leveraging expert knowledge from expert cardiologists to identify and correct estimation errors. A demonstration of this method is available as an Android app on Google Play Store at https://play.google.com/store/activities/details?id=com.example.ecgibiestimate. The overpasses approach, established for matrix singular value decomposition, can be applied to t-SVD by selecting a random subset of data points and summing over the remaining, yielding an accurate solution with a higher number of passes than the matrix counterpart, though still an arbitrary number. The present study builds upon a 2017 framework proposed by Beyer et al., who used 6n passes to obtain an O(n) approximation of the t-SVD solution, improving upon this in 2020 with 3n passes, and now further refines the solution to achieve an O(n) approximation in 2n passes, and even offers a faster method in 1n passes with reduced memory, albeit with potential data corruption. The study provides a detailed analysis of the solution quality and numerical validation of the new method. An implementation of the new method, named tsvd_overpasses, is now available with the PyTensor repository. Deep Metric Learning methods primarily aim to develop a space where data similarities can be accurately maintained. These methods have made substantial improvements in many areas but have failed to account for the broader range of similarity constraints. As a result, metric learning methods only utilize margin parameters that cap similarity values at a specific upper bound. However, this approach leaves unaddressed the similarities that exceed these bounds. Moreover, margins in metric learning often struggle to adapt to diverse data distributions, leading to suboptimal performance. To overcome these limitations, we present a novel objective function that leverages the Sinkhorn Distance, which reflects all the similarities in the dataset. Unlike existing metrics, this distance measure is adaptable to arbitrary similarity distributions. We then develop a method for differentiating the Sinkhorn Distance, which in turn enables us to train Deep Metric Learning models using backpropagation. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments with multiple datasets of varying sizes. Importantly, we demonstrate that our method enhances metric learning models, improving their ability to withstand dataset transformations and outliers. Notably, we apply the Sinkhorn Distance to the field of metric learning, introducing an innovative use of its convexity properties via the optimization of the decision boundary's margin using the Conjugate Gradient method. While the standard formulation of the Sinkhorn Distance is non-differentiable, we present a distinct version that facilitates end-to-end training of deep models. To the best of our knowledge, this differentiation method is originally presented here. We explore the utility of our approach for learning deep embeddings that capture dataset similarities and apply it to the task of metric learning. Focused on the Melotte 72 open star cluster, located 2345+/-108 parsecs away and 1.0+/-0.5 billion years old, our study leverages Gaia DR2's databases and parallax measurements. By only considering stars with expected cluster radial velocity within the survey, we analyzed 661 likely cluster stars, revealing a prominent asymmetry, suggesting Melotte 72 is slightly deformed. Our calculations yield the following cluster parameters: concentration index I_0=0.78, and the L_*
/m_V ratio at the cluster center equal to 7.69. Additionally, our statistical analysis of Melotte 72's radial distribution indicates an irregular and offset main sequence, which could result from a cluster projection and stellar crowding effects. Our study provides a richly detailed cluster radii, ranging from 13 to 16 solar radii, despite some uncertainty. By matching observed and expected cluster radial velocities, we determined the radial velocity of Melotte 72 to be approximately 64.9 km/s. Finally, our analysis of the cluster's proper motion reveals no center of expansion and our calculation of the parallax error for Melotte 72 indicates a margin of error of about 0.12 millparsec. Overall, our analysis presents a comprehensive examination of Melotte 72 using the Gaia DR2 survey. Data analysis applications in medicine, cosmology, and materials science are witnessing growing popularity of random excursion models, which generate threshold-crossing data from local noise. Our research investigates the Betti numbers - a tool for capturing topological features, which often conveys information on the structural organization of the data. By focusing on the sparse regime, we derived precise asymptotic expressions for the first two Betti numbers of the excursion set, building on the Betti numbers' prior study under stronger assumptions. Our results, based on a corrector approach, reveal the precise variate parts of these asymptotics. Furthermore, we established a universal asymptotic formula for the highest Betti number via combinatorial techniques, which also facilitates the identification of the lower threshold for a sparse-excitation transition in exclusion processes. Additionally, we provided novel local limit theorems for homology classes and persistence functions of Gaussian excursions, complementing prior non-asymptotic studies. This enabled us to graphically visualize homology structures via persistence diagrams and to detect their non-stationary, short-range correlations and multivariate patterns resulting, for example, from exclusion processes' quasi-translation invariance. Finally, we verified the asymptotic homogeneity of Gaussian excursion models through a multivariate central limit theorem. This research showcases the asymptotic theory's power in uncovering the complex, hidden structure of the data, as experimentally validated under weakly correlated settings. Such findings are not only desirable but also necessary for the efficient use of topological data analysis methods, given their built-in asymptotic nature. As corroborated by real-world examples, our results provide clear, testable hypotheses for future empirical studies. Although based on precise mathematical assumptions, our model can be applied and tested in various contexts, given the widespread occurrence of Gaussian noise and threshold-crossing data. Artificial intelligence models generate a 3D hand pose estimation, but to compensate for discrepancies, we used both traditional and artificial intelligence-based methods for refining the hand pose estimation and camera calibration parameters.
