One notable strategy to embed prior knowledge about physical systems into machine learning models is physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). These models have been observed to perform well with smaller training datasets, achieve faster training times, and successfully generalize to unobserved conditions. However, the lack of a theoretical basis for PINNs makes it challenging to ensure the reliability of their predictions. This study proposes an a posteriori error estimation technique for PINNs, which enables the evaluation of a posteriori errors in PINNs and PINN-based identification problems. To achieve this goal, we first investigate the deep neural networks consisting of a fully neural network with a ReLU activation function and its associated series expression without any activation function, based on the relevant theory of adaptive finite element methods. Next, we deduce a posteriori error estimators for the solutions of the PINNs and propose an iterative process to guarantee the convergence of the estimated errors. To validate our theoretical findings, we conduct a series of numerical experiments with both PINNs and a PINN-based parameter identification problem for a partial differential equations system describing a resonant cardan degree of freedom. This example shows the significance of accurately estimating the residual errors in PINNs as it is directly related to the accuracy of the solution. This study and the associated findings are expected to contribute significantly to the theoretical research on the PINNs and the deep neural networks, facilitating the reliable use of deep learning methods in scientific and engineering computations. The study was implemented using the open-source libraries PyPINNs and Pytorch, for more details see [22, 23]. Although our research focuses on PINNs, the proposed techniques can be extended to other physics-informed neural networks that satisfy the relevant continuity conditions. Furthermore, the proposed methods can be applied to a variety of PINN-based identification problems where the continuity of the neural networks is an essential factor. To extend the proposed techniques to other types of neural networks, a relevant theory of a posteriori error estimation for the underlying continuity space without activation function is required. For a comprehensive understanding of the proposed techniques and to ensure their successful implementation, we recommend using an object-oriented coding style that separates the code into three layers: the physics, the neural networks, and the approximation layers. Furthermore, using the given and proposed estimators consistently in all layers of the code can help ensure the accurate estimation of the a posteriori errors. For epidemiologic studies of large populations, accurate air pollution modeling is crucial. Leveraging advances in big data analytics and machine learning has led to breakthroughs in air pollution modeling frameworks. This discussion highlights recent breakthroughs and proposes enhancements from the viewpoints of geostatistics and machine learning. Future developments will integrate learning algorithms with spatial analysis, allowing for the incorporation of spatial correlations in the modeling process. This integration is expected to improve the precision of existing air pollution models, thereby enhancing exposure assessments. As a result, researchers can conduct more thorough air pollution and health risk assessments. Moreover, future air pollution models should incorporate essential air pollution variables, such as particulate matter and ozone, to reflect the most recent air pollution monitoring technologies. These enhancements are expected to underpin future air pollution modeling advancements and advance our understanding of the complex links between air pollution and human health, ozone, and climate change. They will also facilitate the optimization of air pollution mitigation strategies, such as carbon pricing and climate change adaptation. To demonstrate the feasibility of these ideas, we show how to incorporate spatial modeling processes into two typical air pollution modeling scenarios for regression models and neural networks. Our study reveals the benefits of combining machine and spatial learning to improve air pollution modeling processes. The growing importance of Adversarial Machine Learning within Computer Science can be attributed to vulnerabilities in models and crowd-sourced attacks on data. Over the past two years, research has expanded to include graph-based data poisoning as a form of adversarial machine learning attack. Unlike traditional data poisoning attacks that target linear models, graph-based poisoning attacks target model predictions on temporal sequences, making them challenging to defend against due to the difficulty in identifying stealthy attacks and limited available training data. Unlike other forms of adversarial machine learning, defenders have a strategic advantage in graph-based poisoning attacks - they have access to a model that is still in training, a Graph Neural Network (GNN) classifier. A natural extension of this is to develop a reinforcement learning agent that actively searches for optimal poisoning strategies in graph-based systems. 

In this study, we employ reinforcement learning to defend against graph-based poisoning attacks. A detailed simulation framework is introduced to evaluate GNN robustness and defend against poisoning attacks. 
The simulation framework is then used to evaluate the effectiveness of reinforcement learning in defending against graph-based poisoning attacks. 
The simulation results show that reinforcement learning is an effective strategy to defend against poisoning attacks in graph-based systems. 
Moreover, the simulation results suggest that there is an inverse relationship between the robustness of a GNN and its level of complexity. 
The simulation results were obtained after extensive testing of over 22,000 GNN models. 
A comprehensive experimental study is also presented to validate the results obtained from the simulation model and provide experimental evidence of the effectiveness of reinforcement learning in graph-based systems. 
Finally, a novel algorithm is presented - the adversarial robust optimization algorithm (ARO) - to defend against poisoning attacks in graph-based systems. 
The ARO algorithm outperforms reinforcement learning in terms of attack success rate and model loss. 
The ARO algorithm achieves an average loss reduction of $\boldsymbol{7.1\pm 0.6\%}$ compared to the baseline loss and this loss reduction holds true for over $\boldsymbol{95\%}$ of the test set. 
The results of our study indicate that the ARO algorithm is a more effective strategy to defend against poisoning attacks in graph-based systems. 
Lastly, a theoretical analysis of the ARO algorithm is provided using concentration inequalities. 
The theoretical analysis confirms that the performance of the ARO algorithm is consistent with the simulation results obtained in this study.

Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected concepts. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly balance the exploration of all concept relationships and large hierarchical structures. OntoPlot's novel hybrid visualisation incorporates icicle plots, interactive elements, and space-efficient visual compression to enhance understanding and reduce visual clutter. Through a user study involving domain experts, we validated OntoPlot's efficacy and obtained valuable feedback, illustrating its potential to streamline ontology-driven software development for large, complex ontologies. By integrating OntoPlot and related visualisation tools, developers can create custom exploration tools for ontologies, encompassing both hierarchical and non-hierarchical structures, to facilitate seamless navigation and understanding between these different types of concept relationships. Inter-domain loss aims to derive a common speech-text representation through a shared neural network, which we found could train end-to-end models even without a label. However, training loss functions can hinder model performance; thus, we explored methods to improve the trained model's effectiveness. By leveraging CycleGAN to transform speech and text into a single domain, we can fine-tune the inter-domain loss and enhance the model's performance, particularly its generalization capabilities. Our approach achieves a high 12% reduction in character error rate on the WSJ dataset, outperforming previous methods that trained only the speaker-dependent model or incorporated an inter-domain loss alone. With this advanced model, we manage to reduce the character error rate on the Voxforge dataset to 15.9, making us the first to achieve an error rate below 16.0. Our study of the Soret effect, conducted under low concentration conditions, revealed that soft molecules exhibit a temperature-dependent Soret coefficient. This behavior can be attributed to the temperature-dependent flexibility of the soft molecules, which allows for a greater contribution of internal degrees of freedom to the Soret effect, as opposed to rigid molecules. Additionally, the effect of molecular flexibility on the Soret effect was found to be temperature-dependent, with greater importance at lower temperatures. This characteristic distinguishes soft molecules from rigid molecules, whose behavior is independent of temperature. To quantify the effect of molecular flexibility on the Soret effect, a new parameter, called the flexibility factor, was defined and evaluated. This parameter was found to significantly impact the Soret effect, with a greater effect observed at lower temperatures. To further investigate the effect of molecular flexibility on the Soret effect, our experiment was conducted under various temperature conditions, revealing a temperature-dependent outcome, which can be accurately explained using the modified Soret coefficient equation. This modified equation incorporates the flexibility factor and has successfully accounted for the experimental results, thus demonstrating its validity. This study not only contributes to our understanding of the Soret effect but also has implications for the application of this phenomenon to the separation of mixtures, with the potential to soft-molecule-based separation methods. To facilitate the practical implementation of this idea, our experimental results are analyzed to identify the optimal temperature conditions for achieving the maximum Soret effect, which can serve as a guiding principle for the development of separation technologies based on this phenomenon. This could potentially lead to the advancement of innovative and effective methods for the separation of mixtures, with the flexibility of soft molecules playing a key role in this process. The development of Automated Essay Scoring involves a fusion of expertise from Education, Linguistics, and Natural Language Processing. Effective evaluation by an NLP model depends on its ability to identify patterns in written content, even in cases where the writing quality is subpar. Despite the current prominence of large transformer-based models in various NLP applications, these models' computational complexity poses significant practical limitations to their deployment. This paper sets out to dispute the prevailing notion that larger models necessarily lead to better performance in Automated Essay Scoring. To this end, the study assesses the capabilities of multiple NLP models with fewer parameters that were fine-tuned on an AES dataset and demonstrates superior results can be achieved by combining these models' outputs, thereby reducing the total number of required parameters. Notably, the best outcomes were achieved by ensemble methods using small models, far exceeding the performance of a large state-of-the-art model, and surpassing the results of a contemporary transformer-based AES model in the process. These findings have implications for the future direction of AES research. Moreover, the study advocates for a more efficient, balanced approach to NLP model development, prioritizing systems that balance performance, size, and adaptability, and highlights the importance of model evaluation strategies that account for diversity and measure the relative usefulness of individual models and their collective contributions. Ultimately, the study's outcomes suggest promising avenues for the advancement of NLP models through the gradual increase in model capabilities, size, and complexity.

One of the false positive issues in pedestrian detection is the dominance of false positives in new domains due to the discrepancy between the distribution of positive boxes and ground truth boxes. This problem can be tackled by suppressing false positives in a pedestrian detection box domain. However, existing suppression methods are impractical for new domains because they rely on positively labeled boxes, which are scarce and biased. To address this challenge, we present a novel method called Box Re-Ranking, which distinguishes false positives from positives without relying on labels, resulting in an improved false positive rate after pedestrian detection. Box Re-Ranking consists of two components: 1) it converts pedestrian detection boxes into dense clusters with a high variance in box coordinates, and 2) it assigns an confidence score to each box as a clustering variant, effectively re-ranking boxes in the pedestrian domain. Our perceptual study revealed that individuals tend to more readily notice errors in underhand rather than overhand throwing gestures. To incorporate syntax-aware decoding into Neural Machine Translation systems, a novel NMT architecture called Seq2Tree is proposed, utilizing a syntactic dependency parsing module to obtain sentence structure. The system leverages the parsing module to determine the sentence structure and utilizes the analysis to compute target language syntax-based representations. These representations, specifically CBOW-style context vectors, encompass both word and sentence context, merging word meanings based on syntax, thus enhancing the translation process. By merging a sentence's representation, hidden states from the encoder are transformed into context vector pairs consisting of a word's CBOW and a sentence's CBOV, guiding decoder decisions. Experimental evaluations on English-to-German and English-to-Russian datasets demonstrate improvements in translation performance, with the proposed Seq2Tree architecture delivering up to a +3.04 BLEU score, compared to a baseline NMT system. Additionally, the proposed method exhibits an on average 4.51 F1-measure increase in parsing accuracy when assessed independently on a parsing dataset. Furthermore, the proposed method generates novel context vector pairs, enabling dependency parsing to obtain extra contextual information not available through parsing alone, resulting in an average 2.31 F1-measure increase in slot filling accuracy, a supporting task of parsing, after slot filling models have been trained independently. Thus, the proposed method demonstrates translations and parses that are aligned and syntax-aware, providing added context to NMT system interpretations. To extend understanding of the proposed method, a game is introduced, allowing the model's behavior to be interactively assessed, providing insight into NMT system decision-making with syntax-aware context, a key capability for generating more informed translations in multiple language contexts. A multiplicative stochastic process with lognormally distributed lower bounds is studied, where a theoretical model of the process is developed and an empirical model based on this formulation is proposed and validated using historical copper price data. The novelty of the approach lies in generating a multiplicative series with a guarantee of at least one data point below a specified threshold, making it suitable for series with extreme values and useful for model development, such as the tails of probability distributions and extreme value prediction in finance. The empirical model's effectiveness is assessed by comparing the properties of the generated series with the actual data. The analysis focuses on three key aspects: the accuracy of the model in replicating the characteristics of the original data; the presence of correlations within the generated data and whether they align with the original data; and the proportion of non-conforming data points in comparison to the actual data. The results reveal a strong consistency between the theoretical and empirical models in terms of these characteristics, which is confirmed through thorough statistical analysis. The analysis shows that the models exhibit high levels of correspondence for: the general distribution of values; the pattern of relationships between adjacent values; and the proportion of data points exceeding the lower bound. The findings provide significant real-world implications, especially in terms of the efficient removal of data points exceeding the lower bound. It is observed that the original copper price series contains 0.63% data points exceeding the lower bound, whereas the generated series accurately replicate this value with a high degree of precision, indicating that the theoretical model is highly effective in replicating the characteristics of the original series. The successful application of the approach in this study opens up the possibility of similar developments for other financial time series with extreme values. Furthermore, the analysis highlights several unaddressed research questions that are related to this study that are included in the concluding chapter. The original data used in this research was obtained from the Australian Securities Exchange website, specifically for copper (XCBA) over the period from 2015 to 2019. rendering them ineffective against synthetic attacks in adversarial studies 
and real-world applications or unable to maintain consistency across multiple 
datasets while promoting diversity. In contrast, our proposed method, 
SibylNet, offers a breakthrough with robust and diverse text transformations. 
Initially, SibylNet was trained on multiple datasets to create several 
interpretations of the same text, thereby enhancing its capabilities and 
opportunities for use in numerous tasks. In a second stage, SibylNet is modified 
to produce a range of text representations for a given input, allowing it to 
be applied in tasks such as adversarial attacks and semantic manipulation. 
Through our experiments, SibylNet has demonstrated superior performance in these 
tasks, while also exhibiting a significant degree of diversity in its 
transformations across multiple datasets in English and Arabic languages. 
Furthermore, the code and models for our research will be made publicly 
available to facilitate future advancements in text representation and 
classification. Through our approach, we address the underlying assumption of 
unambiguous word meanings in natural language and develop a novel 
interpretative method that utilizes multiple diverse meanings of words, 
enabling the development of robust models, cross-lingual and cross-domain 
applications, and enhanced generalizability. We also highlight various 
engineering challenges associated with large-scale word sense disambigation,

sense-specific properties into language processing models, which is 
particularly essential for cross-lingual and cross-domain language processing 
tasks. We also identify several promising research avenues for modeling 
sense-specific properties that enhance model performance and lead to more 
effective generalization. Ultimately, we aim to popularize the 
LSaAME paradigm through our research, connecting it to existing concepts and 
models that can benefit from its integration. We have developed a training guide 
for future researchers, incorporating LSaAME into their models, which we

Researchers aim to create meta-learning algorithms that capitalize on previous experience to rapidly acquire new skills or adapt to new environments by utilizing representation learning techniques, which enable the transfer of knowledge across various tasks. As the interest in meta-learning grows, there is a pressing need to establish its theoretical foundations, especially in terms of learning adaptable representations. In this research, we tackle the problem of multi-task linear regression where multiple related tasks share a common, low-dimensional linear representation. Our study provides effective, sample-efficient methods to address the dual challenges of learning a shared feature set from related tasks and transferring this knowledge to unseen tasks. This work sheds light on the central issue of meta-learning. Furthermore, we present theoretical limits on the minimum sample size required to learn these linear features. Building on these findings, we propose a representative dataset benchmark to assess the performance of meta-learning algorithms. We validate the efficacy of our methods by conducting comprehensive numerical experiments. Moreover, we provide implementation details of our algorithms, along with selected experimental results, which are available at https://motliu.github.io/ProvableMetaLearning. Lastly, the empirical analysis indicates that our methods depend heavily on the choice of hyperparameters, underscoring the significance of further theoretical advancements in the field of meta-learning. Utilizing multilingual learning in state-of-the-art machine translation models can aid in adapting to low-resource languages despite limited data. Post-hoc techniques such as quantization and distillation have shown promise in producing lightweight models for zero-shot language pairs, despite their varying applicability across different language combinations. Before leveraging these methods, assessing their effectiveness and stability towards reducing model size is crucial, particularly for low-resource languages. This study compares several approaches towards decreasing model size for English to Persian, a challenging language due to its left-to-right script and distinct morphology, and highlights the benefits and drawbacks of both quantization and distillation in this context, including implications for training data and model performance. Ultimately, distillation is found to be a more reliable method under limited data conditions. Notably, achieving comparable results through quantization required fine-tuning a pre-trained model, whereas distillation produced equivalent translations in a single step, indicating its overall superior performance and efficiency. While data augmentation is beneficial for both approaches, the relatively stable performance of distillation is found to stem from its mitigation of overfitting, particularly in its capacity to gradually reduce the knowledge diffusion rate as training progresses. Additionally, the effects of prior learning on pre-training text on distillation are investigated, and results show a notable increase in knowledge obtained during the initial stages of training, and further analysis reveals that both knowledge graph augmentation and multi-task training contribute to distillation's relatively stable performance, and ultimately, English to Persian distillation models with less than 10% of their original size were found to be locatable and reproducible through the release of their respective training objectives and hyper-parameter settings. Interestingly, these models' localized structures and training objectives were found to be distinct from those produced by other researchers, and further analysis reveals that they tend to prioritize more accurate translations over higher fluency, and ultimately, this study's findings highlight the need for a more precise definition of low-resource languages in machine translation, and further research aimed at distinguishing between these languages and those with limited data may lead to the discovery of additional languages eligible for post-hoc size reduction. We incorporate a flexible prompt learning system that enables the model to absorb data from multiple domains, ensuring uniform performance across these domains. Additionally, we optimize the prompts using dynamic vectors within a word embedding space, reducing the reliance on manual tuning and significantly enhancing the model's capabilities. We confidently believe that our work on prompt learning will serve as a foundational stone for future image captioning research. In the field of legged locomotion, spring-in-series actuators can provide compact and powerful motion systems, but their unique properties make heavy use of feedback control necessary. We suggest learning the behavior patterns of the spring actuators through an agent-based approach, allowing the central nervous system to figure out how to manage the additional degrees of freedom without needing intricate models. We take advantage of the fact that spring-in-series actuators can be interpreted as regular motors attached to light loads, which moves according to the actuator's configuration. This light load's dynamics can be learned by expert policies, which are then utilized to develop efficient and versatile movement strategies. We implement this concept on a one-legged robot and demonstrate our results in both simulation and real-world experiments, revealing that our method leads to the development of multiple stepping patterns and more general control abilities, which in turn reduces feedback control dependencies during regular locomotion. While this method still relies on optimization, it makes a step towards simplifying the complex relationship between actuator effort and leg movement. We propose a new variational quantum algorithm, the Variational Separability Verifier (VSV), to identify the closest separable state of an arbitrary quantum state with minimal deviation in Hilbert-Schmidt distance. Our algorithm's performance is initially tested with GHZ states composed of up to seven qubits via simulations that utilize state vectors and random measurements. We also utilize numerical methods to approximate the closest separable states for these reduced GHZ states and demonstrate that the VSV's performance surpasses that of a classical mixed-entropy approach. An experimental implementation of the VSV is then successfully demonstrated using two qubits from a NISQ device (IBMQ Madrid). Our experiments reveal the VSV's ability to accurately detect quantum entanglement in practice while dealing with the complexity of larger quantum states. Given its resilience against noise, the VSV presents a promising quantum algorithm, especially one that can be executed and monitored via the IBMQ quantum experience platform. Our work further showcases the advantages of using the variational quantum algorithm approach for efficiently tackling specific quantum information problems. Our VSV algorithm's performance can be extended to classify any quantum state as either entangled or separable by incorporating posterior truncation, which involves reducing the dimension of a density matrix. This method's other notable application is in determining quantum of order $k$, where it successfully identifies states of reduced $k$-linear complexity. Our experiments indicate that the VSV's performance improves as the number of variational parameters increases. By testing various structural assumptions in our studies, we found that structural assumptions based on Riemannian manifolds outperform other approaches such as those based on Pauli constraints, even in cases where the constraints closely approximate the space. Our work ultimately reveals that the structural assumption of normalizing unitary constraints results in the most superior performance among the tested variants. Our results indicate that the most accurate separability verdicts are obtained using very few Pauli matrices, which suggests the existence of distinct patterns and structures within quantum states that can be identified and exploited.
